-1 17 Mar 2026, 18:45:09 GMT+05:30 Here is the complete C program to implement the Circular Queue using an array $A[0..n-1]$. To ensure the queue can hold exactly $n$ elements (instead of the standard $n-1$) while strictly using only head and tail variables, I used a common logic trick: initializing head = -1 to represent an empty state. All operations run in strict $O(1)$ time. I have included Hinglish comments throughout the code to explain the logic clearly. Complete C Program for Circular Queue #include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

// Queue ka structure jisme head, tail, array aur size store hoga
struct Queue {
    int head;
    int tail;
    int* A;   // Array pointer
    int n;    // Maximum capacity
};

// QueueFull(Q): Check karta hai ki queue full hai ya nahi
int QueueFull(struct Queue* Q) {
    // Agar head -1 nahi hai aur head aur tail same jagah point kar rahe hain,
    // iska matlab array ghoom kar wapas aa gaya hai aur full ho chuka hai.
    return (Q->head != -1 && Q->head == Q->tail);
}

// QueueEmpty(Q): Check karta hai ki queue khali hai ya nahi
int QueueEmpty(struct Queue* Q) {
    // Agar head -1 hai, toh queue completely khali hai
    return (Q->head == -1);
}

// Enqueue(Q, k): Naye element ko tail par insert karta hai
void Enqueue(struct Queue* Q, int k) {
    if (QueueFull(Q)) {
        printf("-1\n"); // Full hone par -1 print karo
        return;
    }
    
    if (QueueEmpty(Q)) {
        Q->head = Q->tail; // Agar pehla element aa raha hai, toh head ko tail par set karo
    }
    
    Q->A[Q->tail] = k; // Element insert kiya
    Q->tail = (Q->tail + 1) % Q->n; // Tail ko aage badhaya (circular increment)
}

// Dequeue(Q): Head se element delete karta hai aur print karta hai
void Dequeue(struct Queue* Q) {
    if (QueueEmpty(Q)) {
        printf("-1\n"); // Khali hone par -1 print karo
        return;
    }
    
    int val = Q->A[Q->head]; // Delete hone wala element save kiya
    Q->head = (Q->head + 1) % Q->n; // Head ko aage badhaya
    
    // Agar delete karne ke baad head aur tail barabar ho gaye, 
    // matlab queue ab khali ho chuki hai. Isko wapas empty state mein daal do.
    if (Q->head == Q->tail) {
        Q->head = -1; 
    }
    
    printf("%d\n", val); // Deleted value print kiya
}

int main() {
    int n;
    // Phele line se capacity 'n' read karo
    if (scanf("%d", &n) != 1) return 0;

    struct Queue Q;
    Q.head = -1; // Shuru mein queue khali hai isliye -1
    Q.tail = 0;  // Tail 0 index se start hoga
    Q.n = n;
    Q.A = (int*)malloc(n * sizeof(int)); // Array ke liye memory allocate ki

    char op;
    int k;

    // Infinite loop, 't' aane par break hoga
    while (1) {
        if (scanf(" %c", &op) != 1) break;

        if (op == 't') {
            break; // Program terminate
        } 
        else if (op == 'i') {
            scanf("%d", &k);
            Enqueue(&Q, k);
        } 
        else if (op == 'd') {
            Dequeue(&Q);
        } 
        else if (op == 'f') {
            if (QueueFull(&Q)) {
                printf("-1\n"); // Full hai toh -1
            } else {
                printf("1\n");  // Not full hai toh 1
            }
        } 
        else if (op == 'e') {
            if (QueueEmpty(&Q)) {
                printf("-1\n"); // Empty hai toh -1
            } else {
                printf("1\n");  // Not empty hai toh 1
            }
        }
    }

    free(Q.A); // Memory leak bachane ke liye array free karo
    return 0;
} Key Logic Summary Empty State: We initialize Q.head = -1 . This is the absolute indicator that the queue has nothing in it. Full State: Because Q.tail always points to the next available slot , if the queue is full, the tail wraps around exactly to where the head is. Thus, the condition Q.head == Q.tail (while head != -1 ) proves it is full. Array Wraparound: Both the head and tail use the modulo operator % Q.n to seamlessly loop back to index 0 when they hit the end of the array. No worries at all—this is a classic data structures problem. Managing pointers in a Circular Linked List can definitely get tricky, especially when handling edge cases like deleting the head or inserting into an empty list. I have written the complete C program for you from scratch, strictly following your problem statement's function prototypes and constraints. I've also added the Hinglish comments you requested so you can easily understand the logic behind each step. Complete C Program for Circular Linked List #include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

// Node ka structure define kar rahe hain
struct Node {
    int key;
    struct Node* next;
};

// Circular Linked List ka main structure
struct List {
    struct Node* head;
};

// CREATE-NODE(k): Naya node banata hai memory allocate karke
struct Node* CREATE_NODE(int k) {
    struct Node* newNode = (struct Node*)malloc(sizeof(struct Node));
    newNode->key = k;
    newNode->next = NULL; // Shuru mein next pointer NULL rakhenge
    return newNode;
}

// LIST-SEARCH(L, k): List mein 'k' key wala node dhoondhta hai
struct Node* LIST_SEARCH(struct List* L, int k) {
    if (L->head == NULL) return NULL; // Agar list khali hai toh sidha NULL

    struct Node* curr = L->head;
    do {
        if (curr->key == k) return curr; // Node mil gaya!
        curr = curr->next;
    } while (curr != L->head); // Jab tak ghoom kar wapas head par na aa jayein

    return NULL; // Pura ghoom liya par nahi mila
}

// LIST-INSERT-FRONT(L, x): Naye node ko list ke start mein lagata hai
void LIST_INSERT_FRONT(struct List* L, struct Node* x) {
    if (L->head == NULL) {
        // Agar list bilkul khali hai
        L->head = x;
        x->next = x; // Circular list hai, toh khud ko hi point karega
    } else {
        struct Node* last = L->head;
        // Aakhri node dhoondhne ka loop
        while (last->next != L->head) {
            last = last->next;
        }
        x->next = L->head; // Naye node ko purane head se jodo
        L->head = x;       // Naye node ko naya head bana do
        last->next = x;    // Aakhri node ab naye head ko point karega
    }
}

// LIST-INSERT-TAIL(L, x): Naye node ko list ke end mein lagata hai
void LIST_INSERT_TAIL(struct List* L, struct Node* x) {
    if (L->head == NULL) {
        LIST_INSERT_FRONT(L, x); // Khali list ke liye logic same hi hoga
    } else {
        struct Node* last = L->head;
        while (last->next != L->head) {
            last = last->next;
        }
        last->next = x;    // Purane aakhri node ko naye se jodo
        x->next = L->head; // Naya node ab aakhri hai, toh head ko point karega
    }
}

// LIST-INSERT-AFTER(L, x, y): Node y ke theek baad node x insert karna
void LIST_INSERT_AFTER(struct List* L, struct Node* x, struct Node* y) {
    if (y == NULL) return; // Agar 'y' exist hi nahi karta
    x->next = y->next;
    y->next = x;
}

// LIST-INSERT-BEFORE(L, x, y): Node y ke theek pehle node x insert karna
void LIST_INSERT_BEFORE(struct List* L, struct Node* x, struct Node* y) {
    if (L->head == NULL || y == NULL) return;

    if (L->head == y) {
        LIST_INSERT_FRONT(L, x); // Agar y head hai, toh simple insert front
        return;
    }

    struct Node* curr = L->head;
    // Wo node dhoondho jo y se pehle aata hai
    while (curr->next != y && curr->next != L->head) {
        curr = curr->next;
    }

    if (curr->next == y) {
        curr->next = x;
        x->next = y;
    }
}

// LIST-DELETE(L, x): Node x ko list se hatana aur memory free karna
void LIST_DELETE(struct List* L, struct Node* x) {
    if (L->head == NULL || x == NULL) return;

    // Case 1: Agar list mein sirf ek hi node hai
    if (L->head == x && L->head->next == L->head) {
        free(x);
        L->head = NULL;
        return;
    }

    // Case 2: Agar head node hi delete karna hai
    if (L->head == x) {
        struct Node* last = L->head;
        while (last->next != L->head) {
            last = last->next;
        }
        L->head = x->next; // Naya head set karo
        last->next = L->head; // Aakhri node ko naye head se jodo
        free(x);
        return;
    }

    // Case 3: Beech ka ya end ka koi node delete karna hai
    struct Node* curr = L->head;
    while (curr->next != x && curr->next != L->head) {
        curr = curr->next;
    }

    if (curr->next == x) {
        curr->next = x->next; // Pointers skip karwa diye
        free(x); // Ab memory free kar do
    }
}

// Helper functions for Main() logic to print properly
void handleDelete(struct List* L, int k) {
    struct Node* x = LIST_SEARCH(L, k);
    if (x != NULL) {
        LIST_DELETE(L, x);
        printf("%d\n", k); // Delete hone par key print karo
    } else {
        printf("-1\n"); // Nahi mila toh -1
    }
}

void handleDeleteFirst(struct List* L) {
    if (L->head == NULL) {
        printf("-1\n");
    } else {
        int k = L->head->key;
        LIST_DELETE(L, L->head);
        printf("%d\n", k);
    }
}

void handleDeleteLast(struct List* L) {
    if (L->head == NULL) {
        printf("-1\n");
    } else {
        struct Node* last = L->head;
        while (last->next != L->head) {
            last = last->next;
        }
        int k = last->key;
        LIST_DELETE(L, last);
        printf("%d\n", k);
    }
}

int main() {
    struct List L = {NULL}; // Shuru mein list khali rakhi hai
    char op;
    int k1, k2;

    // Infinite loop jo 'e' aane par break hoga
    while (1) {
        if (scanf(" %c", &op) != 1) break; 

        if (op == 'e') {
            break; // Loop tod do aur program exit karo
        } 
        else if (op == 'f') {
            scanf("%d", &k1);
            LIST_INSERT_FRONT(&L, CREATE_NODE(k1));
        } 
        else if (op == 't') {
            scanf("%d", &k1);
            LIST_INSERT_TAIL(&L, CREATE_NODE(k1));
        } 
        else if (op == 'a') {
            scanf("%d %d", &k1, &k2);
            struct Node* y = LIST_SEARCH(&L, k2);
            if (y != NULL) {
                LIST_INSERT_AFTER(&L, CREATE_NODE(k1), y);
            }
        } 
        else if (op == 'b') {
            scanf("%d %d", &k1, &k2);
            struct Node* y = LIST_SEARCH(&L, k2);
            if (y != NULL) {
                LIST_INSERT_BEFORE(&L, CREATE_NODE(k1), y);
            }
        } 
        else if (op == 'd') {
            scanf("%d", &k1);
            handleDelete(&L, k1);
        } 
        else if (op == 'i') {
            handleDeleteFirst(&L);
        } 
        else if (op == 'l') {
            handleDeleteLast(&L);
        } 
        else if (op == 's') {
            scanf("%d", &k1);
            struct Node* res = LIST_SEARCH(&L, k1);
            if (res != NULL) {
                printf("1\n"); // Mil gaya toh 1
            } else {
                printf("-1\n"); // Nahi mila toh -1
            }
        }
    }
    return 0;
} Quick Test If you run this program and paste your Sample Input , it will exactly match your Sample Output . This plan is structured to serve as the blueprint for an ACL, EMNLP, or ICLR submission, outlining the theoretical foundation, mathematical formulation, and empirical execution. Research Design: Semantic Information Bottleneck for Multi-Agent Communication Governance 1. Abstract & Core Objective Current multi-agent Large Language Model (LLM) systems suffer from communication explosion and error cascades, where verbose or hallucinated reasoning propagates across the agent network. Instead of relying on static consensus rules or binary routing, this research introduces a Semantic Information Bottleneck governed by Reinforcement Learning (Proximal Policy Optimization). The controller learns to dynamically allocate semantic bandwidth—ranging from full transmission to logic filtering to complete blockades—maximizing collective task accuracy while mathematically penalizing excessive mutual information between agents. 2. Problem Statement Multi-agent systems (debate, collaborative reasoning) face two distinct failure modes: Communication Explosion: Unregulated $N \times N$ broadcasting leads to infinite reasoning loops and unsustainable inference costs. Semantic Error Cascades: A highly confident but factually incorrect agent can persuade others, overriding correct minority solutions ("charisma bias"). 3. The Paradigm Shift: From Binary Routing to Semantic Bandwidth Previous works (e.g., Multi-Agent Debate , ChatEval ) treat agent communication as an unalterable text stream. This framework shifts the perspective: communication is a continuous graph where edges represent semantic bandwidth . Instead of deciding if Agent A talks to Agent B, the RL controller learns what specific information Agent A is allowed to transmit. 4. Mathematical & System Architecture The environment is modeled as a dynamic influence graph $G = (V,E)$, where $V$ represents the LLM agents and $E$ represents the directed communication channels governed by the RL controller. A. State Representation ($S_t$) At each communication turn $t$, the controller observes the system state, encoded into a dense continuous vector:
$$S_t = [ H_t \parallel C_t \parallel G_t ]$$ $H_t$ (History): Lightweight embedding (e.g., RoBERTa) of the current prompt and recent message outputs. $C_t$ (Confidence): Vector of the average log-probabilities of the generating agents. $G_t$ (Topology): The current adjacency matrix of the agent network. B. Continuous Action Space ($A_t$) The Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) Actor network outputs a continuous weight matrix $W_t$, where each $w_{ij} \in [0,1]$ dictates the intervention applied to the message from agent $i$ to agent $j$. Action Weight ($w_{ij}$) Semantic Intervention Bandwidth $0.00 \leq w < 0.25$ Sever Edge: Block message entirely. Zero $0.25 \leq w < 0.50$ Summarize: Compress to core claim via a lightweight LLM. Low $0.50 \leq w < 0.75$ Filter Logic: Strip persuasive language; pass only formulas/code. Medium $0.75 \leq w \leq 1.00$ Full Transmit: Pass raw, unaltered text. High C. Information Bottleneck Reward Formulation ($R_t$) The reward function mathematically enforces the bottleneck, forcing the system to find the minimal necessary communication graph.
$$R_{total} = R_{task} - \lambda \sum_{t=1}^{T} ||W_t|| 1 - \gamma \cdot \text{Penalty} {loop}$$ $R_{task}$: $+10$ for the correct final answer, $-10$ for an incorrect answer. $||W_t||_1$: The L1 norm of the action weights. Minimizing this term forces the network to cut edges and compress information. $\lambda$: Hyperparameter controlling the strictness of the bottleneck. D. Policy Optimization The controller is updated using the PPO clipped surrogate objective to ensure stable learning in complex language environments:
$$L^{CLIP}(\theta) = \hat{\mathbb{E}}_t \left[ \min(r_t(\theta) \hat{A}_t, \text{clip}(r_t(\theta), 1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon)\hat{A}_t) \right]$$ 5. Experimental Design & Benchmarks To prove the efficacy of this framework, the evaluation must target environments where collaboration is necessary, but the risk of hallucination is high. A. Datasets Mathematical Reasoning: GSM8K, MATH (requires strict logic filtering). Multi-Hop QA: HotpotQA (requires passing summarized context). Strategic Planning: StrategyQA or ALFWorld (requires diverse agent roles). B. Baseline Comparisons Baseline Description Limitation Addressed Majority Voting (Self-Consistency) Independent sampling, most frequent answer wins. No cross-agent correction. Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) Agents critique each other sequentially. High token cost, prone to error cascades. ChatEval / AutoGen Role-playing agents with static manager rules. Rigid routing; lacks dynamic semantic filtering. C. Evaluation Metrics Task Accuracy: % of correct final answers. Error Propagation Rate: The frequency with which an initially correct agent changes its answer to an incorrect one due to peer influence. Communication Density ($||W||$): Average semantic bandwidth used per task. Token Cost Efficiency: Total inference tokens consumed per task. 6. Phased Implementation Plan Training RL over LLM outputs is computationally intensive. The following execution strategy mitigates API costs and unstable training loops: Phase 1: Static Dataset Generation & Pre-training. * Run standard Multi-Agent Debate on a subset of GSM8K using an open-weights model (e.g., Llama-3). Identify trajectories where an error cascade occurred. Train the PPO controller offline via Supervised/Imitation Learning to predict which edges should have been cut or filtered to prevent the failure. Phase 2: Proxy Environment RL Fine-Tuning. Use highly quantized, fast proxy models (e.g., 8B parameter models) as the conversational agents. Unfreeze the PPO controller and train it actively in this low-cost environment using the Information Bottleneck reward. Phase 3: Zero-Shot Transfer & Final Evaluation. Freeze the PPO controller. Deploy the frozen controller to govern a network of state-of-the-art models (e.g., GPT-4 or Claude 3.5) on the hidden test sets. This proves the controller learns generalized semantic governance, not just model-specific quirks. 7. Expected Scientific Contributions A novel formalization of multi-agent LLM communication as a dynamic, continuous influence graph. The introduction of the Semantic Information Bottleneck, shifting MARL from binary action spaces to semantic interventions. Empirical evidence demonstrating that managed semantic bandwidth simultaneously reduces token cost and prevents error cascades in collaborative reasoning. Summary of the Design To implement this, we must map the messy, high-dimensional text outputs of LLM agents into a continuous mathematical space that an RL algorithm (PPO) can process. We will define the State ($S_t$) as a compressed tensor of the conversation, the Action ($A_t$) as a matrix of semantic routing weights, and the Reward ($R_t$) as a balance between task accuracy and a mathematical penalty for over-communication. Step 1: State Representation ($S_t$) The controller needs a numeric snapshot of the multi-agent system at time step $t$. Since LLMs output text, we must encode this into a dense vector space. The state $S_t$ is a concatenation of three distinct matrices: Task & History Encoding ($H_t$): Pass the initial prompt and the most recent agent messages through a lightweight embedding model (e.g., MiniLM or RoBERTa). Uncertainty/Confidence Vector ($C_t$): Extract the self-evaluated confidence of each agent. If using an open-source model, extract the average log-probabilities of the generated reasoning tokens. Graph Topology ($G_t$): The current adjacency matrix showing which agents are currently connected. The final state vector fed into the PPO policy network is:

For every pair of agents $(i, j)$, the network outputs a weight $w_{ij}^{(t)} \in [0, 1]$. We map these continuous weights to discrete semantic interventions using thresholds: Weight $w_{ij}$ Semantic Action Information Bandwidth $0.00 \leq w < 0.25$ Block: Edge is severed. Agent $j$ does not see Agent $i$'s output. Zero $0.25 \leq w < 0.50$ Summarize: A lightweight LLM compresses Agent $i$'s text into a 1-sentence summary before passing to $j$. Low $0.50 \leq w < 0.75$ Filter Logic: Strip persuasive language. Pass only equations/code/raw facts to prevent "charisma bias". Medium $0.75 \leq w \leq 1.00$ Full Transmit: Agent $i$'s raw text is passed to Agent $j$. High Step 3: The Information Bottleneck Reward Function ($R_t$) This is where the paradigm shift occurs. The reward function must explicitly penalize the system for passing too much information, forcing the PPO agent to find the minimal necessary communication to solve the task. The total reward at the end of an episode (when a final answer is submitted) is calculated as: $$R_{total} = R_{task} - \lambda \sum_{t=1}^{T} ||W_t|| 1 - \gamma \cdot \text{Penalty} {loop}$$ Where: $R_{task}$: The environment reward (+10 for correct, -10 for incorrect). $||W_t||_1$: The $L_1$ norm of the action weight matrix at step $t$. This acts as our Information Bottleneck. By penalizing the sum of the weights, PPO is forced to push as many edges to $0$ (Block) or low values (Summarize) as possible without failing the task. $\lambda$: A tuning parameter controlling the strictness of the bottleneck. $\text{Penalty}_{loop}$: A negative reward if the system exceeds a maximum number of dialogue turns (e.g., -1 per extra step). Step 4: The PPO Objective Formulation To train this controller, you will use the standard PPO clipped surrogate objective. This ensures the policy network does not make drastically destabilizing updates during training. Let $r_t(\theta)$ be the probability ratio of the new policy over the old policy. The objective function you will maximize is: $$L^{CLIP}(\theta) = \hat{\mathbb{E}}_t \left[ \min(r_t(\theta) \hat{A}_t, \text{clip}(r_t(\theta), 1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon)\hat{A}_t) \right]$$ $\hat{A}_t$ is the advantage estimator (how much better a specific semantic routing action was compared to the average expected reward). $\epsilon$ is the clipping hyperparameter (usually set to 0.2). Reinforcement-Learned Communication Governance in Multi-Agent Systems.

The explanation is written like a research design document, which is the way strong papers are planned.
The goal is to move from:

“agents talk too much and propagate errors”
to a general scientific framework for regulating information flow in intelligent agent societies.
1. Problem Statement
Multi-agent AI systems such as debate systems or cooperative reasoning agents suffer from two major problems:

Problem 1 — Communication Explosion
Agents exchange excessive messages.
Example

Agent1 → Agent2 → Agent3 → Agent1 → Agent2 → ...

This causes

inefficiency
long reasoning loops
increased computational cost.
Problem 2 — Error Cascades
If one agent produces an incorrect response, other agents may adopt it.
Example

Agent1 wrong
Agent2 trusts Agent1
Agent3 trusts Agent2
→ system converges to incorrect answer

This phenomenon appears in

AI agents
human collaboration
social networks.
2. Research Goal
Design a learning mechanism that governs communication between agents to:

minimize unnecessary communication
prevent propagation of incorrect information
maintain high collective accuracy.
3. Key Idea
Introduce a communication governance layer.
Instead of agents freely communicating, a controller learns when and how communication should occur.
The controller uses reinforcement learning.
Agents are represented as nodes in a dynamic influence graph.
4. System Architecture
The system contains four components.

1. Task Environment
The environment provides tasks such as reasoning problems.
Examples

math reasoning
multi-hop question answering
planning tasks.
2. Agent Layer
Multiple agents generate candidate solutions.
Example roles

Planner
Solver
Critic
Verifier

Each agent produces reasoning outputs.
3. Influence Graph
Agents form a directed graph.
Nodes represent agents.
Edges represent influence.
Example

Agent1 → Agent2 (influence 0.7)
Agent2 → Agent3 (influence 0.5)
Agent3 → Agent1 (influence 0.3)

This graph models how information spreads.
4. Communication Governance Controller
A reinforcement learning agent decides

which agent can speak
which messages should propagate
when discussion should terminate.
5. Mathematical Model
Define a graph

G = (V,E)

Where

V = agents
E = communication influence edges

Each edge has weight

w_ij

representing how much agent i influences agent j.
Agent belief update can be modeled as

x_j(t+1) = Σ_i w_ij * m_i(t)

where

m_i(t)

is the message from agent i.
This captures information flow in the network.
6. Reinforcement Learning Formulation
The controller learns how to regulate communication.
State
The state describes the current system situation.
Example state components

task_embedding
agent_outputs
communication_history
influence_graph
verification_signals

Verification signals include

missing steps
reasoning inconsistency
confidence estimates.
Actions
The controller chooses a communication decision.
Possible actions

allow(agent_i)
block(agent_i)
request_revision(agent_i)
query_agent_j
terminate_discussion

prevents an unreliable agent from influencing others.
Reward
The reward balances accuracy and efficiency.

reward =

−8 incorrect answer
−1 communication step
−2 revision request

The objective is

maximize reliability
minimize communication cost

7. Learning Algorithm
Start with a simple RL method.

Q-Learning
Update rule

Q(s,a) ← Q(s,a) +
α [ r + γ max_a' Q(s',a') − Q(s,a) ]

Where

α learning rate
γ discount factor

Later, extend to Deep Q Networks if the state becomes high-dimensional.
8. System Workflow
The full pipeline proceeds as follows.
Step 1 — Task Input
A task is given to the system.
Example

Solve a reasoning problem.

Step 2 — Agent Responses
Multiple agents produce candidate reasoning outputs.
Example

Agent1: solution A
Agent2: solution B
Agent3: solution C

Step 3 — Verification
A compliance verifier analyzes outputs.
It extracts signals such as

missing steps
confidence scores
agreement between agents

Step 4 — Influence Graph Update
The system updates the influence graph based on recent behavior.
Example

Agent1 frequently correct → influence increases
Agent3 incorrect → influence decreases

The controller observes the system state and selects an action.
Example

allow(agent1)
block(agent3)

Step 6 — Communication
Allowed agents exchange information.
Blocked agents are excluded.

The system selects a final answer.
Reward is computed.

The RL policy is updated using the reward.

GSM8K

StrategyQA.

3–5 LLM agents with different prompts.

task accuracy
communication cost
prompt adherence
error propagation rate.

Compare against standard methods.
Examples

majority voting
self-consistency
debate frameworks
random communication.
Your system should demonstrate

fewer messages
fewer error cascades
improved reliability.
12. Expected Scientific Contributions
The paper could claim

a framework for communication governance in multi-agent AI systems
a reinforcement learning method that regulates information flow
improved reliability in collaborative reasoning systems.
13. Potential Failure Modes
Understanding failure is important.
Failure 1 — Over-restricting communication
If communication is blocked too aggressively, the system loses diversity of reasoning.
Failure 2 — Incorrect influence estimation
Early mistakes may mislabel good agents as unreliable.
Failure 3 — Collusion
Two agents may consistently agree on incorrect answers.
Agreement does not always mean correctness.
Failure 4 — RL training cost
Training requires many interactions, which may be expensive with LLM inference.

Examples
Learning Communication Governance in Multi-Agent Artificial Intelligence
or
Reinforcement Learning for Regulating Information Flow in Agent Societies
15. Research Impact
If validated, the framework could apply to

LLM agent systems
distributed robotics
human-AI collaboration.
It studies how intelligent agents should communicate efficiently and reliably.

-1 10 Mar 2026, 22:40:21 GMT+05:30 Logic Summary (Step-by-Step) Is program mein hum ek Doubly Linked List (DLL) bana rahe hain. DLL ek aisi list hoti hai jismein har node ke paas do pointers hote hain: ek aage wale node ke liye ( next ), aur ek peeche wale node ke liye ( prev ). Node Structure: Har node mein 3 cheezein hongi: key (data), next pointer, aur prev pointer. Ek head pointer list ki shuruaat ko track karega. CREATE-NODE: Naya node memory mein banata hai aur uske pointers ko NULL set karta hai. Insertions: Front ( f ): Naye node ko sabse aage (head ki jagah) jodta hai. Tail ( t ): List ke aakhir tak jaakar naye node ko sabse last mein jodta hai. After ( a ): Pehle y node ko dhundhta hai, aur uske theek baad x ko insert karta hai. Before ( b ): Pehle y node ko dhundhta hai, aur uske theek pehle x ko insert karta hai. Deletions & Search: Delete ( d , i , l ): Pointers ( prev aur next ) ko adjust karke node ko list se alag karte hain aur uski memory free ( free() ) karte hain. Jo node delete hota hai, uski key print hoti hai. Agar list khali hai ya node nahi mila, toh -1 print hota hai. Search ( s ): Head se lekar aakhir tak linear search karta hai. Mil gaya toh 1 print karta hai, nahi toh -1 . C Program with Hinglish Comments #include <stdio.h>    // Input aur output functions (printf, scanf) ke liye
#include <stdlib.h>   // Memory allocation functions (malloc, free) ke liye

// --- Doubly Linked List ka Node Structure ---
struct Node {         // Node ko define kar rahe hain
    int key;          // Node ka data (integer value)
    struct Node* next; // Agle node ka pointer
    struct Node* prev; // Pichle node ka pointer
};

// List structure jo sirf head pointer rakhega
struct List {         
    struct Node* head; // List ka pehla node
};

// --- Naya Node Banane ka Function ---
struct Node* CREATE_NODE(int k) {
    struct Node* newNode = (struct Node*)malloc(sizeof(struct Node)); // Naye node ke liye memory allocate karna
    newNode->key = k;      // Naye node mein data (key) daalna
    newNode->next = NULL;  // Shuru mein agla pointer khali (NULL) rakhna
    newNode->prev = NULL;  // Shuru mein pichla pointer bhi khali rakhna
    return newNode;        // Naya bana hua node return karna
}

// --- List mein Search karne ka Function ---
struct Node* LIST_SEARCH(struct List* L, int k) {
    struct Node* curr = L->head; // Head se dhoondhna shuru karna
    while (curr != NULL) {       // Jab tak list khatam nahi hoti
        if (curr->key == k) {    // Agar node ki key match ho gayi
            return curr;         // Toh us node ko return kar do
        }
        curr = curr->next;       // Nahi toh agle node par badh jao
    }
    return NULL;                 // Agar poori list mein nahi mila toh NULL return karo
}

// --- List ke Shuru (Front) mein Insert karna ---
void LIST_INSERT_FRONT(struct List* L, struct Node* x) {
    x->next = L->head;           // Naye node ka 'next', current head ko point karega
    if (L->head != NULL) {       // Agar list khali nahi hai
        L->head->prev = x;       // Toh purane head ka 'prev', naye node ko point karega
    }
    L->head = x;                 // Naye node ko naya head bana do
}

// --- List ke Aakhir (Tail) mein Insert karna ---
void LIST_INSERT_TAIL(struct List* L, struct Node* x) {
    if (L->head == NULL) {       // Agar list bilkul khali hai
        L->head = x;             // Toh naya node hi head ban jayega
        return;
    }
    struct Node* curr = L->head; // Aakhiri node dhoondhne ke liye head se shuru karo
    while (curr->next != NULL) { // Jab tak aakhiri node nahi milta
        curr = curr->next;       // Agle node par chalte raho
    }
    curr->next = x;              // Aakhiri node ke 'next' mein naya node jod do
    x->prev = curr;              // Naye node ke 'prev' mein aakhiri node ka pata daal do
}

// --- Kisi Node 'y' ke Baad (After) Insert karna ---
void LIST_INSERT_AFTER(struct List* L, struct Node* x, struct Node* y) {
    if (y == NULL) return;       // Agar node 'y' exist nahi karta, toh kuch mat karo
    x->next = y->next;           // Naye node 'x' ka 'next', 'y' ke agle node ko point karega
    x->prev = y;                 // Naye node 'x' ka 'prev', 'y' ko point karega
    if (y->next != NULL) {       // Agar 'y' aakhiri node nahi tha
        y->next->prev = x;       // Toh 'y' ke agle node ka 'prev', ab 'x' ko point karega
    }
    y->next = x;                 // 'y' ka 'next' ab naye node 'x' ko point karega
}

// --- Kisi Node 'y' se Pehle (Before) Insert karna ---
void LIST_INSERT_BEFORE(struct List* L, struct Node* x, struct Node* y) {
    if (y == NULL) return;       // Agar node 'y' nahi hai, toh return karo
    if (y->prev == NULL) {       // Agar 'y' hi list ka pehla (head) node hai
        LIST_INSERT_FRONT(L, x); // Toh naye node ko Front mein insert kar do
    } else {
        x->next = y;             // Naye node 'x' ka 'next', 'y' ko point karega
        x->prev = y->prev;       // 'x' ka 'prev', 'y' ke pichle node ko point karega
        y->prev->next = x;       // 'y' ke pichle node ka 'next', ab 'x' ko point karega
        y->prev = x;             // 'y' ka 'prev' ab 'x' ho jayega
    }
}

// --- Koi specific Node delete karna ---
void LIST_DELETE(struct List* L, struct Node* x) {
    if (x == NULL) return;       // Agar delete karne wala node NULL hai, toh wapas jao
    if (x->prev != NULL) {       // Agar node list ka pehla node nahi hai
        x->prev->next = x->next; // Uske pichle node ko agle node se jod do
    } else {
        L->head = x->next;       // Agar woh pehla node tha, toh head ko agle node par shift kar do
    }
    if (x->next != NULL) {       // Agar woh aakhiri node nahi tha
        x->next->prev = x->prev; // Uske agle node ko pichle node se jod do
    }
    printf("%d\n", x->key);      // Delete kiye gaye node ki value print karo
    free(x);                     // Node ki memory ko azaad (free) kar do
}

// --- List ka Pehla Node Delete karna ---
void LIST_DELETE_INITIAL(struct List* L) {
    if (L->head == NULL) {       // Agar list khali hai
        printf("-1\n");          // Toh -1 print karo
        return;
    }
    struct Node* x = L->head;    // Pehle node ko 'x' mein save karo
    L->head = x->next;           // Head ko agle node par badha do
    if (L->head != NULL) {       // Agar ab list khali nahi hui hai
        L->head->prev = NULL;    // Naye head ke 'prev' ko NULL kar do
    }
    printf("%d\n", x->key);      // Delete huye node ki value print karo
    free(x);                     // Memory free kar do
}

// --- List ka Aakhiri Node Delete karna ---
void LIST_DELETE_LAST(struct List* L) {
    if (L->head == NULL) {       // Agar list khali hai
        printf("-1\n");          // -1 print karo
        return;
    }
    struct Node* curr = L->head; 
    while (curr->next != NULL) { // Jab tak aakhiri node na mil jaye, aage badhte raho
        curr = curr->next;
    }
    if (curr->prev != NULL) {    // Agar list mein ek se zyada nodes the
        curr->prev->next = NULL; // Uske pichle node ka 'next' NULL kar do (connection tod do)
    } else {
        L->head = NULL;          // Agar list mein sirf ek hi node tha, toh head ko NULL kar do
    }
    printf("%d\n", curr->key);   // Value print karo
    free(curr);                  // Memory free karo
}

// --- Main Menu Driven Program ---
int main() {
    struct List L = {NULL};      // Shuru mein empty list banate hain
    char op;                     // User ki choice (f, t, a, d, etc.) lene ke liye
    int k1, k2;                  // Keys/data lene ke liye variables

Gemini Apps Prompted put more coments explaining 10 Mar 2026, 22:37:57 GMT+05:30 Logic Summary (Step-by-Step) Yahan step-by-step samjhaya gaya hai ki postfix evaluation kaise kaam karta hai aur code mein kya logic use hua hai: Integer Stack ka istemal: Postfix expression mein numbers (operands) hote hain, isliye humein characters nahi, balki int store karne ke liye ek stack chahiye. String Traversing (Looping): Hum input string ko left se right ek-ek character karke padhte hain. Agar koi space ' ' ya newline '\n' aata hai, toh use ignore kar dete hain. Multi-digit Numbers ko handle karna: Agar character ek digit hai (jaise '1', '2'), toh hum check karte hain ki kya uske aage bhi digits hain (jaise "100"). Hum num = num * 10 + (e[i] - '0') formula use karke pure word ko ek integer number mein convert karte hain aur stack mein push kar dete hain. Operators aur Calculation: Agar koi operator ( + , - , * , / ) milta hai, toh stack se do values pop ki jati hain. Pehli nikali gayi value (val1) hamesha Right Operand hoti hai. Dusri nikali gayi value (val2) hamesha Left Operand hoti hai. Un dono par operation perform karke, jo naya result aata hai use wapas stack mein push kar diya jata hai. Final Result: Jab puri string khatam ho jati hai, toh stack ke top par sirf ek hi value bachti hai, jo humara final answer hoti hai. C Program with Detailed Hinglish Comments #include <stdio.h>    // Input/Output functions (jaise printf, fgets) ke liye
#include <stdlib.h>   // Standard library functions ke liye
#include <string.h>   // String manipulation ke liye (agar zarurat ho)
#include <ctype.h>    // isdigit() function use karne ke liye, jo check karta hai ki character number hai ya nahi

#define MAX 1000      // Stack ka maximum size define kar rahe hain

// --- Stack Data Structure ---
// Yahan hum integer stack bana rahe hain kyunki humein numbers par calculation karni hai
struct IntStack {
    int top;          // Stack ka top pointer
    int arr[MAX];     // Integer values store karne ke liye array
};

// Stack ko shuru (initialize) karne ka function
void initStack(struct IntStack* s) {
    s->top = -1;      // -1 ka matlab hai stack abhi poori tarah khali hai
}

// Stack mein value daalne (Push) ka function
void push(struct IntStack* s, int val) {
    if (s->top < MAX - 1) {   // Check karo ki stack mein jagah hai ya nahi
        s->top++;             // Top ko ek step upar badhao
        s->arr[s->top] = val; // Nayi jagah par value ko save kar do
    }
}

// Stack se value nikalne (Pop) ka function
int pop(struct IntStack* s) {
    if (s->top >= 0) {        // Check karo ki stack mein kuch hai ya nahi
        int val = s->arr[s->top]; // Top wali value ko ek variable mein le lo
        s->top--;             // Top ko ek step neeche kar do (value remove ho gayi)
        return val;           // Nikali hui value ko wapas bhej do
    }
    return 0;                 // Agar stack khali hai toh 0 return karo (Error case)
}

// --- Main Logic Function ---
// Postfix expression ko evaluate karne ka function
int EvaluatePostfix(char* e) {
    struct IntStack s;        // Ek naya stack banao
    initStack(&s);            // Stack ko properly initialize karo
    
    int i = 0;                // String ko traverse (padhne) ke liye index variable
    
    // Jab tak string ka end (Null character '\0') nahi aa jata, tab tak loop chalao
    while (e[i] != '\0') {
        
        // Agar current character space ya line-break hai, toh usko chhod do aur aage badho
        if (e[i] == ' ' || e[i] == '\n') {
            i++;
            continue;
        }
        
        // Agar current character ek number (digit) hai
        if (isdigit(e[i])) {
            int num = 0; // Pura number banane ke liye variable
            
            // Ye loop tab tak chalega jab tak lagatar digits milti rahengi (Multi-digit numbers ke liye jaise "100")
            while (isdigit(e[i])) {
                // Character ko integer mein convert kar rahe hain: (e[i] - '0')
                // Aur purane number ko 10 se multiply karke naya digit add kar rahe hain
                num = num * 10 + (e[i] - '0');
                i++; // Agla character check karne ke liye index badhao
            }
            // Pura number banne ke baad usko stack mein push kar do
            push(&s, num);
        } 
        
        // Agar current character operator hai (+, -, *, /)
        else {
            // Stack se top 2 numbers bahar nikalo
            int val1 = pop(&s); // Pehla nikla hua number (Right side wala operand hoga)
            int val2 = pop(&s); // Dusra nikla hua number (Left side wala operand hoga)
            
            // Operator check karo aur calculation karke result wapas push kar do
            switch (e[i]) {
                case '+': 
                    push(&s, val2 + val1); // Dono ko jodo
                    break;
                case '-': 
                    push(&s, val2 - val1); // Dusre mein se pehla ghatao (Order is important!)
                    break;
                case '*': 
                    push(&s, val2 * val1); // Dono ko multiply karo
                    break;
                case '/': 
                    push(&s, val2 / val1); // Dusre ko pehle se divide karo
                    break;
            }
            i++; // Agla character padhne ke liye index badhao
        }
    }
    
    // Pura expression solve hone ke baad, stack mein aakhir mein 1 hi value bachegi wahi final answer hai
    return pop(&s);
}

// --- Main Function ---
int main() {
    char exp[MAX]; // Expression store karne ke liye string array
    
    // User se input le rahe hain. fgets spaces ke sath puri line read karta hai (scanf "%s" sirf pehle space tak padhta hai)
    if (fgets(exp, MAX, stdin) != NULL) {
        int result = EvaluatePostfix(exp); // Function call karo aur result variable mein save karo
        printf("%d\n", result);            // Final result print karo

Spaces aur newlines ko ignore karenge. Agar koi number milta hai (multiple digits ka bhi ho sakta hai), toh usko integer mein convert karke stack mein push kar denge. Agar koi operator ( + , - , * , / ) milta hai, toh stack se aakhiri 2 numbers pop karenge. Pehla pop kiya hua number right operand hoga, aur dusra left operand . Un par operator lagakar result ko wapas stack mein push kar denge. Aakhir mein stack mein sirf ek hi number bachega, jo humara final answer hoga. C Program Yahan code hai jisme sirf zaroori aur chote Hinglish comments diye gaye hain: #include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <ctype.h>

#define MAX 1000

// Integer stack structure banayenge
struct IntStack {
    int top;
    int arr[MAX];
};

// Stack ko initialize karna
void initStack(struct IntStack* s) {
    s->top = -1;
}

// Stack mein value daalna
void push(struct IntStack* s, int val) {
    if (s->top < MAX - 1) {
        s->top++;
        s->arr[s->top] = val;
    }
}

// Stack se value nikalna
int pop(struct IntStack* s) {
    if (s->top >= 0) {
        int val = s->arr[s->top];
        s->top--;
        return val;
    }
    return 0; // Agar stack khali ho
}

// Postfix expression evaluate karne ka function
int EvaluatePostfix(char* e) {
    struct IntStack s;
    initStack(&s);
    
    int i = 0;
    while (e[i] != '\0') {
        // Spaces aur newlines ko ignore karo
        if (e[i] == ' ' || e[i] == '\n') {
            i++;
            continue;
        }
        
        // Agar number hai, toh pura number read karke stack mein push karo
        if (isdigit(e[i])) {
            int num = 0;
            // Jab tak lagatar digits mil rahi hain, number banate jao
            while (isdigit(e[i])) {
                num = num * 10 + (e[i] - '0');
                i++;
            }
            push(&s, num);
        } 
        // Agar operator hai, toh 2 values pop karke calculate karo
        else {
            int val1 = pop(&s); // Pehla pop kiya (Right operand)
            int val2 = pop(&s); // Dusra pop kiya (Left operand)
            
            switch (e[i]) {
                case '+': push(&s, val2 + val1); break;
                case '-': push(&s, val2 - val1); break;
                case '*': push(&s, val2 * val1); break;
                case '/': push(&s, val2 / val1); break;
            }
            i++;
        }
    }
    
    // Final result stack ke top par hoga
    return pop(&s);
}

int main() {

#include <ctype.h>    // isalnum() function use karne ke liye library include kar rahe hain

struct Stack {        // Stack naam ka naya data type bana rahe hain
    int top;          // Sabse upari element ka index track karne ke liye
    char arr[MAX];    // Operators store karne ke liye character array

void initStack(struct Stack* s) { // Stack pointer ko as parameter le rahe hain
    s->top = -1;      // Shuru mein top ko -1 set kar rahe hain kyunki stack khali hai
}                     // Function yahan khatam hota hai

// Stack ke andar element daalne ka function (Push)
void push(struct Stack* s, char c) { // Stack pointer aur character accept kar rahe hain
    if (s->top == MAX - 1) { // Check kar rahe hain ki stack full toh nahi hai
        return;       // Agar full hai toh wapas laut jao (overflow)
    }                 // If condition khatam
    s->top++;         // Top ki value badha rahe hain
    s->arr[s->top] = c; // Array mein naye index par character save kar rahe hain
}                     // Push function khatam

// Stack se element nikalne ka function (Pop)
char pop(struct Stack* s) { // Stack pointer parameter
    if (s->top == -1) { // Check kar rahe hain ki stack khali toh nahi
        return '\0';  // Khali hone par null character return kar rahe hain
    }                 // If condition khatam
    char poppedChar = s->arr[s->top]; // Top element ko ek variable mein nikal rahe hain
    s->top--;         // Top ki value ghata rahe hain (element remove ho gaya)
    return poppedChar; // Nikala gaya character return kar rahe hain

// Operator ki precedence (prathmikta) batane ka function
int precedence(char op) { // Operator accept kar rahe hain
    if (op == '*' || op == '/') { // Agar multiply ya divide hai
        return 2;     // Toh highest precedence 2 return karo
    }                 // Pehla if khatam
    if (op == '+' || op == '-') { // Agar plus ya minus hai
        return 1;     // Toh low precedence 1 return karo
    }                 // Dusra if khatam
    return 0;         // Agar '(' hai ya kuch aur, toh 0 return karo

// Infix expression ko Postfix mein convert karne ka function
char* InfixToPostfix(char* e) { // Infix string pointer as input le rahe hain
    struct Stack s;             // Ek naya stack variable bana rahe hain
    initStack(&s);              // Stack ko initialize kar rahe hain
    
    static char postfix[MAX];   // Postfix result store karne ke liye static array bana rahe hain (taaki function ke bahar bhi access ho sake)
    int i = 0;                  // Infix string (e) ko padhne ke liye index

            postfix[j] = current; // Operand ko seedhe postfix array mein daal do
            j++;                // Postfix ka index badha do
        }                       // If condition khatam
        
        // Agar character '(' hai
        else if (current == '(') { // Check kar rahe hain opening bracket ke liye
            push(&s, current);  // Ise seedhe stack mein push kar do
        }                       // Else-if khatam
        
        // Agar character ')' hai
        else if (current == ')') { // Check kar rahe hain closing bracket ke liye
            while (s.top != -1 && s.arr[s.top] != '(') { // Jab tak stack khali na ho aur '(' na mil jaye
                postfix[j] = pop(&s); // Stack se pop karke postfix mein daalte raho
                j++;            // Postfix ka index badhaate raho
            }                   // While loop khatam
            pop(&s);            // Aakhir mein stack se '(' ko bhi pop karke hata do (discard kar do)
        }                       // Else-if khatam
        
        // Agar character operator (+, -, *, /) hai
        else {                  // Uppar di gayi condition nahi hai toh operator hi hoga
            while (s.top != -1 && precedence(s.arr[s.top]) >= precedence(current)) { 
                // Jab tak stack ke top element ki precedence naye operator se badi ya barabar hai
                postfix[j] = pop(&s); // Top operator ko pop karke postfix mein daal do

    }                           // Main while loop khatam

        j++;                    // Postfix ka index badhaate jao
    }                           // Aakhiri while loop khatam
    
    postfix[j] = '\0';          // Postfix string ko properly band (terminate) karne ke liye null character laga rahe hain
    return postfix;             // Final postfix string return kar rahe hain
}                               // InfixToPostfix function khatam

// C program ka main function jahan execution shuru hota hai

    char infix[MAX];            // User ka input lene ke liye array

Gemini Apps Prompted Blunt verdict: the idea is promising, but in its current form it is not yet a strong main-track paper. The reason is not that it is bad; it is that the space has moved fast. Dynamic team selection already exists in DyLAN, sparse communication already has dedicated study, message-pruning/topology-economy already exists in AgentPrune, task-adaptive topology design already exists in G-Designer, graph orchestration has already been pushed to over 1,000 agents in MacNet, and late-2025 work has already gone beyond text into latent/thought communication with LatentMAS and ThoughtComm. A reviewer could easily say “interesting combination, but novelty is incremental” unless you sharpen the claim a lot. (OpenReview)
Your own critiques are basically correct. The “quantum” framing is a metaphor risk, raw concatenation is still a context bomb, and easy benchmarks will not impress reviewers anymore. The good news is that there is still real headroom on harder agent benchmarks: the current verified GAIA leaderboard tops out at 74.55% overall and 65.39% on level 3; the current verified ScienceAgentBench leaderboard tops out at 33.33%; SciCode contains 338 subproblems from 80 real scientific problems and its paper reports only 4.6% solved in the most realistic setting; SWE-bench Verified is a human-validated set of 500 coding tasks. That means the field is still wide open on difficult, tool-using, open-ended problems. (hal.cs.princeton.edu)
So my honest assessment is:

As written: publishable as a workshop/system paper or arXiv project, assuming solid experiments.
As a flagship paper: not yet.
After redesign: yes, it could become a serious paper.
The gap you can still own
Do not try to own “dynamic sparse multi-agent routing.” That lane is crowded.
Do not try to own “latent communication” alone. That lane is now active too.
The gap worth owning is:
Under a fixed compute/token budget, can a multi-agent system route only the messages that materially change the solution, while attaching enough evidence and uncertainty to prevent echo chambers and hallucination cascades?
From the sources I checked, adjacent work covers dynamic selection, sparse topologies, pruning, task-adaptive graph design, and latent/thought communication, but I did not find one unifying budgeted online routing + proof-carrying structured messages + optional latent side channel into one verifiable agent system. That is an inference from the literature I checked, not a proof that no prior paper exists, but it is the cleanest novelty slot I see. (OpenReview)

The version I would build
Call it something like:
Budgeted Belief Routing for Multi-Agent LLMs
or
VoI-Router: Value-of-Information Routing for Agent Societies
That is much stronger than a quantum metaphor.

Core idea
Agents should not mostly talk in free-form chat.
They should emit belief packets.
Each packet is a structured object like:

{
  "claim": "...",
  "evidence": ["tool result / code diff / citation / observation"],
  "uncertainty": 0.27,
  "proposed_action": "...",
  "verification_test": "...",
  "compact_summary": "...",
  "embedding_or_latent": "optional"
}
Now the system routes packets, not conversations.

Better formalism
Let agent (j) emit packets (p_{j,k}(t)).
Let (M_i(t)) be agent (i)’s local memory slice.
Let the router estimate utility:
[
U(p_{j,k}\to i, t)
\widehat{\Delta I}(y; p_{j,k}\mid M_i(t))

\eta , \text{DisagreementGain}
\lambda , \text{TokenCost}
\mu , \text{Redundancy}
\gamma , \text{Risk}
]
Then select packets under a budget:

[
S_t
\arg\max_{S}
\sum_{(p \to i)\in S} U(p\to i,t)
\quad
\text{s.t. }
\sum_{p\in S}\text{cost}(p)\le B_t
]
Then update edge weights using verified contribution, not only agreement:

[
w_{ij}(t+1)
\rho w_{ij}(t)

\alpha ,\text{verified_gain}_{ij}
\beta ,\text{redundancy}_{ij}
\delta ,\text{error_propagation}_{ij}
]
This is much better than “who talked to whom.” It becomes “who delivered useful, verifiable information.”

Why this is more novel
It shifts the paper from topology aesthetics to decision-theoretic communication.
It solves the biggest practical problem: context overflow.
It gives you a built-in anti-hallucination mechanism because messages must carry evidence, a test, or both.
It gives you reviewer-friendly ablations: no budget, no verifier, no uncertainty, no structured packets, no latent side-channel.

The mindblowing but still doable extension
The bold extension is a dual-channel agent society:

Public channel: structured text packets for interpretability, tools, and logging.
Private channel: compact latent/vector packets for speed and dense semantic transfer.
Use the public channel for anything that must be auditable.
Use the private channel for fast internal coordination.
That is still doable, but only really practical with open-weight models where you can access hidden states or KV-cache-like internals. Recent latent/thought communication work makes this direction exciting, but it is no longer empty territory, so treat it as a second-phase upgrade rather than the only novelty claim. (arXiv)

Step-by-step build plan
Step 1: Freeze the paper thesis
Use one sentence and do not drift from it:

“We propose a budgeted, verifiable communication protocol for multi-agent LLM systems that routes only high-value belief updates and improves the accuracy-cost-robustness Pareto frontier on hard agent benchmarks.”
That sentence is publishable. “Quantum society of minds” is not.

Step 2: Drop nonessential complexity from v1
For the first serious version, remove prompt crossover/evolution. It is flashy, but it adds confounds and makes ablations messier. Put it in appendix or future work.
Also do not lead with “1,000 agents.” MacNet already owns the giant-scale headline. Beat baselines with 8–32 agents under strict budgets. (OpenReview)

Step 3: Build the packet schema
Implement a strict typed output format for every agent:

claim
evidence
confidence
proposed next action
verification hook
compact summary
Force every agent to speak this language. This alone will make your system cleaner than most multi-agent chat pipelines.

Step 4: Replace chat history with a belief graph
Do not keep one giant transcript. Maintain a graph:

nodes = claims, subgoals, tests, code artifacts, observations
edges = supports / contradicts / depends-on / verified-by
Each agent retrieves only the local subgraph relevant to its subproblem. This is how you break the concatenation bottleneck.

Step 5: Start with a simple router, not a learned one
Use a hand-designed utility score first:

uncertainty reduction bonus
disagreement bonus
novelty bonus
token-cost penalty
redundancy penalty
Do greedy routing under a budget. Only after the whole system works should you replace the heuristic with a learned scorer or contextual bandit.

This is essential.
The verifier checks:

code execution / unit tests
tool outputs
factual consistency
internal contradictions
whether a proposed action actually moved the task forward
Only verified gains should strengthen graph edges. This directly attacks hallucination propagation, which is already recognized as a major problem in multi-agent systems. (Springer)

Step 7: Add anti-echo-chamber control
When too many agents converge too early:

spawn a critic or contrarian agent
force cross-cluster review
increase disagreement bonus
penalize repeated semantically similar packets
This is where your system becomes more than “debate with a graph.”

Primary set:

GAIA for general agentic reasoning, web/tool use, and multi-step autonomy. (hal.cs.princeton.edu)
ScienceAgentBench for real scientific workflow tasks with very large headroom. (hal.cs.princeton.edu)
SciCode for scientific coding and decomposition-heavy research tasks. (scicode-bench.github.io)
SWE-bench Verified for realistic software engineering. (SWE-bench)
Secondary:

AssistantBench if you want realistic web task evaluation. (AssistantBench)
Avoid leading with GSM8K. At most use it as a sanity check.

single-agent ReAct/tool-use baseline
dense full-communication multi-agent baseline
sparse fixed-topology baseline
dynamic-team baseline
pruning baseline
Reviewer mindset is simple: “Did this really beat existing ways to coordinate agents?” Make that answer obvious.

no verifier
no budget constraint
no structured packets
no disagreement bonus
no redundancy penalty
no topology adaptation
no latent side-channel
If the full system only barely beats a simpler variant, the paper is weak.

Step 11: Measure the right metrics
Do not only measure final accuracy.
Track:

task success
tokens
wall-clock latency
dollar cost
redundancy rate
verifier-confirmed error propagation
robustness to one malicious or noisy agent
calibration of final confidence
This turns the paper from “clever prompting” into a systems contribution.

Step 12: Only then add the latent side-channel
Once the text-structured version works, add optional latent packets for open-weight models:

encode packet summary into hidden-state or KV-style representation
transmit to selected peers
keep public text trace for auditing
If this part fails, you still have a strong paper.
If it works, you have a stronger one.

same or better success with 30–60% lower token cost
better robustness when one agent is noisy or adversarial
better performance on open-ended tool benchmarks, not just toy QA
evidence that routing decisions correlate with verified progress
clean ablations proving the gain is from budgeted verified communication, not prompt luck
That is the bar.

Problem: multi-agent systems waste tokens, propagate bad info, and collapse into redundant chat.
Method: budgeted routing of proof-carrying belief packets over an adaptive graph.
Insight: message value matters more than message volume.
Result: better accuracy-cost-robustness frontier on hard agent benchmarks.
That is crisp and respectable.

Your current idea is not yet strong enough for a major paper, but the core instinct is excellent; reframe it as budgeted, verifiable belief routing over adaptive multi-agent graphs, and it becomes a plausible, genuinely interesting research project.
