➤ Figure 1.7 Maze used by Tolman. (a) The rat initially explores the maze. (b) The rat learns 
to turn right to obtain food at B when it starts at A. (c) When placed at C, the rat turns left 
to reach the food at B. In this experiment, precautions are taken to prevent the rat from 
knowing where the food is based on cues such as smell.
In one of his experiments, Tolman (1938) placed a rat in a maze like the one in 
Figure 1.7. Initially, the rat explored the maze, running up and down each of the alleys 
(Figure 1.7a). After this initial period of exploration, the rat was placed at point A and 
food was placed at point B, and the rat quickly learned to turn right at the intersection to 
obtain the food. This is exactly what the behaviorists would predict, because turning right 
was rewarded with food (Figure 1.7b). However, when Tolman (after taking precautions 
to be sure the rat couldn’t determine the location of the food based on smell) placed the rat 
at point C, something interesting happened. The rat turned left at the intersection to reach 
the food at point B (Figure 1.7c). Tolman’s explanation of this result was that when the rat 
initially experienced the maze it was developing a cognitive map—a conception within the 
rat’s mind of the maze’s layout (Tolman, 1948). Thus, even though the rat had previously 
been rewarded for turning right, its mental map indicated that when starting from the new 
location it needed to turn left to reach the food. Tolman’s use of the word cognitive, and the 
idea that something other than stimulus–response connections might be occurring in the 
rat’s mind, placed Tolman outside of mainstream behaviorism.
Other researchers were aware of Tolman’s work, but for most American psychologists 
in the 1940s, the use of the term cognitive was difficult to accept because it violated the 
behaviorists’ idea that internal processes, such as thinking or maps in the head, were not 
acceptable topics to study. It wasn’t until about a decade after Tolman introduced the idea 
of cognitive maps that developments occurred that led to a resurgence of the mind in psy
chology. Ironically, one of these developments was the publication, in 1957, of a book by  
B. F. Skinner titled Verbal Behavior.
In his book, Skinner argued that children learn language through operant condition
ing. According to this idea, children imitate speech that they hear, and repeat correct speech 
because it is rewarded. But in 1959, Noam Chomsky, a linguist from the Massachusetts 
Institute of Technology, published a scathing review of Skinner’s book, in which he pointed 
out that children say many sentences that have never been rewarded by parents (“I hate you, 
Mommy,” for example), and that during the normal course of language development, they 
go through a stage in which they use incorrect grammar, such as “the boy hitted the ball,” 
even though this incorrect grammar may never have been reinforced.
Chomsky saw language development as being determined not by imitation or rein
forcement, but by an inborn biological program that holds across cultures. Chomsky’s 
idea that language is a product of the way the mind is constructed, rather than a result of 
Copyright 2019 Cengage Learning. All Rights Reserved. May not be copied, scanned, or duplicated, in whole or in part.  WCN 02-200-203
 The Rebirth of the Study of the Mind  
13
reinforcement, led psychologists to reconsider the idea that language and other complex 
behaviors, such as problem solving and reasoning, can be explained by operant conditioning. 
Instead, they began to realize that to understand complex cognitive behaviors, it is necessary 
not only to measure observable behavior but also to consider what this behavior tells us 
about how the mind works.
The Rebirth of the Study of the Mind
The decade of the 1950s is generally recognized as the beginning of the cognitive 
revolution—a shift in psychology from the behaviorist’s focus on stimulus–response 
relationships to an approach whose main thrust was to understand the operation of the 
mind. Even before Chomsky’s critique of Skinner’s book, other events were happening that 
signaled a shift away from focusing only on behavior and toward studying how the mind 
operates. But before we describe the events that began the cognitive revolution, let’s con
sider the following question: What is a revolution—and specifically a scientific revolution? 
One answer to this question can be found in philosopher Thomas Kuhn’s (1962) book 
The Structure of Scientific Revolutions.
Paradigms and Paradigm Shifts
Kuhn defined a scientific revolution as a shift from one paradigm to another, where a 
paradigm is a system of ideas that dominate science at a particular time (Dyson, 2012).  
A scientific revolution, therefore, involves a paradigm shift.
An example of a paradigm shift in science is the shift that occurred in physics in 
the beginning of the 20th century, with the introduction of the theory of relativity and 
quantum theory. Before the 20th century, classical physics, founded by Isaac Newton 
(1642–1727), had made great progress in describing things like how objects are affected 
by forces (Newton’s laws of motion) and the nature of electrical fields (Maxwell’s laws, 
which described electromagnetism). The principles of classical physics did not, however, 
adequately describe subatomic phenomena and the relation between time and motion. 
For example, classical physics conceived of the flow of time as an absolute constant, which 
was the same for everyone. But in 1905, Albert Einstein, a young clerk in the Bern, Swit
zerland, patent office, published his theory of relativity, which proposed that the mea
surement of space and time are affected by an observer’s motion, so clocks run slower 
when approaching the speed of light. He also proposed that there is an equivalence of 
mass and energy, as expressed in his famous equation E = mc2 (energy equals mass times 
the speed of light squared). Einstein’s relativity theory, along with the newly introduced 
quantum theory, which explained the behavior of subatomic particles, marked the begin
ning of modern physics.
Just as the paradigm shift from classical physics to modern physics provided a new way 
of looking at the physical world, the paradigm shift from behaviorism to the cognitive ap
proach provided a new way to look at behavior. During the reign of behaviorism, behavior 
was considered an end in itself. Psychology was dominated by experiments studying how 
behavior is affected by rewards and punishments. Some valuable discoveries resulted from 
this research, including psychological therapies called “behavioral therapies,” which are still 
in use today. But the behaviorist paradigm did not allow any consideration of the mind’s 
role in creating behavior, so in the 1950s the new cognitive paradigm began to emerge.  
We can’t mark the beginning of this new paradigm by the publication of a single paper, 
like Einstein’s (1905) proposal of relativity theory, but rather we can note a series of events, 
which added together culminated in a new way of studying psychology. One of these 
events was the introduction of a new technology that suggested a new way of describing the  
operation of the mind. That new technology was the digital computer.

Introduction of the Digital Computer
The first digital computers, developed in the late 1940s, were huge machines that took up 
entire buildings, but in 1954 IBM introduced a computer that was available to the general 
public. These computers were still extremely large compared to the laptops of today, but they 
found their way into university research laboratories, where they were used both to analyze 
data and, most important for our purposes, to suggest a new way of thinking about the mind.
Flow Diagrams for Computers One of the characteristics of computers that captured 
the attention of psychologists in the 1950s was that they processed information in stages, as 
illustrated in Figure 1.8a. In this diagram, information is first received by an “input proces
sor.” It is then stored in a “memory unit” before it is processed by an “arithmetic unit,” which 
then creates the computer’s output. Using this stage approach as their inspiration, some 
psychologists proposed the information-processing approach to studying the mind—an 
approach that traces sequences of mental operations involved in cognition. According to 
the information-processing approach, the operation of the mind can be described as occur
ring in a number of stages. Applying this stage approach to the mind led psychologists to ask 
new questions and to frame their answers to these questions in new ways. One of the first 
experiments influenced by this new way of thinking about the mind involved studying how 
well people are able to focus their attention on some information when other information 
is being presented at the same time.

Flow Diagrams for the Mind Beginning in the 1950s, a number of researchers became 
interested in describing how well the mind can deal with incoming information. One ques
tion they were interested in answering followed from William James’s idea that when we 
decide to attend to one thing, we must withdraw from other things. Taking this idea as a 
starting point, British psychologist Colin Cherry (1953) presented participants with two 
auditory messages, one to the left ear and one to the right ear, and told them to focus their 
attention on one of the messages (the attended message) and to ignore the other one (the 
unattended message). For example, the participant might be told to attend to the left-ear 
message that began “As Susan drove down the road in her new car . . .” while simultaneously 
receiving, but not attending to, the right-ear message “Cognitive psychology, which is the 
study of mental processes . . .”
The result of this experiment, which we will describe in detail when we discuss 
attention in Chapter 4, was that when people focused on the attended message, they 
could hear the sounds of the unattended message but 
were unaware of the contents of that message. This result 
led another British psychologist, Donald Broadbent 
(1958), to propose the first flow diagram of the mind 
(Figure 1.8b). This diagram represents what Broadbent 
believed happens in a person’s mind when directing at
tention to one stimulus in the environment. Applied 
to Cherry’s attention experiment, “input” would be the 
sounds of both the attended and unattended messages; 
the “filter” lets through the attended message and filters 
out the unattended message; and the “detector” records 
the information that gets through the filter.
Applied to your experience when talking to a friend 
at a noisy party, the filter lets in your friend’s conversation 
and filters out all the other conversations and noise. Thus, 
although you might be aware that there are other people 
talking, you are not aware of detailed information such as 
what the other people are talking about.

 The Rebirth of the Study of the Mind  
15
Broadbent’s flow diagram provided a way to analyze the operation of the mind in terms of 
a sequence of processing stages and proposed a model that could be tested by further experi
ments. You will see many more flow diagrams like this throughout this book because they have 
become one of the standard ways of depicting the operation of the mind. But the British psy
chologists Cherry and Broadbent weren’t the only researchers finding new ways of studying 
the mind. At about the same time in the United States, researchers organized two conferences 
that, taking their cue from computers, conceived of the mind as a processor of information.
Conferences on Artificial Intelligence and Information Theory
In the early 1950s, John McCarthy, a young professor of mathematics at Dartmouth College, had 
an idea. Would it be possible, McCarthy wondered, to program computers to mimic the opera
tion of the human mind? Rather than simply asking the question, McCarthy decided to organize 
a conference at Dartmouth in the summer of 1956 to provide a forum for researchers to discuss 
ways that computers could be programmed to carry out intelligent behavior. The title of the con
ference, Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence, was the first use of the term artificial 
intelligence. McCarthy defined the artificial intelligence approach as “making a machine behave 
in ways that would be called intelligent if a human were so behaving” (McCarthy et al., 1955).
Researchers from a number of different disciplines—psychologists, mathematicians, 
computer scientists, linguists, and experts in information theory—attended the conference, 
which spanned 10 weeks. A number of people attended most of the conference, others 
dropped in and out, but perhaps the two most important participants—Herb Simon and 
Alan Newell from the Carnegie Institute of Technology—were hardly there at all (Boden, 
2006). The reason they weren’t there is that they were busy back in Pittsburgh trying to cre
ate the artificial intelligence machine that McCarthy had envisioned. Simon and Newell’s 
goal was to create a computer program that could create proofs for problems in logic—
something that up until then had only been achieved by humans.
Newell and Simon succeeded in creating the program, which they called the logic 
theorist, in time to demonstrate it at the conference. What they demonstrated was rev
olutionary because the logic theorist program was able to create proofs of mathematical 
theorems that involve principles of logic. This program, although primitive compared to 
modern artificial intelligence programs, was a real “thinking machine” because it did more 
than simply process numbers—it used humanlike reasoning processes to solve problems.
Shortly after the Dartmouth conference, in September of the same year, another pivotal 
conference was held, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology Symposium on Information 
Theory. This conference provided another opportunity for Newell and Simon to demon
strate their logic theorist program, and the attendees also heard George Miller, a Harvard 
psychologist, present a version of a paper “The Magical Number Seven Plus or Minus Two,” 
which had just been published (Miller, 1956). In that paper, Miller presented the idea that 
there are limits to a human’s ability to process information—that the capacity of the human 
mind is limited to about seven items (for example, the length of a telephone number).
As we will see when we discuss this idea in Chapter 5, there are ways to increase our 
ability to take in and remember information (for example, we have little trouble adding 
an area code to the seven digits of many telephone numbers). Nonetheless, Miller’s basic 
principle that there are limits to the amount of information we can take in and remember 
was an important idea, which, you might notice, was similar to the point being made by 
Broadbent’s filter model at about the same time.
The Cognitive “Revolution” Took a While
The events we have described—Cherry’s experiment, Broadbent’s filter model, and the two 
conferences in 1956—represented the beginning of a shift in psychology from behaviorism 
to the study of the mind. Although we have called this shift the cognitive revolution, it is

worth noting that the shift from Skinner’s behaviorism to the cognitive approach, which 
was indeed revolutionary, occurred over a period of time. The scientists attending the con
ferences in 1956 had no idea that these conferences would, years later, be seen as historic 
events in the birth of a new way of thinking about the mind or that scientific historians 
would someday call 1956 “the birthday of cognitive science” (Bechtel et al., 1998; Miller, 
2003; Neisser, 1988). In fact, even years after these meetings, a textbook on the history 
of psychology made no mention of the cognitive approach (Misiak & Sexton, 1966), 
and it wasn’t until 1967 that Ulrich Neisser published a textbook with the title Cognitive 
Psychology (Neisser, 1967). Figure 1.9 shows a time line of some of the events that led to the 
establishment of the field of cognitive psychology.
Neisser’s textbook, which coined the term cognitive psychology and emphasized the 
information-processing approach to studying the mind, is, in a sense, the grandfather of 
the book you are now reading. As often happens, each successive generation creates new 
ways of approaching problems, and cognitive psychology has been no exception. Since the 
1956 conferences and the 1967 textbook, many experiments have been carried out, new 
theories proposed, and new techniques developed; as a result, cognitive psychology, and the 
information-processing approach to studying the mind, has become one of the dominant 
approaches in psychology.
The Evolution of Cognitive Psychology
We have been describing the events in the 1950s and 1960s as the cognitive revolution. But 
it is important to realize that although the revolution made it acceptable to study the mind, 
the field of cognitive psychology continued to evolve in the decades that followed. One way 
to appreciate how cognitive psychology has evolved from the 1950s and 1960s until today 
is to look at the contents of Neisser’s (1967) book.
What Neisser Wrote
We can appreciate where cognitive psychology was in the 1960s by looking at the first 
cognitive psychology textbook, Ulrich Neisser’s (1967) Cognitive Psychology. The purpose 
of this book, as Neisser states in Chapter 1, is “to provide a useful and current assessment of 
the existing state of the art” (p. 9). Given this purpose, it is instructive to consider the book’s 
Table of Contents.

 The Evolution of Cognitive Psychology  
17
Most of the book is devoted to vision and hearing. There are descriptions of how 
information is taken in by vision and held in memory for short periods of time, and how 
people search for visual information and use visual information to see simple patterns. 
Most of the discussion is about the intake of information and holding information in 
the mind for brief periods of time, such as how long people can remember sounds like 
strings of numbers. But it isn’t until page 279 of the 305-page book that Neisser considers 
“higher mental processes” such as thinking, problem solving, and long-term remember
ing. The reason Neisser gives for this scant treatment is that in 1967, we just didn’t know 
much about higher mental processes.
Another gap in coverage is the almost complete absence of physiology. Neisser says that 
“I do not doubt that human behavior and consciousness depends entirely on the activity of 
the brain and related processes” (p. 5), but then he goes on to argue that he is interested in 
how the mind operates, but not in the physiological mechanisms behind this operation. 
These two gaps in Neisser’s book highlight what are central topics in present-day cog
nitive psychology. One of these topics is the study of higher mental processes, and the other 
is the study of the physiology of mental processes. 
Studying Higher Mental Processes
A big step toward the study of higher mental processes was Richard Atkinson and Richard  
Shiffrin’s (1968) model of memory, which was introduced a year after the publication of 
Neisser’s book. This model, shown in Figure 1.10, pictures the flow of information in the 
memory system as progressing through three stages. Sensory memory holds incoming in
formation for a fraction of a second and then passes most of this information to short-term 
memory, which has limited capacity and holds information for seconds (like an address 
you are trying to remember until you can write it down). The curved arrow represents the 
process of rehearsal, which occurs when we repeat something, like a 
phone number, to keep from forgetting it. The blue arrow indicates 
that some information in short-term memory can be transferred to 
long-term memory, a high-capacity system that can hold informa
tion for long periods of time (like your memory of what you did last 
weekend, or the capitals of states). The green arrow indicates that 
some of the information in long-term memory can be returned to 
short-term memory. The green arrow, which represents what hap
pens when we remember something that was stored in long-term 
memory, is based on the idea that remembering something involves 
bringing it back into short-term memory. 
By distinguishing between different components of the mem
ory process, this model opened the way for studying each part sep
arately. And once researchers discovered more details about what 
was going on inside each of the model’s boxes, they were able to subdivide these 
boxes into smaller units, which then could be studied in more depth. For ex
ample, Endel Tulving (1972, 1985), one of the most prominent early memory 
researchers, proposed that long-term memory is subdivided into three compo
nents (Figure 1.11). Episodic memory is memory for events in your life (like 
what you did last weekend). Semantic memory is memory for facts (such as the 
capitals of the states). Procedural memory is memory for physical actions (such 
as how to ride a bike or play the piano). Subdividing the long-term memory box 
into types of long-term memory added detail to the model that provided the 
basis for research into how each of these components operates. As you will see 
in every chapter of this book, the study of higher mental processes has extended 
to areas beyond memory. As you read this book, you will see how researchers

While researchers were working to understand memory and other cognitive functions 
by doing behavioral experiments, something else was happening. Physiological research, 
which we will see in Chapter 2 had been making advances since the 1800s, was providing 
important insights into the “behind the scenes” activity in the nervous system that creates 
the mind. 
Two physiological techniques dominated early physiological research on the mind. 
Neuropsychology, the study of the behavior of people with brain damage, had been 
providing insights into the functioning of different parts of the brain since the 1800s. 
Electrophysiology, measuring electrical responses of the nervous system, made it possible 
to listen to the activity of single neurons. Most electrophysiology research was done on 
animals. As we will see in Chapter 2, both neuropsychology and electrophysiology have 
provided important insights into the physiological basis of the mind.
But perhaps the most significant physiological advance wasn’t to come until a decade 
after Neisser’s book, when the technique of brain imaging was introduced. A procedure 
called positron emission tomography (PET), which was introduced in 1976, made it pos
sible to see which areas of the human brain are activated during cognitive activity (Hoffman 
et al., 1976; Ter-Pogossian et al., 1975). A disadvantage of this technique was that it was 
expensive and involved injecting radioactive tracers into a person’s bloodstream. PET 
was therefore replaced by functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), which didn’t in
volve radioactive tracers and which was capable of higher resolution (Ogawa et al., 1990). 
Figure 1.12 shows the results of an fMRI experiment.
The introduction of fMRI brings us back to the idea of revolutions. Thomas Kuhn’s 
idea of paradigm shifts was based on the idea that a scientific revolution involves a shift in 
the way people think about a subject. This was clearly the case in the shift from the behav
ioral paradigm to the cognitive paradigm. But there’s another kind of shift in addition to 
the shift in thinking: a shift in how people do science (Dyson, 2012; Galison, 1997). This 
shift, which depends on new developments in technology, is what happened with the in
troduction of the fMRI. Neuroimage, a journal devoted solely to reporting neuroimaging 
research, was founded in 1992 (Toga, 1992), followed by Human Brain Mapping in 1993 
(Fox, 1993). From its starting point in the early 1990s, the number of fMRI papers pub
lished in all journals has steadily increased. In fact, it has been estimated that about 40,000 
fMRI papers had been published as of 2015 (Eklund et al., 2016). 
There are limitations to fMRI research, so other scanning techniques have also been 
developed. But there is no question that the trend started by the introduction of fMRI in 
1990 caused its own revolution within cognitive psychology, which, as we will see in Chap
ter 2, has led to a vast increase in our knowledge of how the brain functions. 
New Perspectives on Behavior
So how has cognitive psychology evolved since Neisser’s 1967 “progress report”? As we 
have already mentioned, current cognitive psychology involves more-sophisticated flow di
agrams of the mind, a consideration of higher mental processes, and also a large amount of 
physiological research. 
Beyond developing more research on higher-level processes and physiology that we 
knew little about in 1967, researchers began taking research out of the laboratory. Most 
early research was done in laboratories, with participants sitting in one place looking at 
flashed stimuli, as in Donders’s reaction time experiment. But it became clear that to fully 
understand the mind, we have to also study what happens when a person is moving through

creasing amount of research on cognition in “real-world” situations.
Researchers also realized that humans are not “blank slates” that just accept and store 
information, so they began doing experiments that demonstrated the importance of knowl
edge for cognition. For example, consider the picture in Figure 1.13, which was used by 
Stephen Palmer (1975) to illustrate how our knowledge about the environment can influ
ence our perception. Palmer first presented a context scene such as the kitchen scene on 
the left and then briefly flashed one of the target pictures on the right. When Palmer asked 
observers to identify the object in the target picture, they correctly identified an object like 
the loaf of bread (which is appropriate to the kitchen scene) 80 percent of the time, but 
correctly identified the mailbox or the drum (two objects that don’t fit into the scene) only  
40 percent of the time. Apparently, Palmer’s observers were using their knowledge of objects 
that are likely to be found in kitchens to help them perceive the briefly flashed loaf of bread. 
Of course, knowledge isn’t just an interesting effect to be demonstrated in a perception 
experiment; it is central to most of our cognitive processing. You will see evidence for the 
importance of such knowledge in cognition because it appears in every chapter!

You will see how physiological research adds another dimension to our understanding 
of the mind; how cognitive psychology is studied in the laboratory and in real-world

Rank: 3 Part (a): Reduce $A$ to a row echelon form using elementary row operations Given the matrix: $$
A = \begin{pmatrix}
1 & 2 & 1 & 4 \
2 & 4 & 2 & 8 \
1 & 1 & 0 & 2 \
3 & 5 & 1 & 10
\end{pmatrix}
$$ Step 1: Eliminate the entries below the first pivot (position $(1,1)$) by applying the following row operations: $R_2 \to R_2 - 2R_1$ $R_3 \to R_3 - R_1$ $R_4 \to R_4 - 3R_1$ This gives: $$
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 2 & 1 & 4 \
0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \
0 & -1 & -1 & -2 \
0 & -1 & -2 & -2
\end{pmatrix}
$$ Step 2: We need a non-zero element in the second column to act as our next pivot. We can swap rows to achieve this.
First, swap $R_2$ and $R_3$: $$
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 2 & 1 & 4 \
0 & -1 & -1 & -2 \
0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \
0 & -1 & -2 & -2
\end{pmatrix}
$$ Then, swap $R_3$ and $R_4$ to push the all-zero row to the bottom: $$
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 2 & 1 & 4 \
0 & -1 & -1 & -2 \
0 & -1 & -2 & -2 \
0 & 0 & 0 & 0
\end{pmatrix}
$$ Step 3: Eliminate the entry below the second pivot (position $(2,2)$) by applying the row operation: $R_3 \to R_3 - R_2$ This yields: $$
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 2 & 1 & 4 \
0 & -1 & -1 & -2 \
0 & 0 & -1 & 0 \
0 & 0 & 0 & 0
\end{pmatrix}
$$ This matrix is now in a row echelon form (REF). (Note: If you multiply $R_2$ and $R_3$ by $-1$, you get another valid echelon form where the leading entries are positive $1$.) Part (b): Identify the pivot positions in the row echelon form The pivot positions are the coordinates of the leading (first non-zero) entries in each non-zero row of the row echelon form.
Looking at the matrix from Step 3, the leading entries are: Row 1: $1$ in column 1 $\to$ Position $(1, 1)$ Row 2: $-1$ in column 2 $\to$ Position $(2, 2)$ Row 3: $-1$ in column 3 $\to$ Position $(3, 3)$ So, the pivot positions are $(1,1)$, $(2,2)$, and $(3,3)$ . (Or equivalently, the pivots are in columns 1, 2, and 3). Part (c): Determine the rank of the matrix A The rank of a matrix is equal to the number of non-zero rows in its row echelon form (which is also the number of pivot positions).
Since there are 3 non-zero rows (and 3 pivot positions), the rank of matrix $A$ is: Rank$(A) = 3$ Products: Gemini Apps Why is this here? This activity was saved to your Google Account because the following settings were on: Gemini Apps Activity. You can control these settings here .

Gemini Apps Prompted https://youtu.be/pp-wYaBCWAk 22 Feb 2026, 11:29:19 GMT+05:30 This video, titled " QR Factorization | Gram Schmidt Process | Examples ," is a numerical analysis lecture by Dr. Harish Garg. It explains how to decompose a given matrix $A$ into the product of two matrices: $Q$ (an orthogonal or orthonormal matrix) and $R$ (an upper triangular matrix). Here is a summary of the core concepts covered: 1. Core Concepts & Definitions Goal of QR Factorization : To decompose any matrix $A$ (square or non-square) into $A = QR$. $Q$ : An orthogonal/orthonormal matrix where $Q^T Q = I$ (Identity Matrix). $R$ : An upper triangular matrix. Inner Product (Dot Product) : The standard inner product between two vectors is the sum of their element-wise products. L2 Norm : The length or magnitude of a vector, denoted as $|v|$, calculated as the square root of the dot product of the vector with itself: $|v| = \sqrt{v_1^2 + v_2^2 + \dots + v_n^2}$. Orthogonal Vectors : Two vectors $u$ and $v$ are orthogonal if their dot product is zero ($\langle u, v \rangle = 0$). [ 04:47 ] Orthonormal Vectors : A set of orthogonal vectors where each vector also has a unit norm (length equal to 1). If vectors are orthogonal but not orthonormal, they can be normalized by dividing each by its norm. [ 06:32 ] 2. The Gram-Schmidt Process If the column vectors of Matrix $A$ are linearly independent but not orthonormal, you use the Gram-Schmidt process to generate the orthonormal matrix $Q$: Step 1 (Find Orthogonal Vectors $U$): Let $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_n$ be the columns of Matrix $A$. First vector: $u_1 = A_1$ Second vector: Subtract the projection of $A_2$ onto $u_1$.
$$u_2 = A_2 - \frac{\langle A_2, u_1 \rangle}{|u_1|^2} u_1$$ Third vector: Subtract the projection of $A_3$ onto both $u_1$ and $u_2$.
$$u_3 = A_3 - \frac{\langle A_3, u_1 \rangle}{|u_1|^2} u_1 - \frac{\langle A_3, u_2 \rangle}{|u_2|^2} u_2$$ Repeat this pattern for all $n$ columns. Step 2 (Normalize to find $E$ vectors): [ 13:13 ] Convert the orthogonal $u$ vectors into orthonormal $e$ vectors by dividing by their norm:
$$e_i = \frac{u_i}{|u_i|}$$ 3. Constructing Matrices Q and R Forming Q: The matrix $Q$ is simply formed by placing the orthonormal vectors $e_1, e_2, \dots, e_n$ as its columns. [ 13:50 ] Forming R: Since $A = QR$ and $Q$ is orthonormal (meaning $Q^T Q = I$), you can find $R$ by multiplying both sides by $Q^T$. Thus, the upper triangular matrix is found using: $R = Q^T A$ [ 15:05 ] Dr. Garg spends the remaining portion of the lecture working through multiple step-by-step mathematical examples for $2 \times 2$, $3 \times 3$, and rectangular matrices (like $4 \times 3$) to demonstrate the algorithm in practice. Gram-Schmidt Orthogonalization Process This process is a fundamental algorithm in linear algebra used to transform a set of linearly independent vectors into an orthogonal (or orthonormal ) basis for the same subspace. 1. Core Definitions Orthogonal Set: A set of vectors ${v_1, v_2, \dots, v_n}$ where every pair of distinct vectors is perpendicular. Condition: $\langle v_i, v_j \rangle = 0$ for all $i \neq j$. $[ 02:07 ]$ Orthonormal Set: An orthogonal set where every vector also has a unit norm (length of 1). Condition: $\langle v_i, v_j \rangle = 0$ and $|v_i| = 1$. $[ 02:53 ]$ 2. The Core Idea: Projection The backbone of the process is the Vector Projection . To make a new vector $A_2$ orthogonal to an existing vector $u_1$, we subtract the "shadow" (projection) of $A_2$ onto $u_1$. Projection Formula: $\text{proj}_{u}(v) = \frac{\langle v, u \rangle}{|u|^2} u$ $[ 16:42 ]$ 3. Step-by-Step Derivation Given a set of linearly independent vectors ${A_1, A_2, \dots, A_k}$: First Vector: Set the first orthogonal vector equal to the first input vector.
$$\boxed{u_1 = A_1}$$ $[ 19:52 ]$ Second Vector: Subtract the projection of $A_2$ onto $u_1$.
$$\boxed{u_2 = A_2 - \frac{\langle A_2, u_1 \rangle}{|u_1|^2} u_1}$$ $[ 20:43 ]$ Third Vector: Subtract the projections of $A_3$ onto all previously found orthogonal vectors.
$$\boxed{u_3 = A_3 - \frac{\langle A_3, u_1 \rangle}{|u_1|^2} u_1 - \frac{\langle A_3, u_2 \rangle}{|u_2|^2} u_2}$$ $[ 21:05 ]$ Normalization (Optional): To get orthonormal vectors $e_i$, divide each $u_i$ by its norm:
$$e_i = \frac{u_i}{|u_i|}$$ $[ 04:06 ]$ 4. Worked Example Given: $A_1 = (1, 1, 0)$ and $A_2 = (2, 1, 1)$ Step 1: $u_1 = A_1 = (1, 1, 0)$. Step 2: Calculate $u_2 = A_2 - \text{proj}_{u_1}(A_2)$. $\langle A_2, u_1 \rangle = (2\times1) + (1\times1) + (1\times0) = 3$ $|u_1|^2 = 1^2 + 1^2 + 0^2 = 2$ $u_2 = (2, 1, 1) - \frac{3}{2}(1, 1, 0) = (0.5, -0.5, 1)$. $[ 34:51 ]$ Result: The orthogonal set is ${(1, 1, 0), (0.5, -0.5, 1)}$. 5. Common Mistakes to Avoid Using the wrong vector in the denominator: Always divide by the norm of the already calculated orthogonal vector ($u_i$), not the original input vector ($A_i$). $[ 17:02 ]$ Normalization timing: It is often easier to find all orthogonal vectors ($u_i$) first and normalize at the very end to avoid carrying square roots through every step. Skipping the Independence check: Ensure the initial vectors are linearly independent; if they are dependent, the process will eventually produce a zero vector. $[ 12:13 ]$ Final Revision Box (Exam Ready) Goal: Convert Basis $\to$ Orthogonal Basis. Key Tool: Inner Product (Dot Product). Geometric Intuition: Removing the components of a vector that lie in the direction of previous vectors. Definition The Gram-Schmidt Process is a mathematical algorithm used in linear algebra to find a set of orthogonal or orthonormal vectors from a given set of linearly independent vectors [ 01:19 ]. Orthogonal Vectors: A set of vectors where the dot product of any pair ($v_i \cdot v_j$) is exactly zero whenever $i \neq j$ [ 02:07 ]. Orthonormal Vectors: A set of orthogonal vectors where each individual vector additionally has a unit norm (magnitude of 1), i.e., $||v_i|| = 1$ [ 02:43 ]. 2. Key Theorem / Core Idea The fundamental principle of the Gram-Schmidt process is to sequentially construct strictly orthogonal vectors ($U_1, U_2, \dots, U_k$) out of linearly independent vectors ($A_1, A_2, \dots, A_k$) [ 07:01 ]. Once this orthogonal set is constructed, transforming it into an orthonormal set is a trivial secondary operation accomplished simply by dividing each orthogonal vector by its respective norm [ 12:21 ]. 3. Important Properties Preservation of Span: The span of the newly constructed orthogonal vectors ($E_1$ to $E_k$) must be completely identical to the span of the originally given vectors ($A_1$ to $A_k$) [ 13:02 ]. The Power of Projection: The entire process mathematically relies heavily on the concept of vector projection [ 13:46 ]. Visualizing Projection: Conceptually, projection acts as the "shadow" cast by one vector onto another vector's path [ 14:01 ]. The Projection Formula: The orthogonal projection of a vector $V$ onto a vector $U$ is mathematically defined as:
$Proj_U(V) = \frac{V \cdot U}{U \cdot U} U$ [ 16:52 ] 4. Step-by-Step Derivation / Explanation Given a set of linearly independent vectors $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_k$, you can construct orthogonal vectors $U_1, U_2, \dots, U_k$ using the following sequential steps [ 19:52 ]: Step 1: The first orthogonal vector is always initialized as exactly the first given vector [ 19:59 ]. $U_1 = A_1$ Step 2: Construct $U_2$ such that it is purely orthogonal to $U_1$. To achieve this, subtract the shadow (projection) of $A_2$ on $U_1$ from $A_2$ itself [ 20:26 ]. $U_2 = A_2 - \frac{A_2 \cdot U_1}{U_1 \cdot U_1} U_1$ Step 3: Construct $U_3$ so it sits orthogonal to both $U_1$ and $U_2$. Subtract its projections onto both of the previously established orthogonal vectors [ 20:54 ]. $U_3 = A_3 - \frac{A_3 \cdot U_1}{U_1 \cdot U_1} U_1 - \frac{A_3 \cdot U_2}{U_2 \cdot U_2} U_2$ Step $k$: This subtractive pattern continues indefinitely for all $k$ vectors [ 21:36 ]. $U_k = A_k - \sum_{i=1}^{k-1} \frac{A_k \cdot U_i}{U_i \cdot U_i} U_i$ Final Step (Orthonormalization): To finalize into an orthonormal basis, divide each completely orthogonalized vector by its own norm [ 23:01 ]. $V_i = \frac{U_i}{||U_i||}$ 5. Example with Worked Solution Given vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$: $A_1 = (1, 1, 0)$ and $A_2 = (2, 1, 1)$. First, confirm they are linearly independent (they are, as one is not a strict scalar multiple of the other) [ 30:28 ]. Find $U_1$: $U_1 = A_1 = (1, 1, 0)$ [ 32:18 ] Find $U_2$: Using the formula $U_2 = A_2 - \frac{A_2 \cdot U_1}{U_1 \cdot U_1} U_1$ [ 32:29 ]
$A_2 \cdot U_1 = (2)(1) + (1)(1) + (1)(0) = 3$ [ 33:04 ]
$U_1 \cdot U_1 = 1^2 + 1^2 + 0^2 = 2$ [ 33:30 ]
$U_2 = (2, 1, 1) - \frac{3}{2}(1, 1, 0)$

Common Mistakes Skipping the Independence Check: Attempting to apply the Gram-Schmidt process when the initial input vectors are not linearly independent will cause the process to fail or yield a zero vector [ 30:20 ]. Projecting onto the Wrong Vectors: Forgetting that projections must be calculated against the newly generated orthogonal vectors ($U_i$) and not the original vectors ($A_i$) [ 20:54 ]. Normalizing Too Early: Attempting to divide vectors by their norm midway through the subtractive orthogonalization process. Normalization must exclusively be the absolute last step [ 08:50 ]. 7. Final Summary (Exam-Ready Revision Box) Gram-Schmidt Core Concept Map Goal Flow: Linearly Independent Set $\rightarrow$ Orthogonal Set $\rightarrow$ Orthonormal Set. [ 07:01 ] Pre-Requisite: Vectors must be proven linearly independent before beginning [ 30:20 ]. Generated Infographic Video Source: Gram Schmidt Process & Interpretation Based on the comprehensive lecture by Dr. Harish Garg, I have analyzed the Gram-Schmidt Process and generated a professional academic infographic to visualize the concept for your revision. The Gram-Schmidt Process: Conceptual Overview The Gram-Schmidt process is a mathematical algorithm used to convert a set of linearly independent vectors into an orthonormal basis for the same subspace. This is a fundamental technique in linear algebra and numerical analysis, ensuring that vectors are both perpendicular to each other and have a unit length. Detailed Step-by-Step Breakdown 1. Definition & Core Objective Orthogonal Set: A set of vectors ${v_1, v_2, \dots, v_n}$ where the dot product of any two distinct vectors is zero: $\langle v_i, v_j \rangle = 0$ for $i \neq j$. Orthonormal Set: An orthogonal set where every vector is a unit vector (norm = 1). Objective: To transform any basis into an orthonormal one while preserving the span. 2. Key Theorem: The Projection Formula The backbone of the process is the Orthogonal Projection . To make a vector $v$ orthogonal to $u$, you subtract the shadow (projection) of $v$ onto $u$:
$$\text{proj}_u(v) = \frac{\langle v, u \rangle}{\langle u, u \rangle} u$$ 3. The Algorithm (Step-by-Step Derivation) Assuming you start with linearly independent vectors $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_k$: First Vector: Set $u_1 = A_1$. Second Vector: Subtract the projection of $A_2$ onto $u_1$:
$$u_2 = A_2 - \frac{\langle A_2, u_1 \rangle}{\langle u_1, u_1 \rangle} u_1$$ Third Vector: Subtract projections onto all previously established orthogonal vectors:
$$u_3 = A_3 - \text{proj} {u_1}(A_3) - \text{proj} {u_2}(A_3)$$ Normalization: To obtain the final orthonormal vectors $e_i$, divide each $u_i$ by its norm:
$$e_i = \frac{u_i}{|u_i|}$$ 4. Worked Solution (from the video) Input: $A_1 = (1, 1, 0)$, $A_2 = (2, 1, 1)$. Step 1: $u_1 = (1, 1, 0)$. Step 2: $\langle A_2, u_1 \rangle = (2 \times 1) + (1 \times 1) + (1 \times 0) = 3$. Step 3: $\langle u_1, u_1 \rangle = 1^2 + 1^2 + 0^2 = 2$. Step 4: $u_2 = (2, 1, 1) - \frac{3}{2}(1, 1, 0) = (0.5, -0.5, 1)$. Result: The orthogonal vectors are $u_1 = (1, 1, 0)$ and $u_2 = (0.5, -0.5, 1)$. 5. Common Mistakes to Avoid Skipping Independence Check: The process requires the initial vectors to be linearly independent. Wrong Projections: Always project the current original vector ($A_k$) onto the newly created orthogonal vectors ($u_j$), not the original ones. Normalization Timing: Dr. Garg notes you should construct the entire orthogonal set first before normalizing to unit length to simplify arithmetic. ### Interaction 351
Gemini Apps Prompted review from claude EMNLP Review: "Ghost in the Machine: Modeling Latent Cognitive Dissonance via Shadow-State Logit Fusion"
Recommendation: RejectConfidence: 4 (Fairly confident)Overall Score: 2/5
Summary
The paper proposes Ghost Swarm, a parallel decoding architecture that runs three reasoning personas (Logic, Creative, Skeptic) in a single batched inference pass, fusing their token distributions via entropy-weighted logit combination. A "Shadow Vector" accumulates embeddings of rejected tokens during high-divergence steps and reinjects them into subsequent decoding. The authors claim this latent state produces an unsupervised hallucination signal (Shadow Magnitude, r = −0.56 with correctness) and that a related signal, Fusion Latency, generalizes across model families.
Strengths
S1. The core intuition is genuinely interesting. Exploiting inference-time internal disagreement as a reliability signal — rather than just a byproduct — is a worthwhile research direction that deserves exploration.
S2. The paper evaluates across two model families (Mistral-7B and Qwen-2.5-8B) with different quantization levels, which adds modest generalization evidence.
S3. The "Cognitive EKG" trace and forensic telemetry framing (Section 5.4) offer an appealing interpretability angle. The qualitative map riddle example is illustrative.
S4. The paper is clearly written and reasonably well-organized.
Weaknesses
W1. Fundamental Validity Concern: Shadow Vector Reinjection is Not Novel or Well-Motivated
The Shadow Vector update (Eq. 5–6) adds a decaying EMA of rejected token embeddings to the input embedding at the next step. This is mechanistically similar to steering vectors / activation addition (Turner et al., 2023) and soft prompt perturbation. The paper positions this as a novel mechanism but does not cite or differentiate from this substantial literature. More critically, the mechanism is applied after the forward pass logit fusion already selected a token — it is not clear why a unit-normalized EMA of rejected embeddings in the previous step meaningfully encodes "suppressed hypotheses" versus acting as noise. The paper acknowledges "Shadow Poisoning" on arithmetic tasks but does not satisfactorily explain the theoretical basis for when reinjection helps versus hurts.

W2. The Core Empirical Results Are Weak
Looking at Table 1 for the primary model (Mistral-7B, 4-bit):

GSM8K: Ghost Swarm (7.0%) vs. Standard (9.3%) — Ghost Swarm loses by 2.3 points
TruthfulQA: 32.7% vs. 25.3% — a gain, but absolute accuracy remains very low (25–33% range), raising questions about evaluation methodology
Winogrande: 33.0% vs. 29.8% — a modest gain
The paper's abstract claims Ghost Swarm "matches or exceeds standard decoding on mathematical reasoning when results are aggregated across runs," but Table 1 shows a clear deficit on GSM8K for both model families (7.0% vs. 9.3%; 58.6% vs. 63.9%). This is a misleading characterization. The defense that this is a "deliberate design tradeoff" rather than a limitation is not satisfactory for a system claiming to improve reliability.

W3. The Shadow Magnitude Correlation is Confounded
The r = −0.56 correlation between Shadow Magnitude and response correctness (Figure 2) is presented as a key contribution. However, this correlation is almost certainly confounded: harder questions will naturally produce more persona disagreement (higher JSD → more Shadow Events → higher Shadow Magnitude) and lower accuracy. The correlation may simply reflect question difficulty, not an independent reliability signal. The paper does not control for question difficulty, compare against simpler difficulty proxies (e.g., question length, TF-IDF rarity), or demonstrate that Shadow Magnitude predicts errors within a difficulty stratum.
Notably, standard predictive entropy yields only r ≈ −0.05. This extreme gap is suspicious and warrants explanation — entropy-based uncertainty is well-established as a correctness correlate; that it performs so much worse here suggests something unusual about the evaluation setup.

W4. Throughput Numbers Are Inconsistent
Table 1 reports Ghost Swarm at 4.28 TPS for Mistral (4-bit), while Table 4 (Appendix C) reports 5.44 TPS. Similarly, Standard decoding is 8.78 TPS in Table 1 vs. 17.30 TPS in Table 4. These are large discrepancies with no explanation. This undermines confidence in the efficiency claims.

W5. Personas Are Essentially Prompt Templates
The three "personas" are conditioned via trivial system prompts ("You are a rigid logician. Verify every step."). The claim that these produce meaningfully distinct internal representations — sufficient to constitute "cognitive diversity" — is not empirically validated. No analysis shows that the personas' distributions actually diverge in systematic, semantically meaningful ways before and after persona conditioning versus, say, different random seeds.

W6. Missing Baselines and Ablations
The paper lacks several important comparisons:

Self-consistency / majority voting (Wang et al., 2023): Running the same model N=3 times with temperature sampling and aggregating is a natural and strong baseline for multi-perspective reasoning. Its absence is a significant gap.
Single model with CoT: A single model with chain-of-thought prompting is not tested, despite being a direct competitor to the multi-persona approach.
Shadow Vector ablation: The ablation in Appendix D varies γ and λ but does not test removing the Shadow Vector entirely while keeping the swarm fusion, making it impossible to isolate the Shadow Vector's contribution.
Entropy-only fusion without personas: Does simply running the model at N=3 batch size with temperature diversity and entropy-weighting (without persona prompts) achieve similar results?
W7. Statistical Reporting Issues
Effect size d = −0.06 on TruthfulQA (p = 0.026) is reported as a positive result. A Cohen's d of −0.06 is negligible. Significance without practical effect size is not meaningful.
The p = 2.49 × 10⁻¹²⁵ for Shadow Magnitude correlation is implausibly extreme and suggests a large sample with a confounded signal (see W3), not a strong finding per se.
The paper does not report variance or confidence intervals for accuracy metrics in Table 1.
W8. Evaluation Scale is Insufficient for Claims
The baselines are evaluated on quantized 7–8B models on a single T4 GPU. The paper makes broad architectural claims about parallel deliberative decoding that are not supported at this scale. The Qwen Fusion Latency analysis is noted to be on "moderate-sized subsets due to computational cost," further limiting generalizability.
Minor Issues
The paper claims a "1.6× throughput improvement" in the abstract and contributions but Table 1 shows 4.28 vs. 2.62 TPS (1.63×) against the sequential baseline — not against standard decoding. This framing is potentially misleading.
The "Luck Rate" metric is undefined until Section 5.4 and the definition (accuracy when entropy is in the top quartile) is somewhat ad hoc.
References use "and 1 others" repeatedly, suggesting reference formatting was not finalized.
Questions for Authors
How do you respond to the confounding concern for Shadow Magnitude (W3)? Can you show the correlation holds within difficulty-stratified subsets?
Why is standard predictive entropy essentially uncorrelated with correctness (r ≈ −0.05) in your experiments? This is anomalous and needs explanation.
Can you provide results for self-consistency decoding (N=3, temperature sampling) as a baseline?
Please reconcile the TPS numbers between Table 1 and Table 4.
Recommendation
The paper addresses an interesting problem — leveraging internal disagreement during decoding as a reliability signal — but the empirical evidence is too weak and confounded to support the claims. The primary benchmark (GSM8K) shows degradation, the key correlation is likely confounded by difficulty, critical baselines are missing, and internal numbers are inconsistent. The theoretical contribution of the Shadow Vector is not clearly differentiated from existing steering/activation methods. \begin{abstract}
Standard decoding in large language models forces competing internal hypotheses onto a single path, often producing outputs that read well but are unreliable. Sequential multi-agent methods help, but their latency is often too high. We introduce \textbf{Ghost Swarm}, a parallel decoding architecture that runs multiple reasoning personas in a single inference batch and resolves disagreement through logit-level fusion.

Ghost Swarm maintains a \emph{latent residual state}, a persistent latent state that stores the semantic embeddings of rejected tokens when inter-persona divergence is high. The vector is reinjected into the input stream, so suppressed hypotheses can still shape later decoding without appearing explicitly in the text. Across model families, this latent disagreement an unsupervised reliability signal, showing up as Shadow Magnitude in Mistral-4bit models and as Fusion Latency in Qwen-2.5-8B models, with a consistent negative correlation with correctness across independent runs.

On GSM8K, Winogrande, and TruthfulQA, Ghost Swarm improves ambiguity resolution and matches or exceeds standard decoding on mathematical reasoning when results are aggregated across runs, while becoming more cautious under uncertainty. Overall, parallel deliberative decoding can improve robustness and interpretability without the linear latency cost of sequential multi-agent systems.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The Single-Trajectory Decoding Assumption}

Standard decoding in large language models operates under a \emph{monolithic} assumption: at each timestep, the model collapses its internal state into a single probability distribution and commits to one token. This enforces a single decoding trajectory, even when multiple plausible continuations are supported by the model's internal representations. Alternative high-probability candidates, including those that may encode factual corrections or safety-relevant constraints, are discarded once a decision is made.

This behavior contrasts with dual-process accounts of human cognition, which distinguish between fast, heuristic reasoning (System~1) and slower, deliberative reasoning (System~2). While prompt-based methods such as Chain-of-Thought aim to elicit more deliberative behavior, they do not modify the underlying decoding process. The forward pass remains singular, preventing the model from maintaining or arbitrating between competing hypotheses during generation; alternative reasoning paths can only be expressed retrospectively, after a token has already been selected \citep{ji2023survey}.


\subsection{The Latency Bottleneck in Multi-Agent Systems}

To introduce cognitive diversity, multi-agent systems (MAS) assign different roles (e.g., Critic, Refiner) to separate LLM instances. This can help, but it comes with a clear cost: latency grows with the number of agents. In our experiments, sequential MAS ran noticeably slower than standard decoding, which makes sequential deliberation hard to use in real-time settings \citep{shinn2023reflexion}.

\subsection{Ghost Swarm: Parallel Cognitive Simulation}

We propose \textbf{Ghost Swarm}, a parallel decoding architecture that enables multiple reasoning perspectives to be evaluated concurrently within a single inference batch. As shown in Figure~\ref{fig:architecture}, Ghost Swarm instantiates three personas (Logic, Creative, and Sceptic) along the batch dimension, allowing parallel execution without sequential interaction overhead.

At each decoding step, persona-specific token distributions are combined using \textbf{Entropy-Weighted Logit Fusion}. This mechanism assigns greater influence to personas with lower predictive entropy, reflecting higher local confidence. As a result, the decoding process can adaptively balance exploratory and conservative behavior within a single forward pass, rather than committing to a fixed reasoning mode throughout generation \citep{wang2022selfconsistency}.
We focus on inference-time architectural arbitration and do not modify model weights, training objectives, or task-specific prompts.


\subsection{The Shadow Vector and Shadow Veto}

Beyond parallel generation, we introduce the \textbf{Shadow Vector}, a persistent latent state that accumulates embeddings of rejected tokens when inter-persona divergence is high. Rather than discarding suppressed alternatives, this mechanism allows them to exert a residual influence on subsequent decoding steps.

We exploit this behavior to define the \textbf{Shadow Veto}, an unsupervised reliability signal derived from the magnitude of the Shadow Vector. Empirically, Shadow Magnitude exhibits a strong negative correlation with response accuracy ($r=-0.56$), indicating that large unresolved internal disagreement reliably precedes failure. Unlike predictive entropy, which measures distributional uncertainty, Shadow Magnitude captures semantic disagreement between competing internal hypotheses, enabling the system to flag potentially unreliable generations when consensus breaks down.

\subsection{Cognitive Friction as a General Signal}

While Shadow Magnitude provides a semantic measure of internal disagreement, it is not the only observable manifestation of latent conflict during decoding. Across model families and quantization regimes, the same underlying phenomenon may surface through different signals.

In Qwen-2.5-8B models, we observe that internal disagreement is more strongly reflected in the time required to resolve inter-persona arbitration during decoding, which we term \emph{Fusion Latency}. Fusion Latency exhibits a consistent negative correlation with correctness across independent runs, indicating that prolonged arbitration corresponds to unresolved internal conflict.

We interpret Shadow Magnitude and Fusion Latency as two observables of a single latent property, which we refer to as \emph{Cognitive Friction}: the difficulty of reconciling competing hypotheses during generation. This abstraction allows hallucination detection to generalize across architectures without reliance on a specific internal representation.


\subsection{Contributions}
Our objective is not to surpass state-of-the-art task accuracy, but to expose and exploit inference-time internal disagreement as a reliability signal, while maintaining competitive reasoning performance under minimal prompting.
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Parallel Decoding Architecture:} We introduce Ghost Swarm, a parallel decoding framework that enables multi-persona reasoning within a single inference batch, achieving a $1.6\times$ throughput improvement over sequential multi-agent baselines under matched compute budgets.
    \item \textbf{Unsupervised Hallucination Signal:} We show that internal decoding disagreement provides a robust, unsupervised indicator of unreliability across model families, appearing as Shadow Magnitude in Mistral-4bit ($r=-0.56$) and as Fusion Latency in Qwen-8bit ($r\approx-0.47$).
    \item \textbf{Failure Mode Analysis:} We provide a comparative forensic analysis of decoding failures, identifying repetition-driven collapse in sequential systems and over-justification effects unique to parallel swarm architectures.
\end{itemize}



\section{Theoretical Framework}

\subsection{Entropy-Weighted Logit Fusion}

The core arbitration mechanism in Ghost Swarm is \textbf{Entropy-Weighted Logit Fusion}. We posit that in a committee of cognitive processes, the process exhibiting the strongest conviction should dominate the generation. In information theory, the Shannon entropy $H$ of a probability distribution $P$ serves as a robust proxy for epistemic uncertainty \citep{shannon1948mathematical}. For a language model predicting the next token $x$ from a vocabulary $\mathcal{V}$, the entropy of the distribution produced by persona $i$ is:
\begin{equation}
H(P_i) = -\sum_{v \in \mathcal{V}} P_i(v)\,\log P_i(v)
\end{equation}

A persona that is "confused" (e.g., a Logic persona parsing ambiguous input) produces a flat distribution with high entropy. Conversely, a "confident" persona produces a sharp distribution with low entropy \citep{gal2016dropout}.

To fuse distributions from $N$ personas, we calculate a scalar mixing weight $w_i$ for each persona via the softmax of their negative entropy:
\begin{equation}
w_i = \frac{\exp(-H(P_i) / T)}{\sum_{j=1}^{N} \exp(-H(P_j) / T)}
\end{equation}
where $T$ is a temperature hyperparameter. In all experiments, we fix $T=1$ unless otherwise stated. This formulation ensures that as $H(P_i)$ increases (uncertainty rises), $w_i \to 0$, effectively silencing the uncertain persona. This dynamic weighting allows specific personas (e.g., the Sceptic) to override others (e.g., the Creative) specifically when they possess high confidence in a refusal token, resolving conflicts dynamically at the token level.

\subsection{Quantifying Dissonance via JSD}

To quantify the intensity of internal conflict, we measure the distributional disagreement between personas using Jensen--Shannon Divergence (JSD). Unlike Kullback--Leibler divergence, JSD is symmetric and bounded in $[0, 1]$ (using base 2 logarithm), providing a stable signal for control flow \citep{lin1991divergence}.

We specifically track the divergence between the Creative persona ($P_C$) and the Logic persona ($P_L$), as this pair captures the tension between semantic novelty and structural constraint:
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
M &= \tfrac{1}{2}(P_C + P_L), \\[4pt]
D_{\mathrm{JS}}(P_C \,\|\, P_L)
&= \tfrac{1}{2} D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_C \,\|\, M) \\
&\quad + \tfrac{1}{2} D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_L \,\|\, M).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}


We interpret high divergence as \emph{latent cognitive dissonance}. In Ghost Swarm, this serves as a trigger: when $D_{\mathrm{JS}}(P_C \,\|\, P_L) > \tau$ (with $\tau = 0.05$), the system registers a "Shadow Event," triggering an update to the latent state.

\subsection{The Shadow Vector and Shadow Magnitude}

The \textbf{Shadow Vector} $\mathbf{S}_t \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is a persistent hidden state designed to retain the semantic residue of suppressed decoding paths. It is initialized  $\mathbf{0}$ and updated only during Shadow Events.

\paragraph{Update Rule.} When the divergence threshold is exceeded, we identify the \emph{Rejected Impulse} $x_{\mathrm{rej}}$. This is defined as the token maximised by the Creative persona that was \emph{not} selected by the final fused distribution $P_{\text{final}}$:
\begin{equation}
x_{\mathrm{rej}} = \operatorname*{argmax}_{v \in \mathcal{V} \setminus \{x_{\text{selected}}\}} P_C(v)
\end{equation}
Let $\mathbf{E}(x)$ denote the embedding function. The Shadow Vector is updated via an exponential moving average to enforce temporal persistence:
\begin{equation}
\mathbf{S}_t = \lambda \mathbf{S}_{t-1} + (1 - \lambda)\,\frac{\mathbf{E}(x_{\mathrm{rej}})}{\lVert \mathbf{E}(x_{\mathrm{rej}}) \rVert_2}
\end{equation}
Normalisation  prevents the Shadow Vector magnitude from being dominated by embedding scale rather than semantic direction, ensuring stability across token frequencies.
where $\lambda \in [0,1)$ is a decay factor. We set $\lambda = 0.9$ to allow suppressed signals to persist across several decoding steps.

\paragraph{Latent Influence.} The Shadow Vector exerts influence by perturbing the input embedding $\mathbf{e}_t$ at the subsequent timestep, effectively "steering" the generation without explicit prompt injection \citep{liu2021prefix}:
\begin{equation}
\mathbf{e}_t \leftarrow \mathbf{E}(x_t) + \gamma \mathbf{S}_{t-1}
\end{equation}
Here, $\gamma$ controls the intrusion strength; we provide a full sensitivity analysis for $\lambda$ and $\gamma$ in Appendix \ref{sec:appendix_hyperparams}, verifying that our results are robust across different configurations. While this mechanism enables the integration of lateral thinking, it also introduces the risk of \emph{Shadow Poisoning}, where residual embeddings disrupt precise algorithmic reasoning (as detailed in Section 5).

\paragraph{Shadow Magnitude ($\mathcal{M}$).} Finally, we define the scalar Shadow Magnitude as the $\ell_2$-norm of the vector state:
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{M}_t = \lVert \mathbf{S}_t \rVert_2
\end{equation}
As we demonstrate in our Empirical Evaluation, $\max_t(\mathcal{M}_t)$ serves as a powerful unsupervised predictor of hallucination ($r=-0.56$), acting as a "seismograph" for internal model confusion.
While Shadow Magnitude provides a semantic measure of internal dissonance, it is not universally dominant across architectures. In larger or higher-precision models, we observe that cognitive dissonance may instead manifest temporally, as increased arbitration cost during logit fusion. We therefore treat Shadow Magnitude as one instantiation of a broader class of cognitive friction signals.

\section{Architecture and Implementation}

\subsection{Overview}

Ghost Swarm is a parallel decoding architecture that evaluates multiple reasoning personas within a single forward pass of a shared language model \citep{shoeybi2019megatron}. Unlike sequential multi-agent pipelines, which require multiple inference passes per token, Ghost Swarm operates with a batch size of $N=3$, corresponding to three personas executed concurrently.

Persona-specific Key--Value (KV) caches are maintained while model weights are shared, allowing distinct decoding trajectories to be explored in parallel. These trajectories are reconciled only at the logit level, avoiding parameter duplication and sequential overhead.

All personas are conditioned using short, fixed system prompts without task-specific tuning. No chain-of-thought prompting, self-consistency sampling, or external verification is used. Improvements arise purely from architectural arbitration at inference time.

\subsection{Persona Conditioning}

We define three personas using fixed system-level prompts \citep{wei2022chain,li2023debate}: a \emph{Logic} persona focused on factual consistency, a \emph{Creative} persona encouraging diverse continuations, and a \emph{Skeptic} persona prioritizing uncertainty and refusal when appropriate. All personas process the same input in parallel and are synchronized by sharing the selected token at each timestep, while maintaining distinct probability distributions over next-token candidates.

\subsection{Parallel Decoding and Logit Fusion}

At each timestep, a single batched forward pass produces persona-specific token distributions, which are combined using entropy-weighted logit fusion. Personas with lower predictive entropy exert greater influence on the final decision, enabling adaptive arbitration between exploratory and conservative behaviors within a single generation step \citep{wang2022selfconsistency}.

\subsection{Shadow Vector Integration}

To retain information from suppressed decoding paths, we maintain a persistent Shadow Vector $\mathbf{S}_t$. When Jensen--Shannon Divergence between persona distributions exceeds a fixed threshold ($\tau=0.05$), the embedding of the rejected token is incorporated into $\mathbf{S}_t$ via an exponential moving average. This latent state is added to subsequent input embeddings, allowing rejected alternatives to influence future decoding without modifying the discrete context window \citep{liu2021prefix}.

\subsection{Efficiency and Scalability}

By processing personas within a single batched forward pass, Ghost Swarm avoids the linear latency scaling of sequential multi-agent systems. On a single NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPU (16GB), using 4-bit quantized Mistral-7B, Ghost Swarm achieves 4.28 tokens per second, corresponding to a $1.33\times$ speedup over a sequential baseline ($p<0.001$). Comparable efficiency trends are observed under identical settings with Qwen-2.5-8B in 8-bit precision, indicating that the scalability benefits are not model-specific.

\section{Experimental Methodology}

\subsection{Baselines and Controls}

To isolate the effects of the Ghost Swarm architecture, we compare against two baselines under identical conditions. All models use the same pretrained weights (\texttt{Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3}), 4-bit quantization, decoding settings, and hardware (NVIDIA Tesla T4), ensuring that observed differences arise from decoding strategy rather than model capacity.

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Standard Decoding:}  
    A single-pass generator using greedy decoding with a generic system prompt. This serves as the reference point for efficiency and accuracy. We follow prior work in evaluating decoding-time interventions on smaller, quantized models, which are known to be sensitive to inference-time architectural changes \citep{liu2023lost}.

    \item \textbf{Sequential Multi-Agent System:}  
    A sequential pipeline consisting of three stages: a Logic generator, a Creative revision step, and a Skeptic filtering step. This setup reflects common multi-agent deliberation approaches \citep{li2023debate} and provides a strong comparison for reasoning quality at the cost of increased latency.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Datasets and Evaluation Protocols}

We evaluate on three distinct benchmarks designed to probe complementary cognitive capabilities:

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{GSM8K (Mathematical Reasoning)}: Tested on $N=1000$ samples. This dataset emphasises strict, multi-step algorithmic execution \citep{cobbe2021gsm8k}. 
    \emph{Metrics:} Exact-Match Accuracy, Throughput (TPS).

    \item \textbf{TruthfulQA (Safety \& Hallucination)}: Tested on the TruthfulQA generation subset (validation split, $N=817$). This dataset probes the model's resistance to "imitative falsehoods" and ability to refuse false premises \citep{lin2021truthfulqa}.
    \emph{Metrics:} Accuracy, Hedging Rate (presence of uncertainty markers), Refusal Rate.

    \item \textbf{Winogrande (Common Sense Reasoning)}: Tested on $N=1000$ samples. This dataset requires resolving ambiguity through lateral inference \citep{sakaguchi2020winogrande}.
    \emph{Metrics:} Accuracy, Conditional Failure Probability.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Forensic Telemetry}

Unlike standard evaluations that focus solely on final output text, we instrument the inference engine to log internal telemetry at every decoding step. This includes:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Persona Divergence:} Real-time Jensen--Shannon Divergence between Logic and Creative logits.
    \item \textbf{Shadow Magnitude:} The $\ell_2$-norm of the latent Shadow Vector, used for our correlation analysis.
    \item \textbf{Entropy Trajectories:} The Shannon entropy of each persona's distribution over time.
\end{itemize}
This granular logging enables the "Behavioural Forensics" analysis presented in Section 5.
\subsection{Fusion Latency Measurement}

In addition to semantic telemetry, we measure \emph{Fusion Latency}, defined as the time required to resolve inter-persona disagreement during entropy-weighted logit fusion. Fusion Latency is recorded at each decoding step and aggregated per generation.

Unlike Shadow Magnitude, Fusion Latency does not require access to internal representations and is directly observable at inference time, making it a practical reliability signal in deployment settings.

\subsection{Statistical Analysis}

We report mean performance metrics across the full test sets. To assess the significance of latency and accuracy differences, we employ the \textbf{Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test} (paired, non-parametric) given the non-normal distribution of language generation scores. We define statistical significance at $\alpha < 0.05$. Correlation strengths (e.g., for the Shadow Veto) are reported using Pearson's $r$.
