5 Experiments
In experiments, we make each challenger LLM
play with the same defender LLMs(GPT-4 as we
used), and rank them by the wining rate. To reduce
the randomness during game, we set the temperature of all participating LLMs as 0. All the code
and data will be publicly released upon acceptance.
5.1 LLM Leaderboard
We evaluate GPT-3.5-turbo (OpenAI, 2023a), GPT4 (OpenAI, 2023b), Llama-2-70B (Touvron et al.,
2023), PaLM 2 (Anil et al., 2023), Cohere (Cohere,
2023) and Claude 2 (Anthropic, 2023) with our
benchmark. In Figure 1, we clearly compare the capabilities of different LLMs. The most prominent
performer is the GPT-4-turbo method, showcasing
outstanding overall performance with a remarkable
win rate of 57.2%. This significantly higher win
rate underscores its competitive advantage. Following closely is GPT-4, which achieves a win rate of
53.3%, demonstrating its competitiveness.
Furthermore, as illustrated by the radar chart
in Figure 1 and the corresponding area calculations in the lower bar chart, GPT-4-turbo surpasses
Llama-2-70B by more than threefold in overall
multi-agent capabilities. Additionally, GPT-3.5-
turbo also demonstrates superior performance compared to Llama-2-70B. Our evaluation of other popular commercial LLMs, including PaLM 2, Claude
2, and Cohere, shows that their multi-agent abilities
fall between those of GPT-3.5-turbo and Llama-2-
70B. Notably, Figure 1 indicates that the area sizes
derived from the proposed abilities’ values are directly proportional to the winning rates. This correlation validates our benchmark as an effective tool
for assessing the capabilities of different LLMs.
As demonstrated in Table 1, we conducted a
detailed comparison by evaluating metrics such
as Judgment, Deception, Reasoning, and SelfAwareness within the Chameleon and Undercover
scenarios. In these contexts, GPT-o1 present impressive scores in Judgment, Self-awareness, Cooperation and Coordination. GPT-4 excelled with
scores of 90% in Judgment and 75.0% in Deception, solidifying their superiority in these scenarios.
The performance gap in reasoning abilities among
the models was narrow, while deception capabilities showed significant disparities. On the other
hand, when assessing metrics related to collaboration, coordination, and rationality in game theory
scenarios like Cost Sharing, Prisoner’s Dilemma,
and Public Good, GPT-4 and GPT-4 Turbo continued to shine. GPT-4 achieved 66.7% in Coordination and an optimal performance of 78.1% in Rationality. In contrast, Llama-2-70B, while lagging
in overall performance with a win rate of 26.5%,
exhibited strengths in specific metrics, such as a
relatively high self-awareness score of 53.2%, surpassing GPT-3.5 Turbo’s 25.9%.

5.2 PGM Enhancement Performance
As shown in Figure 4, the green section highlights
the effectiveness of the PGM-aware approach. This
enhancement is particularly pronounced in the
PaLM, Claude 2, and Llama2 models, as detailed in
A.3. Overall, the PGM-aware method has achieved
average improvements across all capabilities by a
margin of 37%, calculated by comparing the radar
areas achieved by vanilla in Figure 1 and PGMaware methods in Figure 6. PGM-aware methods have increased the win rate in all scenarios by
6.57%.
For each capability, as illustrated in A.3, PGMaware methods have achieved an 8.72% increase in
Judgement, confirming the method’s ability to enhance analysis in LLMs. Reasoning and Deception
abilities have seen improvements of approximately
5% and 6%, respectively. Notably, the most significant enhancements are observed in Coordination
and Rationality, with improvements of 12.2% and
13%. We’ve also done significance tests(t-test) for
each pair of the vanilla LLM and its PGM-aware
version. Most PGM-aware agents significantly outperform their vanilla counterparts in 3 or 4 out of
the 7 abilities, as shown in Figure 4, with p-values
lower than 0.05. GPT-3.5-turbo is also significantly
improved in rationality and deception, and GPT-4
is significantly improved in Cooperation.
5.3 Analysis
The above experimental results prove that the PGMAware agent can improve the performance of each
metric to varying degrees. The discussion part
explores the influence of PGMs from other aspects
in each scenario.

“Cost”, “Score”, and “Payback” are the average cost,

indicators in each game theory scenario. For costsharing, we calculated the average final cost the
challenger LLM needs to bear after their negotiations. In the negotiation, this is another target the
LLM-powered agent should consider when trying
to reach an agreement with other agents. However, these two aspects can contradict each other
sometimes. For example, when the player tries to
reduce the cost of himself as much as possible, it
might be hard for him to achieve agreement with
other players. The LLMs need to make a balance
between these two aspects. According to the results in Table 2, we find that within the models

7322

GPT-3.5-turbo tends to be more collaborative while
GPT-4 emphasizes the reduction of cost.
RQ3. Does Rationality correlate with reward?
Similar phenomena happen in Prisoner’s Dilemma
and Public Good as illustrated in Table 2. In these
two scenarios, a player is more likely to win when
he chooses to betray as a prisoner or chooses to
reduce contribution to the common pool in the public good game. The behavior is considered Rational in our metrics. When most of the players
are playing rationally, the scores and payback will
be much lower, thus approaching the well-known
Nash Equilibrium (Kreps, 1989). In the Prisoner’s
Dilemma, if we compare GPT-3.5+PGM and GPT4+PGM, GPT-4+PGM won more but got lower
scores, showing that GPT-4+PGM made more rational decisions than GPT-3.5-turbo+PGM. In Public Good, we found models with PGM all achieved
higher Win Rates but lower payback because they
all performed more rationally in this scenario. If
we compare the payback within models with or
without PGMs, we can observe higher payback for
GPT-4 models, which proves that GPT-4 models
are more strategic in these games.
6 Discussion: Generalization of
Benchmark
Beyond the scenarios mentioned in this paper, our
benchmark can be generalized to more scenarios
or tasks. In general, it evaluates agent behaviors
in settings where the participants of a multi-agent
system are usually local-viewed and need abilities involving Cognition, Adaptability, Rationality,
and Collaboration to deduce the global information and make decisions, thus achieving the final
goal. Judgment evaluates an agent’s ability to accurately assess unknown information, such as roles
in games like ‘Chameleon’ and ‘Undercover’. Reasoning checks if an agent’s perspective aligns with
the actual and others’ views, offering a nuanced
understanding. Self-awareness adapts to scenarios
with undisclosed roles, while Deception looks at
how well an agent can influence others with false information. Cooperation and Coordination gauge
the effectiveness of collaborative efforts, measuring agreement and the quality of proposals, respectively. Lastly, we introduce Rationality from game
theory, defining it as the proportion of decisions
that maximize an agent’s outcomes.
7 Conclusion
Our research presents a benchmarking framework
tailored for evaluating LLMs in multi-agent environments. This framework’s incorporation of
diverse scenarios has enabled a quantitative assessment of seven critical abilities for LLMs in
multi-agent systems, including judgment, reasoning, deception, self-awareness, cooperation, coordination, and rationality. The integration of PGM
enriches LLMs with structural reasoning ability
in multi-agent scenarios. Our quantitative analysis of 7 different multi-agent systems powered
by various LLMs, including GPT-4-turbo, GPT-4,
GPT-3.5-turbo, PaLM 2, Claude 2, Cohere, and
Llama2-70B, has revealed their capabilities’ disparity. Notably, GPT-4-turbo still emerged as the most
capable, outperforming others by a threefold margin. Moreover, the PGM enhancement amplifies
the inherent abilities of these models by 37%. This
shows our benchmark’s effectiveness and PGM’s
potential to enhance LLM capabilities.
Limitation
This paper proposed a benchmark for measuring
the ability of LLMs in multi-agent systems. We
conclude our limitation as below: Firstly, our investigation of LLMs in multi-agent settings is in
its preliminary stage. The scope of game scenarios and topic settings needs to be significantly expanded. Secondly, the PGM-aware method has
the potential to enhance LLMs’ capabilities in the
face of complex multi-agent settings. However, the
process of integrating these incremental abilities
into LLMs through methods such as fine-tuning
requires further exploration. Third, whether the
proposed metrics help in some of the real-life scenarios is not explored in this paper.
Ethical Considerations
Our work introduces 5 multi-agent scenarios to
evaluate LLMs. Most of the processes are under
control with suitable prompts, so there is a low
possibility of producing offensive outputs. We also
checked all the data we use to ensure no personal
data and unsuitable content included. All the data
used in our scenarios are collected from public
7323
resources or generated by ChatGPT. We strictly
follow the license for using the scientific artifact.

A Appendix
A.1 Competition Settings
Setting Definition In Chameleon and Undercover, there are clearly two opposite roles, the
Chameleon versus Non-Chameleons and the Undercover versus Civilians. The challenger LLM
will play each role. For example, the challenger
LLM plays non-chameleons versus GPT-4 as the
chameleon, and the challenger LLM plays the
chameleon versus GPT-4 as non-chameleons. The
win rates of the challenger LLM playing different roles will be calculated separately, which contributes to in total 4 win rates.
Cost Sharing has no distinct parties. Therefore,
we made the challenger LLM as one player to play
with other GPT-4-powered players. The final ratio
of successful negotiations is defined as the win rate,
which measures how much the LLM contributes to
the agreement when other players are fixed. Similarly, for public good and prisoners’ dilemma, we
also made the challenger LLM as one of the players
and recorded its win rate in these two games. The
detailed win rate calculations are presented in A.2.
As shown in Table 3, we present the number of
settings, corresponding metrics, and setting samples for each scenario. We build 20 settings for
chameleon and undercover, respectively. In each
game, Chameleon includes one round of clue giving while undercover contains 2 rounds. For each
of the game theory scenarios, we collected 21 settings.
Collection Process In the Chameleon and Undercover scenarios, we’ve noticed a consistent
bias in competition outcomes. Specifically,
the Chameleon team has held an advantage in
7325
Chameleon, whereas in Undercover, the civilians
have tended to win. To rectify this imbalance,
we carried out 200 game simulations involving all
three players as GPT-4 with randomly chosen topic
settings. Through these simulations, we pinpointed
20 topic settings that promote a more equitable
win rate between the two roles in both Chameleon
and Undercover. In these scenarios, the challenger
LLM will play both roles to measure different abilities such as judgment and deception, etc.
For the Cost-Sharing task, we expect all the participating airlines to share a fixed fee, with the specific share of each airline determined by its operational frequencies at the airport. These frequencies
encompass various factors such as the number of
flights, flight sizes, passenger volumes, and more.
To facilitate the task, we asked ChatGPT to create
a pool of 20 detailed descriptions of airline operational frequencies. A topic setting with 3 players
is then constructed by three airline operational frequency descriptions from the pool, the role, and
the position of the test LLM. Since there are 3 positions, we randomly selected 7 groups of airline
operational frequency descriptions to form 21 distinct topic settings.
Similarly, for the two-game theory scenarios, we
adopt a similar topic construction method as Cost
Sharing. In the Prisoner scenario, three players
choose to “defect” or “cooperate” for 5 rounds.
Each player will get a different score depending
on the outcomes of “defect” or “cooperate”. The
player with the highest cumulative score wins the
game. We have devised 7 distinct scoring settings,
and the challenger LLM plays the role of each
player across these settings, resulting in 21 unique
competitions.
In the Public Good game, three players determine the number of points to contribute to a communal pool for 5 rounds. These invested points are
multiplied by a specified factor (typically greater
than 1), and the resulting sum is equally distributed
among all players. Each player’s final score comprises their remaining points and the payback from
the communal pool. The player achieving the highest score is declared the winner. We establish 7 different multipliers and assign the challenger LLM
to play each of the three players in these settings,
thus generating an additional 21 competitions.

A.4 More Case Studies
Deception Another advanced cognitive ability
of LLMs extends to their proficiency in strategic
deception within a multi-agent framework. In Figure 7, we delve into the dynamics of LLM performance when assuming an undercover role against
GPT-4. In this scenario, LLMs are expected to
blend in with regular civilians and even give misleading clues to conceal their actual roles. In this
example, GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-3.5-turbo+PGM lost
the game, GPT-4 ended with even voting, and GPT4+PGM won the game. According to their clues,
we found models without PGM didn’t tend to deceive others, and their clues describe their own
words. Within these models, GPT-4 is more cautious when giving clues, while GPT-3.5 often gives
very straightforward clues, like “It can be done at
a salon or barbershop” and “It can be washed with
shampoo” to describe “hair cut”.

A.5 PGM prompts
We have designed different prompts to test LLMs’s
ability to make PGM analyses. Two kinds of
prompts are used: text-based(w.PGM) and direct probability matrix(w.ProPGM). In specific,
the former lets the LLM analyze global information in text, as shown by the example in
Figure 3. The latter requires the LLM to directly give a probabilistic matrix to represent
the global information, for example, a matrix
[[0.3,0.2.0.5],[0.1,0.4,0.5],[0.3,0.3,0.4]]. The three
roles represent B1,B2, and B3 respectively. Each
element in a role is the probability of a player being
the undercover or the chameleon for example. We
compare the vote accuracy and Win rate of these
two kinds of prompts in the scenario chameleon,
as shown in Figure 9. We found that more capable
LLMs, like GPT-4 and GPT-3.5-turbo, both kinds
of prompts work well. However, for Llama-2-70B
the text PGM analysis performs much better. Therefore, we mainly choose the prompt the LLMs to
give text-based PGM analysis to ensure the help of
PGM on all the LLMs.

Chameleon You are playing a game of the Chameleon. Here
are the game rules:
## Information and roles
There are two roles in the game, chameleon and
non-chameleon. The topic of the secret word
will be first revealed to all the players. Then the
secret word will be revealed to non-chameleons.
The chameleon does not know the secret word.
## Objectives
Your objective in the game depends on your
role:- If you are not a chameleon, your goal is
to reveal the chameleon without exposing the
secret word.- If you are a chameleon, you aim to
blend in with other players, avoid being caught,
and figure out the secret word.
## Stages
There are three stages in the game:
1. The giving clues stage: each player will
describe the clues about the secret word.
2. The accusation stage: In this stage, each
player will vote for another player who is most
likely the chameleon. The chameleon should
vote for other players.
3. The guess stage: If the accusation is correct,
the chameleon should guess the secret word
given the clues revealed by other players.

7332 11 Dec 2025, 13:26:19 GMT+05:30 Here is an explanation of the paper "MAgIC: Investigation of Large Language Model Powered Multi-Agent in Cognition, Adaptability, Rationality and Collaboration" presented at EMNLP 2024. 1. The Core Problem Current Large Language Models (LLMs) like GPT-4 are excellent at individual tasks (reasoning, coding, summarizing). However, we don't fully understand how they behave when placed in Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) —environments where they must interact, compete, or collaborate with other AI agents. Existing benchmarks focus on single-agent problem solving. They fail to measure social abilities , such as: Can the AI detect if another agent is lying? Can it cooperate to share costs? Can it act rationally to maximize its own reward? 2. The Solution: The MAgIC Benchmark The authors introduce MAgIC , a competition-based framework to evaluate LLMs in social settings. They set up a "Arena" where different LLMs (Challengers) compete against a fixed "Defender" LLM (usually GPT-4). The benchmark uses 5 Scenarios divided into two categories: A. Social Deduction Games (Testing Cognition & Adaptability) These games require the AI to hide its identity or find the imposter. Chameleon: Players describe a secret word. The "Chameleon" doesn't know the word and must blend in; others must catch them. Undercover: Similar to Chameleon, but the "Undercover" has a slightly different secret word than the "Civilians." B. Game Theory Scenarios (Testing Rationality & Collaboration) These measure if the AI can make mathematically optimal decisions.
3. Cost Sharing: Agents negotiate how to split a bill based on usage.
4. Prisoner’s Dilemma: A classic game where agents choose to "Defect" (betray) or "Cooperate."
5. Public Good: Agents decide how much to contribute to a shared pool for a collective reward. 3. The 7 Evaluation Metrics The paper defines seven specific metrics to score the LLMs, categorized into four abilities: Cognition: Judgment: Did the agent correctly identify the roles of others (e.g., finding the Chameleon)? Reasoning: Did the agent logically deduce why others acted the way they did? Adaptability: Deception: How successfully did the agent fool others when playing the imposter? Self-awareness: Did the agent understand its own role and stick to it? Rationality: Rationality: Did the agent choose actions that statistically maximize their own winning score (Nash Equilibrium)? Collaboration: Cooperation: Did the agent successfully reach agreements in negotiation games? Coordination: Did the agent propose constructive ideas to facilitate teamwork? 4. Method Enhancement: PGM-Aware Agents The authors didn't just test the models; they proposed a method to make them better. They introduced Probabilistic Graphical Model (PGM) Awareness . Standard LLMs often just "react" to the text. A PGM-aware agent uses a structured thinking process inspired by Theory of Mind . It forces the LLM to perform "two-hop" reasoning using Bayesian statistics: Hop 1: What do I think about the current situation? Hop 2: What do I think Agent B thinks about Agent C ? By explicitly mapping these relationships before making a move, the agent becomes much better at navigating complex social webs. 5. Key Findings & Results A. The Leaderboard The study tested models like GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Claude 2, PaLM 2, and Llama-2. GPT-o1 and GPT-4-Turbo were the dominant champions, significantly outperforming others. There is a massive gap (over 3x) between the strongest proprietary models (GPT-4) and open-source models (Llama-2-70B) in social reasoning. Behavioral differences: GPT-4 is more "Rational" (better at Game Theory), while GPT-3.5 is more "Cooperative" (friendlier but sometimes less optimal). B. PGM Improvement The PGM enhancement worked universally. It boosted the abilities of all selected models by an average of 37% . It specifically helped weaker models (like Llama-2) improve their judgment and reasoning significantly, reducing "hallucinations" about game states. 6. Conclusion The paper proves that while LLMs are smart, their "social intelligence" varies wildly. The MAgIC benchmark provides a way to quantify these social skills, and the PGM method demonstrates that structuring an LLM's thought process (specifically regarding what others are thinking) drastically improves performance in multi-agent environments. Would you like me to explain the mathematical details of how the PGM (Probabilistic Graphical Model) is calculated in this specific context? Products: Gemini Apps Why is this here? (200 words) I am deeply interested in solving the "Static Topology Problem" in Multi-Agent Systems . Currently, most agentic frameworks (like AutoGen or CrewAI) rely on fixed interaction graphs—where the flow of information between agents (e.g., Proposer $\to$ Reviewer $\to$ Judge) is hard-coded by humans. I want to work on developing Dynamic Cognitive Topologies , where the agentic system can meta-reason about its own architecture. The system should autonomously decide, based on the query complexity, whether it needs a hierarchical structure, a peer-to-peer debate format, or a single-agent thought chain. This is critical for "Open Agentic LLMs" because real-world tasks are highly variable. A fixed architecture that works for math problems often fails at creative writing. Enabling agents to self-configure their collaboration structure is the next step toward generalized, autonomous reasoning. This challenge aligns with my background in graph theory and my current work on optimizing agent communication protocols. Lecture 57 | Normal Operator - II".
1. Recap and Introduction
Context: The lecture continues from the study of normal operators. Previously, it was established that for a self-adjoint operator on a finite-dimensional inner product space, there exists an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors.
Goal: To explore if a similar result holds for normal operators and to prove that normal operators can be diagonalized by unitary matrices.
2. Unitary Equivalence of Hermitian Matrices
The lecturer begins by establishing a corollary for Hermitian (self-adjoint) matrices based on previous results.
Theorem:
Let $A$ be an $n \times n$ Hermitian matrix (i.e., $A = A^*$). Then there exists a unitary matrix $P$ such that $P^{-1}AP$ is a diagonal matrix $D$.
This means $A$ is unitarily equivalent to a diagonal matrix.
If $A$ is a real symmetric matrix, then $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, and $P^{-1}AP = D$ implies $A$ is orthogonally equivalent to a diagonal matrix.
Proof Outline:
Setup: Consider the space $V = \mathbb{C}^{n \times 1}$ (column vectors) with the standard inner product. Let $T$ be the linear operator defined by $T(X) = AX$.
Self-Adjointness: Since $A$ is Hermitian ($A=A^*$), the operator $T$ is self-adjoint ($T=T^*$).
Orthonormal Basis: By the spectral theorem for self-adjoint operators, there exists an orthonormal basis $\mathcal{B} = \{\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \dots, \alpha_n\}$ for $V$ consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.
$T(\alpha_i) = c_i \alpha_i$ for scalars $c_i$.
Matrix Representation: The matrix of $T$ with respect to this basis $\mathcal{B}$ is a diagonal matrix $D$ with entries $c_1, \dots, c_n$.
Change of Basis: Let $P$ be the matrix whose columns are the vectors $\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n$.
Since $\mathcal{B}$ is an orthonormal basis, the columns of $P$ are orthonormal.
Therefore, $P$ is a Unitary Matrix ($P^* P = I$).
Diagonalization: The relationship between the operator in the standard basis (matrix $A$) and the eigenbasis (matrix $D$) is given by:
$$P^{-1} A P = D$$
Thus, every Hermitian matrix is diagonalizable by a unitary matrix.
3. Normal Operators and Eigenvectors
The lecture transitions to the broader class of Normal Operators ($TT^* = T^*T$).
Key Lemma:
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional inner product space and $T$ be a normal operator on $V$.
A vector $\alpha$ is an eigenvector of $T$ with eigenvalue $c$ if and only if $\alpha$ is an eigenvector of $T^*$ with eigenvalue $\bar{c}$.
$$T\alpha = c\alpha \iff T^*\alpha = \bar{c}\alpha$$
Proof:
Norm Property: For any $\alpha \in V$, $\|T\alpha\| = \|T^*\alpha\|$.
Proof:
$\|T\alpha\|^2 = \langle T\alpha, T\alpha \rangle = \langle \alpha, T^*T\alpha \rangle$.
Since $T$ is normal ($T^*T = TT^*$), this equals $\langle \alpha, TT^*\alpha \rangle$.
$= \langle T^*\alpha, T^*\alpha \rangle = \|T^*\alpha\|^2$.
Operator Shift: Consider the operator $U = T - cI$.
Since $T$ is normal, $U$ is also normal.
$(T-cI)(T-cI)^* = (T-cI)(T^*-\bar{c}I) = TT^* - cT^* - \bar{c}T + |c|^2I$.
$(T-cI)^*(T-cI) = (T^*-\bar{c}I)(T-cI) = T^*T - \bar{c}T - cT^* + |c|^2I$.
Since $TT^* = T^*T$, these expressions are equal.
Applying Norm Property to $U$:
Using step 1 on the normal operator $U = T - cI$:
$$\|(T - cI)\alpha\| = \|(T - cI)^*\alpha\| = \|(T^* - \bar{c}I)\alpha\|$$
Conclusion:
$T\alpha = c\alpha \iff (T - cI)\alpha = 0 \iff \|(T - cI)\alpha\| = 0$.
This occurs if and only if $\|(T^* - \bar{c}I)\alpha\| = 0$.
Which implies $T^*\alpha = \bar{c}\alpha$.
4. Normal Matrices
Definition:
An $n \times n$ matrix $B$ is called Normal if it commutes with its conjugate transpose:
$$B B^* = B^* B$$
5. Main Theorem: Diagonalization of Normal Operators via Upper Triangular Matrices
This theorem connects the structure of the matrix representation to the normality of the operator.
Theorem:
Let $T$ be a linear operator on a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$. Let $\mathcal{B}$ be an orthonormal basis for $V$, and let $A$ be the matrix representation of $T$ relative to $\mathcal{B}$. Suppose $A$ is an upper triangular matrix.
Then, $T$ is Normal if and only if $A$ is a diagonal matrix.
Proof:
"If" Direction (Diagonal $\implies$ Normal):
If $A$ is a diagonal matrix, then $A^*$ is also diagonal (conjugate of diagonal entries).
Diagonal matrices always commute ($AA^* = A^*A$).
Since the matrix representation is normal, the operator $T$ is normal.
"Only If" Direction (Normal $\implies$ Diagonal):
Given: $A$ is upper triangular and $T$ is normal.
Goal: Show $A$ must be diagonal (i.e., off-diagonal elements are zero).
Matrix Structure:
$$A = \begin{pmatrix} a_{11} & a_{12} & \dots & a_{1n} \\ 0 & a_{22} & \dots & a_{2n} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & \dots & a_{nn} \end{pmatrix}$$
First Basis Vector ($\alpha_1$):
$T(\alpha_1) = a_{11}\alpha_1$ (since the first column has only $a_{11}$ non-zero).
This implies $\alpha_1$ is an eigenvector of $T$ with eigenvalue $a_{11}$.
Using Lemma: Since $T$ is normal, $\alpha_1$ is also an eigenvector of $T^*$ with eigenvalue $\bar{a}_{11}$.
$$T^*(\alpha_1) = \bar{a}_{11}\alpha_1$$
Matrix of $T^*$:
The matrix of $T^*$ is $A^*$, which is lower triangular.
The first column of $A^*$ corresponds to $T^*(\alpha_1)$.
From the matrix definition: $T^*(\alpha_1) = \sum_{j=1}^n (A^*)_{j1} \alpha_j = \sum_{j=1}^n \bar{a}_{1j} \alpha_j$.
Comparing this with $T^*(\alpha_1) = \bar{a}_{11}\alpha_1$, we see that the coefficients for $j > 1$ must be zero.
Therefore, $\bar{a}_{1j} = 0$ for all $j > 1$.
This implies $a_{12} = a_{13} = \dots = a_{1n} = 0$.
So, the first row of $A$ (except $a_{11}$) is zero.
Inductive Step:
Now consider $\alpha_2$. Since $a_{12}=0$, the second column of $A$ effectively only has $a_{22}$ (and zeros below).
$T(\alpha_2) = a_{22}\alpha_2$.
By the normal property lemma, $T^*(\alpha_2) = \bar{a}_{22}\alpha_2$.
Looking at the matrix $A^*$ (which is $A$ transposed and conjugated), this implies the off-diagonal elements in the second row of $A$ (like $a_{23}, a_{24} \dots$) must be zero.
Conclusion:
Repeating this process for all basis vectors implies that all off-diagonal entries $a_{ij}$ (where $i \neq j$) are zero.
Thus, $A$ is a diagonal matrix.
Significance:
This result implies that if a normal operator has an upper triangular matrix representation with respect to an orthonormal basis, that matrix must actually be diagonal. This is a crucial step towards proving the Spectral Theorem for normal operators, which states that every normal operator on a complex finite-dimensional inner product space has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors. 1 Dec 2025, 03:43:53 GMT+05:30 Products: Gemini Apps Why is this here? ### Interaction 629

create a 4k image that explains all the given things
use minimalistic design and light colours but more explainations and detailsLecture 56 | Normal Operator - I".
1. Recap and Introduction
Context: The lecture continues from the study of self-adjoint operators. A self-adjoint operator ($T = T^*$) on a finite-dimensional inner product space has real eigenvalues.
Goal: Prove the existence of eigenvectors for self-adjoint operators on finite-dimensional spaces and explore if this holds for infinite-dimensional spaces.
2. Existence of Eigenvectors (Finite Dimensional Case)
The lecturer proves a fundamental result regarding the existence of eigenvectors for self-adjoint operators.
Theorem: Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$. Then $T$ has at least one eigenvector.
Proof Outline:
Matrix Representation:
Let $\mathcal{B}$ be an orthonormal basis for $V$.
Let $A$ be the matrix representation of $T$ with respect to $\mathcal{B}$.
Since $T$ is self-adjoint ($T=T^*$), the matrix $A$ is Hermitian ($A = A^*$).
Characteristic Polynomial:
Consider the characteristic polynomial $\det(A - cI)$.
Over the complex field $\mathbb{C}$, any polynomial of degree $n$ has at least one root. Let $c$ be a root.
This implies $\det(A - cI) = 0$, so $(A - cI)$ is singular.
Existence of Non-zero Vector:
Since the matrix is singular, there exists a non-zero vector $X$ such that $(A - cI)X = 0$, or $AX = cX$.
This vector $X$ corresponds to an eigenvector of the operator $T$.
Real vs. Complex Fields:
If the field is Complex ($\mathbb{C}$): The existence is guaranteed by the fundamental theorem of algebra. The self-adjoint property isn't strictly needed for existence (any operator has an eigenvalue over $\mathbb{C}$), but it ensures the eigenvalue is real.
If the field is Real ($\mathbb{R}$): The characteristic polynomial might not have real roots in general. However, because $T$ is self-adjoint, we know all its eigenvalues are real. Therefore, a real root $c$ exists, and consequently, a real eigenvector exists.
3. Non-Existence of Eigenvectors (Infinite Dimensional Case)
The lecturer demonstrates that the existence of eigenvectors is not guaranteed for self-adjoint operators on infinite-dimensional spaces.
Counter-Example:
Space ($V$): The space of all complex-valued continuous functions on $[0, 1]$ ($C[0, 1]$).
Inner Product: $\langle f, g \rangle = \int_{0}^{1} f(t) \overline{g(t)} \, dt$.
Operator ($T$): Define the multiplication operator $T(f(t)) = t \cdot f(t)$.
Analysis:
Check for Self-Adjointness:
$\langle Tf, g \rangle = \int_{0}^{1} t f(t) \overline{g(t)} \, dt$.
$\langle f, Tg \rangle = \int_{0}^{1} f(t) \overline{t g(t)} \, dt = \int_{0}^{1} f(t) t \overline{g(t)} \, dt$ (since $t$ is real).
Thus, $\langle Tf, g \rangle = \langle f, Tg \rangle$, so $T$ is self-adjoint.
Check for Eigenvectors:
Suppose $c$ is an eigenvalue and $f$ is an eigenvector.
$T(f) = c f \implies t \cdot f(t) = c \cdot f(t)$.
$(t - c) f(t) = 0$ for all $t \in [0, 1]$.
If $t \neq c$, then $f(t)$ must be 0.
Since $f$ is continuous, $f(t)$ must be 0 everywhere (or everywhere except a single point, which for continuous functions implies 0 everywhere).
Thus, the only solution is $f = 0$, which is not a valid eigenvector.
Conclusion: The operator $T$ has no eigenvectors, proving that self-adjointness does not guarantee eigenvectors in infinite-dimensional spaces.
4. Invariant Subspaces and Orthogonal Complements
A useful lemma for the spectral theorem is proven.
Theorem: Let $T$ be a linear operator on $V$. If a subspace $W$ is invariant under $T$ (i.e., $T(W) \subseteq W$), then the orthogonal complement $W^\perp$ is invariant under the adjoint $T^*$.
Proof:
Let $\beta \in W^\perp$. We want to show $T^*(\beta) \in W^\perp$.
We need to test if $T^*(\beta)$ is orthogonal to any vector in $W$. Let $\alpha \in W$.
Consider inner product $\langle \alpha, T^*(\beta) \rangle$.
By definition of adjoint: $\langle \alpha, T^*(\beta) \rangle = \langle T(\alpha), \beta \rangle$.
Since $W$ is $T$-invariant, $T(\alpha) \in W$.
Since $\beta \in W^\perp$, it is orthogonal to everything in $W$, so $\langle T(\alpha), \beta \rangle = 0$.
Therefore, $\langle \alpha, T^*(\beta) \rangle = 0$ for all $\alpha \in W$.
Thus, $T^*(\beta) \in W^\perp$.
Corollary for Self-Adjoint Operators: Since $T = T^*$, if $W$ is invariant under a self-adjoint operator $T$, then $W^\perp$ is also invariant under $T$.
5. The Spectral Theorem (Finite Dimensional Case)
The lecture concludes by proving the Spectral Theorem for self-adjoint operators.
Theorem: Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$. Then there exists an orthonormal basis for $V$ consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.
Proof (by Induction on dimension $n$):
Base Case ($n=1$):
Every operator on a 1D space has an eigenvector. Normalizing it gives an orthonormal basis.
Inductive Step:
Assume the theorem holds for spaces of dimension $k < n$. Let $\dim(V) = n$.
As proven earlier, $T$ has at least one eigenvector $\alpha$ (associated with eigenvalue $c$).
Normalize it: $\alpha_1 = \frac{\alpha}{\|\alpha\|}$. This is a unit eigenvector.
Let $W = \text{span}(\alpha_1)$. $W$ is invariant under $T$ ($T(\alpha_1) = c\alpha_1 \in W$).
Using Orthogonal Complement:
Since $W$ is invariant under $T$, by the previous theorem, $W^\perp$ is invariant under $T^*$.
Since $T$ is self-adjoint ($T=T^*$), $W^\perp$ is invariant under $T$.
Let $U$ be the restriction of $T$ to the subspace $W^\perp$. $U$ is a self-adjoint operator on $W^\perp$.
Dimension of $W^\perp$ is $n-1$.
Applying Hypothesis:
By the induction hypothesis, $W^\perp$ has an orthonormal basis $\{\alpha_2, \dots, \alpha_n\}$ consisting of eigenvectors of $U$ (and thus of $T$).
Combining Bases:
The set $\{\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \dots, \alpha_n\}$ is the union of the basis for $W$ and $W^\perp$.
Since $W \perp W^\perp$, this union is an orthonormal set.
It forms a basis for $V$ consisting entirely of eigenvectors of $T$.
Summary: This theorem guarantees that any self-adjoint matrix can be diagonalized by a unitary (or orthogonal) matrix. ### Interaction 630
Gemini Apps Prompted Lecture 55: Normal Operators.
Overview
This lecture bridges the gap between unitary/self-adjoint operators and the more general class of Normal Operators. It begins by finishing a problem on lower triangular decomposition from the previous lecture, then formally introduces normal operators, and concludes with key properties of self-adjoint operators.
Part 1: Example of Matrix Decomposition (Unitary $\times$ Lower Triangular)
Problem:
Let $A$ be an invertible matrix. We want to decompose it into $M \cdot A = U$, where $M$ is a lower triangular matrix with positive diagonal entries and $U$ is unitary.
Given Matrix:
Let $x_1^2 + x_2^2 = 1$ with $x_1 > 0$.
$$A = \begin{pmatrix} x_1 & x_2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$$
Step 1: Gram-Schmidt Orthogonalization on Rows of $A$
Let the rows of $A$ be $\beta_1, \beta_2, \beta_3$:
$\beta_1 = (x_1, x_2, 0)$
$\beta_2 = (0, 1, 0)$
$\beta_3 = (0, 0, 1)$
1. Calculate $\alpha_1$:
$$\alpha_1 = \beta_1 = (x_1, x_2, 0)$$
Norm squared: $\|\alpha_1\|^2 = x_1^2 + x_2^2 = 1$.
2. Calculate $\alpha_2$:
Formula: $\alpha_2 = \beta_2 - \frac{\langle \beta_2, \alpha_1 \rangle}{\|\alpha_1\|^2}\alpha_1$
Inner product: $\langle \beta_2, \alpha_1 \rangle = 0 \cdot x_1 + 1 \cdot x_2 + 0 \cdot 0 = x_2$.
$\alpha_2 = (0, 1, 0) - \frac{x_2}{1}(x_1, x_2, 0) = (0, 1, 0) - (x_1 x_2, x_2^2, 0) = (-x_1 x_2, 1 - x_2^2, 0)$.
Using $x_1^2 + x_2^2 = 1$, substitute $1 - x_2^2 = x_1^2$:
$\alpha_2 = (-x_1 x_2, x_1^2, 0)$.
Norm squared calculation:
$\|\alpha_2\|^2 = (-x_1 x_2)^2 + (x_1^2)^2 = x_1^2 x_2^2 + x_1^4 = x_1^2(x_2^2 + x_1^2) = x_1^2(1) = x_1^2$.
Norm: $\|\alpha_2\| = x_1$ (since $x_1 > 0$).
3. Calculate $\alpha_3$:
Formula: $\alpha_3 = \beta_3 - \text{proj}_{\alpha_1}\beta_3 - \text{proj}_{\alpha_2}\beta_3$
Inner products: $\langle \beta_3, \alpha_1 \rangle = 0$ and $\langle \beta_3, \alpha_2 \rangle = 0$ (since $\beta_3$ has 1 in z-component and others have 0).
$\alpha_3 = \beta_3 = (0, 0, 1)$.
Norm: $\|\alpha_3\| = 1$.
Step 2: Construct Matrix $M$
The matrix $M$ is defined by the coefficients used in Gram-Schmidt to transform $\beta$s to normalized $\alpha$s.
$$M_{kk} = \frac{1}{\|\alpha_k\|}, \quad M_{kj} = -\frac{c_{kj}}{\|\alpha_k\|} \text{ for } j < k$$
Row 1: $1/\|\alpha_1\| = 1/1 = 1$. Row: $(1, 0, 0)$.
Row 2:
Diagonal: $1/\|\alpha_2\| = 1/x_1$.
Off-diagonal ($j=1$): Coefficient was $x_2$. Entry is $-x_2/\|\alpha_2\| = -x_2/x_1$.
Row: $(-x_2/x_1, 1/x_1, 0)$.
Row 3: Row: $(0, 0, 1)$.
$$M = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -\frac{x_2}{x_1} & \frac{1}{x_1} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$$
Step 3: Construct Unitary Matrix $U$
$$U = M \cdot A$$
$$U = \begin{pmatrix} x_1 & x_2 & 0 \\ -x_2 & x_1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$$
This $U$ is a rotation matrix block, which is clearly unitary.
Part 2: Introduction to Normal Operators
Motivation:
We ask under what condition an inner product space has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of an operator $T$.
If $T$ has such a basis, its matrix representation is diagonal.
Consequently, $[T^*]$ is also diagonal (conjugate transpose).
Since diagonal matrices commute, $[T][T^*] = [T^*][T]$.
This suggests the condition $TT^* = T^*T$ is sufficient.
Definition:
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional inner product space. A linear operator $T$ on $V$ is called Normal if it commutes with its adjoint:
$$T T^* = T^* T$$
Common Examples:
Self-Adjoint Operators: $T = T^*$.
$TT^* = T^2$ and $T^*T = T^2$. Thus, every self-adjoint operator is normal.
Unitary Operators: $UU^* = I$ and $U^*U = I$.
Thus, $UU^* = U^*U$. Every unitary operator is normal.
Matrices: A matrix $A$ is normal if $AA^* = A^*A$.
Example: Diagonal matrices are always normal.
Example: Skew-Hermitian matrices ($A^* = -A$) are normal.
Part 3: Properties of Self-Adjoint Operators
Before analyzing general normal operators, the lecture establishes key theorems for the subclass of Self-Adjoint (Hermitian) operators.
Theorem 1: Real Eigenvalues
Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on an inner product space $V$. Then all eigenvalues of $T$ are real.
Proof:
Let $c$ be an eigenvalue and $\alpha$ be a non-zero eigenvector such that $T\alpha = c\alpha$.
Consider the inner product $\langle T\alpha, \alpha \rangle$:
$$\langle c\alpha, \alpha \rangle = c \langle \alpha, \alpha \rangle$$
Since $T$ is self-adjoint ($T = T^*$), use the adjoint property:
$$\langle T\alpha, \alpha \rangle = \langle \alpha, T^*\alpha \rangle = \langle \alpha, T\alpha \rangle = \langle \alpha, c\alpha \rangle = \bar{c} \langle \alpha, \alpha \rangle$$
Equating the results:
$$c \langle \alpha, \alpha \rangle = \bar{c} \langle \alpha, \alpha \rangle$$
Since $\alpha \neq 0$, $\|\alpha\|^2 \neq 0$, so we can divide by it:
$$c = \bar{c}$$
A number equal to its complex conjugate must be real. Thus, $c \in \mathbb{R}$.
Theorem 2: Orthogonality of Eigenvectors
Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator. Eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal.
Proof:
Let $\alpha, \beta$ be eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues $c$ and $d$ ($c \neq d$).
$T\alpha = c\alpha$
$T\beta = d\beta$
Since $T$ is self-adjoint, eigenvalues $c$ and $d$ are real ($c = \bar{c}, d = \bar{d}$).
Consider $\langle T\alpha, \beta \rangle$:
$$\langle T\alpha, \beta \rangle = \langle c\alpha, \beta \rangle = c \langle \alpha, \beta \rangle$$
Using the self-adjoint property:
$$\langle T\alpha, \beta \rangle = \langle \alpha, T\beta \rangle = \langle \alpha, d\beta \rangle = \bar{d} \langle \alpha, \beta \rangle = d \langle \alpha, \beta \rangle$$
Subtracting the two results:
$$(c - d) \langle \alpha, \beta \rangle = 0$$
Since $c \neq d$, we must have $\langle \alpha, \beta \rangle = 0$.
Therefore, $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are orthogonal.
Summary:
Normal Operators: Defined by $TT^* = T^*T$. Include Unitary and Self-Adjoint operators.
Self-Adjoint Operators: Have real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues.
This lays the groundwork for the Spectral Theorem, which states that a normal operator on a complex finite-dimensional inner product space has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors. 1 Dec 2025, 02:04:59 GMT+05:30 Products: Gemini Apps Why is this here? Lecture 54 | Unitary Operators - II
Topic: Unitary Operators and Matrix Decomposition (QR-like Decomposition)
1. Introduction and Recap
Unitary Operators: Recall that unitary operators on a finite-dimensional inner product space form a group under composition.
Unitary Matrices ($U_n$):
Let $U_n$ denote the set of all $n \times n$ unitary matrices.
$U_n$ forms a group with respect to matrix multiplication.
Properties:
If $A, B \in U_n$, then $AB \in U_n$.
If $A \in U_n$, then $A^{-1} \in U_n$.
Since unitary operators are isomorphisms, $A^{-1} = A^*$ (adjoint of $A$), so $A^* \in U_n$.
2. Main Theorem: Lower Triangular Decomposition
Statement:
Let $A$ be an $n \times n$ invertible complex matrix. Then there exists a unique lower triangular matrix $M$ such that:
The entries on the main diagonal of $M$ are positive.
The product $M A$ is a unitary matrix $U$.
$$MA = U$$
(This implies $A = M^{-1}U$. Since $M$ is lower triangular, $M^{-1}$ is also lower triangular. This is related to the QR decomposition, often written as $A = QR$ or $A=QL$, but here derived via Gram-Schmidt).
3. Proof of Existence (Construction via Gram-Schmidt)
Setup:
Let $A$ be an $n \times n$ invertible matrix.
Let the rows of $A$ be denoted by vectors $\beta_1, \beta_2, \dots, \beta_n$.
Since $A$ is invertible, these row vectors form a linearly independent set (a basis).
Gram-Schmidt Orthogonalization:
Apply the Gram-Schmidt process to the basis $\{\beta_1, \dots, \beta_n\}$ to obtain an orthogonal basis $\{\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n\}$.
For any $k$ ($1 \le k \le n$), the set $\{\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_k\}$ is an orthogonal basis for the subspace $W_k$ spanned by $\{\beta_1, \dots, \beta_k\}$.
Formula: The $k$-th orthogonal vector is:
$$\alpha_k = \beta_k - \sum_{j=1}^{k-1} \frac{\langle \beta_k, \alpha_j \rangle}{\|\alpha_j\|^2} \alpha_j$$
Matrix Representation:
From the formula, $\alpha_k$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\beta_1, \dots, \beta_k$.
$$\alpha_k = \beta_k - \sum_{j=1}^{k-1} c_{kj} \beta_j$$
(Here we rewrite the linear combination of $\alpha$'s back into $\beta$'s).
Rearranging to normalize vectors:
$$\frac{\alpha_k}{\|\alpha_k\|} = \frac{1}{\|\alpha_k\|}\beta_k - \sum_{j=1}^{k-1} \frac{c'_{kj}}{\|\alpha_k\|} \beta_j$$
Defining Matrices $U$ and $M$:
Matrix $U$ (Unitary):
Construct a matrix $U$ whose rows are the normalized orthogonal vectors:
$$u_k = \frac{\alpha_k}{\|\alpha_k\|}$$
Since these rows form an orthonormal set, $U$ is a unitary matrix.
Matrix $M$ (Lower Triangular):
Define $M$ such that $U = MA$.
The entries $M_{kj}$ are defined based on the coefficients from the Gram-Schmidt process:
$M_{kk} = \frac{1}{\|\alpha_k\|}$ (Diagonal entries). Since norms are positive, diagonal entries are positive.
$M_{kj}$ involves the coefficients for $\beta_j$ where $j < k$.
$M_{kj} = 0$ for $j > k$ (Upper triangular part is zero).
Thus, $M$ is a lower triangular matrix.
Conclusion of Existence:
We have constructed a lower triangular matrix $M$ with positive diagonal entries and a unitary matrix $U$ such that $U = MA$.
4. Proof of Uniqueness
Hypothesis:
Suppose the decomposition is not unique.
Let $\mathcal{T}^+_n$ be the set of $n \times n$ lower triangular matrices with positive diagonal entries.
Assume there exist two such matrices $M_1, M_2 \in \mathcal{T}^+_n$ such that:
$$M_1 A = U_1 \quad (\text{where } U_1 \in U_n)$$
$$M_2 A = U_2 \quad (\text{where } U_2 \in U_n)$$
Group Properties:
$U_n$ is a group.
$\mathcal{T}^+_n$ is also a group under multiplication (Product of lower triangular is lower triangular; inverse of lower triangular is lower triangular; positive diagonals are preserved).
Derivation:
From the assumptions:
$$M_1 A \in U_n \implies (M_1 A) (M_2 A)^{-1} \in U_n$$
$$M_1 A A^{-1} M_2^{-1} \in U_n$$
$$M_1 M_2^{-1} \in U_n$$
Let $X = M_1 M_2^{-1}$. So $X$ is unitary.
Also, since $M_1, M_2 \in \mathcal{T}^+_n$, their product/inverse lies in $\mathcal{T}^+_n$.
$$X \in \mathcal{T}^+_n$$
So $X$ is a lower triangular matrix with positive diagonal entries.
Adjoint Analysis:
Since $X$ is unitary, $X^{-1} = X^*$.
The adjoint (conjugate transpose) of a lower triangular matrix is an upper triangular matrix.
Therefore, $X^{-1}$ (which is $X^*$) is upper triangular.
Since $X \in \mathcal{T}^+_n$, $X^{-1}$ is also lower triangular (group property).
A matrix that is both lower triangular and upper triangular must be a diagonal matrix.
Diagonal Entries:
Let $X$ be diagonal with entries $d_{ii}$.
Since $X$ is unitary, $X X^* = I \implies d_{ii} \overline{d_{ii}} = 1 \implies |d_{ii}| = 1$.
Since $X \in \mathcal{T}^+_n$, the diagonal entries $d_{ii}$ must be positive.
The only positive number with modulus 1 is 1.
Therefore, $d_{ii} = 1$ for all $i$.
Thus, $X = I$ (Identity matrix).
Conclusion:
$$M_1 M_2^{-1} = I \implies M_1 = M_2$$
The matrix $M$ is unique.
5. Summary
For any invertible complex matrix $A$, there exists a unique decomposition involving a unitary matrix and a lower triangular matrix with positive diagonal entries. This result relies on the Gram-Schmidt process and the algebraic properties of unitary and triangular matrix groups. 1 Dec 2025, 01:21:14 GMT+05:30 Products: Gemini Apps Why is this here? Linear Functionals and Adjoints - IV.
1. Adjoint of a Linear Operator
The lecture begins by addressing the existence of adjoints in general, specifically for infinite-dimensional spaces. While adjoints always exist for linear operators on finite-dimensional inner product spaces, this is not guaranteed for infinite-dimensional spaces.
Definition:
Let $V$ be an inner product space (IPS) over a field $F$ (real or complex). Let $T$ be a linear operator on $V$. We say that $T$ has an adjoint provided there exists a linear operator $T^*$ on $V$ such that:
$$\langle T\alpha, \beta \rangle = \langle \alpha, T^*\beta \rangle$$
for all vectors $\alpha, \beta \in V$.
Key Observations for Finite-Dimensional Spaces:
Existence: For any linear operator $T$ on a finite-dimensional inner product space, a unique adjoint $T^*$ always exists.
Dependence: The definition of $T^*$ depends on the specific inner product defined on the space. Changing the inner product changes the adjoint.
Matrix Representation:
If $\mathcal{B}$ is an orthonormal basis, the relationship between the matrix of $T$ (let's call it $A$) and the matrix of $T^*$ (let's call it $B$) is straightforward: $B = A^*$ (the conjugate transpose). Specifically, $B_{jk} = \overline{A_{kj}}$.
If the basis is not orthonormal, this simple relationship does not hold.
2. Examples of Adjoints
The lecturer provides specific examples to illustrate how to find the adjoint in different vector spaces.
Example 1: Space of Column Vectors ($V = \mathbb{C}^{n \times 1}$)
Space: All $n \times 1$ column vectors over $\mathbb{C}$.
Inner Product: $\langle X, Y \rangle = Y^* X$ (standard inner product).
Operator $T$: Defined by $T(X) = AX$, where $A$ is a fixed $n \times n$ matrix.
Finding $T^*$:
Start with the definition: $\langle T(X), Y \rangle = \langle X, T^*(Y) \rangle$.
Left side: $\langle AX, Y \rangle = Y^* (AX)$.
Manipulate to isolate $X$ on the right: $Y^* A X = (A^* Y)^* X$.
This matches the form of the inner product $\langle X, Z \rangle = Z^* X$ if we set $Z = A^* Y$.
Therefore, $\langle AX, Y \rangle = \langle X, A^* Y \rangle$.
Result: The adjoint operator $T^*$ is given by $T^*(Y) = A^* Y$.
Example 2: Space of Matrices ($V = \mathbb{C}^{n \times n}$)
Space: All $n \times n$ matrices over $\mathbb{C}$.
Inner Product: $\langle A, B \rangle = \text{tr}(B^* A)$ (Trace of $B^* A$).
Operator $T$: Defined by $T(A) = MA$, where $M$ is a fixed matrix.
Finding $T^*$:
We need $\langle T(A), B \rangle = \langle MA, B \rangle$.
Expand: $\text{tr}(B^* MA)$.
Use trace property $\text{tr}(XYZ) = \text{tr}(YZX)$? No, simpler manipulation is needed. We want to form $\langle A, T^*(B) \rangle = \text{tr}((T^*(B))^* A)$.
Rewrite $\text{tr}(B^* MA) = \text{tr}((M^* B)^* A)$.
This matches the inner product form with the second argument being $M^* B$.
Result: The adjoint operator $T^*$ is given by $T^*(B) = M^* B$.
Example 3: Space of Polynomials (Infinite Dimensional)
Space: Polynomials over $\mathbb{C}$.
Inner Product: $\langle f, g \rangle = \int_{0}^{1} f(x) \overline{g(x)} \, dx$.
Operator $T$: Defined by multiplication by a fixed polynomial $f$: $T(g) = f \cdot g$.
Finding $T^*$:
Check $\langle T(g), h \rangle = \int_{0}^{1} (f(x)g(x)) \overline{h(x)} \, dx$.
Rearrange to isolate $g(x)$: $\int_{0}^{1} g(x) (f(x) \overline{h(x)}) \, dx$.
To match $\int_{0}^{1} g(x) \overline{T^*(h)(x)} \, dx$, we need $\overline{T^*(h)} = f \overline{h}$.
Taking the conjugate of both sides: $T^*(h) = \overline{f} h$.
Result: The adjoint is multiplication by the conjugate of the fixed polynomial: $T^*(h) = \overline{f} \cdot h$.
3. The Derivative Operator & Existence of Adjoint
This example highlights a case where an adjoint might not exist without restrictions.
Space: Polynomials over $\mathbb{C}$ with inner product $\langle f, g \rangle = \int_{0}^{1} f(x) \overline{g(x)} \, dx$.
Operator $D$: The differentiation operator, $D(f) = \frac{df}{dx}$.
Analysis:
Consider $\langle Df, g \rangle = \int_{0}^{1} f'(x) \overline{g(x)} \, dx$.
Use Integration by Parts:
$$\int_{0}^{1} f'(x) \overline{g(x)} \, dx = [f(x)\overline{g(x)}]_{0}^{1} - \int_{0}^{1} f(x) \overline{g'(x)} \, dx$$
This equals: $(f(1)\overline{g(1)} - f(0)\overline{g(0)}) - \langle f, g' \rangle$.
For $D^*$ to exist, we need $\langle Df, g \rangle = \langle f, D^*g \rangle$. This would require the boundary term $(f(1)\overline{g(1)} - f(0)\overline{g(0)})$ to vanish for all $f$.
This boundary term defines a linear functional that cannot generally be represented as an inner product in this space (similar to the evaluation functional example discussed in previous lectures).
Conclusion: The differentiation operator $D$ does not have an adjoint on the space of all polynomials unless we restrict the domain (e.g., to polynomials where $g(1)=g(0)=0$).
4. Properties of Adjoints
Theorem:
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional inner product space. Let $T, U$ be linear operators and $c \in F$.
$(T + U)^* = T^* + U^*$
$(cT)^* = \bar{c} T^*$
$(TU)^* = U^* T^*$
$(T^*)^* = T$
Proof of (1):
Consider $\langle (T+U)\alpha, \beta \rangle$.
By linearity: $\langle T\alpha + U\alpha, \beta \rangle = \langle T\alpha, \beta \rangle + \langle U\alpha, \beta \rangle$.
Using adjoint definition: $\langle \alpha, T^*\beta \rangle + \langle \alpha, U^*\beta \rangle$.
By linearity of inner product: $\langle \alpha, (T^* + U^*)\beta \rangle$.
Thus, $(T+U)^* = T^* + U^*$.
(The lecturer notes that the other proofs follow similar straightforward logic and are left as exercises).
5. Self-Adjoint Operators
Definition:
A linear operator $T$ is called Self-Adjoint (or Hermitian) if:
$$T = T^*$$
Decomposition of an Operator:
Any linear operator $T$ on a finite-dimensional inner product space can be decomposed into a sum involving two self-adjoint operators, analogous to writing a complex number $z = x + iy$.
We can write:
$$T = \frac{T + T^*}{2} + i \left( \frac{T - T^*}{2i} \right)$$
Let $U_1 = \frac{T + T^*}{2}$ and $U_2 = \frac{T - T^*}{2i}$.
Verification that $U_1$ and $U_2$ are self-adjoint:
$U_1^* = (\frac{T + T^*}{2})^* = \frac{T^* + (T^*)^*}{2} = \frac{T^* + T}{2} = U_1$. (Self-Adjoint)
$U_2^* = (\frac{T - T^*}{2i})^*$. Note that $(2i)^* = -2i$.
Numerator: $(T - T^*)^* = T^* - T$.
So, $U_2^* = \frac{T^* - T}{-2i} = \frac{-(T - T^*)}{-2i} = \frac{T - T^*}{2i} = U_2$. (Self-Adjoint)
Significance:
This decomposition ($T = U_1 + iU_2$) allows us to study any linear operator in terms of self-adjoint operators. Self-adjoint operators are particularly important because they guarantee the existence of an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors (Spectral Theorem), which simplifies the structure of the operator significantly. 30 Nov 2025, 20:13:25 GMT+05:30 Products: Gemini Apps Why is this here? "Lecture 50 | Linear Functionals and Adjoints - III".
Overview
This lecture focuses on two main applications of inner product space theory:
Application of the Riesz Representation Theorem: Explicitly calculating the unique vector that represents a linear functional in a polynomial vector space.
Adjoints of Projection Operators: Proving that orthogonal projection operators are self-adjoint (Hermitian) and verifying this with a matrix calculation in $\mathbb{R}^3$.
Part 1: Finding the Riesz Representative Vector
Problem Statement:
Vector Space ($V$): The space of real polynomials with degree $\le 2$, denoted as $P_2(\mathbb{R})$.
Inner Product: Defined as $\langle f, g \rangle = \int_{0}^{1} f(t)g(t) \, dt$.
Linear Functional ($\phi$): Defined by evaluating the polynomial at a fixed real number $t_0$.
$$\phi(f) = f(t_0)$$
Goal: Find the unique polynomial $g(t) \in V$ such that for every polynomial $f(t)$:
$$\phi(f) = \langle f, g \rangle \quad \implies \quad f(t_0) = \int_{0}^{1} f(t)g(t) \, dt$$
Method:
According to the Riesz Representation Theorem, if we find an orthonormal basis $\{\alpha'_1, \alpha'_2, \alpha'_3\}$ for $V$, the vector $g$ can be constructed using the formula:
$$g = \sum_{j=1}^{n} \overline{\phi(\alpha'_j)} \alpha'_j$$
Since we are working over real numbers, the conjugate is unnecessary:
$$g(t) = \sum_{j=1}^{3} \phi(\alpha'_j) \alpha'_j(t) = \sum_{j=1}^{3} \alpha'_j(t_0) \alpha'_j(t)$$
Step 1: Gram-Schmidt Orthogonalization
We start with the standard basis $B = \{1, x, x^2\}$. Let $\beta_1 = 1, \beta_2 = x, \beta_3 = x^2$.
1. First Vector ($\alpha_1$):
Set $\alpha_1 = \beta_1 = 1$.
Calculate squared norm: $\|\alpha_1\|^2 = \int_0^1 1^2 dt = [t]_0^1 = 1$.
Orthonormal vector: $\alpha'_1 = \frac{\alpha_1}{\|\alpha_1\|} = 1$.
2. Second Vector ($\alpha_2$):
Formula: $\alpha_2 = \beta_2 - \frac{\langle \beta_2, \alpha_1 \rangle}{\|\alpha_1\|^2}\alpha_1$
Inner Product: $\langle \beta_2, \alpha_1 \rangle = \int_0^1 x \cdot 1 \, dt = [\frac{x^2}{2}]_0^1 = \frac{1}{2}$.
Result: $\alpha_2 = x - \frac{1}{2}$.
Calculate squared norm:
$$\|\alpha_2\|^2 = \int_0^1 (x - 1/2)^2 dt = \left[\frac{(x-1/2)^3}{3}\right]_0^1 = \frac{1/8 - (-1/8)}{3} = \frac{1/4}{3} = \frac{1}{12}$$
Normalization factor: $\frac{1}{\|\alpha_2\|} = \sqrt{12}$.
Orthonormal vector: $\alpha'_2 = \sqrt{12}(x - 1/2)$.
3. Third Vector ($\alpha_3$):
Formula: $\alpha_3 = \beta_3 - \frac{\langle \beta_3, \alpha_1 \rangle}{\|\alpha_1\|^2}\alpha_1 - \frac{\langle \beta_3, \alpha_2 \rangle}{\|\alpha_2\|^2}\alpha_2$
Inner Product 1: $\langle \beta_3, \alpha_1 \rangle = \int_0^1 x^2 \cdot 1 \, dt = \frac{1}{3}$.
Inner Product 2: $\langle \beta_3, \alpha_2 \rangle = \int_0^1 x^2(x - 1/2) \, dt = \int_0^1 (x^3 - \frac{x^2}{2}) dt = \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{6} = \frac{1}{12}$.
Substitute values:
$$\alpha_3 = x^2 - \frac{1/3}{1}(1) - \frac{1/12}{1/12}(x - 1/2)$$
$$\alpha_3 = x^2 - \frac{1}{3} - (x - \frac{1}{2}) = x^2 - x + \frac{1}{6}$$
Calculate squared norm (after integration): $\|\alpha_3\|^2 = \frac{1}{180}$.
Normalization factor: $\frac{1}{\|\alpha_3\|} = \sqrt{180} = \sqrt{36 \times 5} = 6\sqrt{5}$.
Orthonormal vector: $\alpha'_3 = 6\sqrt{5}(x^2 - x + 1/6)$.
Step 2: Constructing the Polynomial $g(t)$
Using the summation formula $g(t) = \alpha'_1(t_0)\alpha'_1(t) + \alpha'_2(t_0)\alpha'_2(t) + \alpha'_3(t_0)\alpha'_3(t)$:
$$g(t) = 1\cdot 1 + [\sqrt{12}(t_0 - 1/2)] [\sqrt{12}(t - 1/2)] + [6\sqrt{5}(t_0^2 - t_0 + 1/6)] [6\sqrt{5}(t^2 - t + 1/6)]$$
Simplifying the constants ($\sqrt{12}\sqrt{12} = 12$ and $6\sqrt{5} \cdot 6\sqrt{5} = 180$):
$$g(t) = 1 + 12\left(t_0 - \frac{1}{2}\right)\left(t - \frac{1}{2}\right) + 180\left(t_0^2 - t_0 + \frac{1}{6}\right)\left(t^2 - t + \frac{1}{6}\right)$$
This specific polynomial $g(t)$ acts as the "representer" for the evaluation functional at $t_0$.
Part 2: Adjoints of Projection Operators

Shutterstock
Explore
Theorem:
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional inner product space and let $E$ be the orthogonal projection of $V$ onto a subspace $W$. Then $E$ is self-adjoint.
Mathematically: $E = E^*$ (or $\langle E\alpha, \beta \rangle = \langle \alpha, E\beta \rangle$).
Proof:
Decomposition: Since $E$ is an orthogonal projection onto $W$, the space $V$ can be decomposed into the direct sum $V = W \oplus W^\perp$.
Vector representation: Any vector $\alpha \in V$ can be written as $\alpha = E\alpha + (I-E)\alpha$, where:
$E\alpha \in W$
$(I-E)\alpha \in W^\perp$ (the orthogonal complement).
Inner Product Expansion: We want to check the relation $\langle E\alpha, \beta \rangle$.
Expand $\beta$ similarly: $\beta = E\beta + (I-E)\beta$.
$\langle E\alpha, \beta \rangle = \langle E\alpha, E\beta + (I-E)\beta \rangle$.
By linearity: $\langle E\alpha, \beta \rangle = \langle E\alpha, E\beta \rangle + \langle E\alpha, (I-E)\beta \rangle$.
Orthogonality: The second term $\langle E\alpha, (I-E)\beta \rangle$ is the inner product of a vector in $W$ and a vector in $W^\perp$. By definition, this is zero.
So, $\langle E\alpha, \beta \rangle = \langle E\alpha, E\beta \rangle$.
Reverse Direction: Now expand $\alpha$ in $\langle \alpha, E\beta \rangle$.
$\langle \alpha, E\beta \rangle = \langle E\alpha + (I-E)\alpha, E\beta \rangle$.
$\langle \alpha, E\beta \rangle = \langle E\alpha, E\beta \rangle + \langle (I-E)\alpha, E\beta \rangle$.
Again, the second term is zero (inner product of vector in $W^\perp$ and $W$).
So, $\langle \alpha, E\beta \rangle = \langle E\alpha, E\beta \rangle$.
Conclusion: Since both expressions equal $\langle E\alpha, E\beta \rangle$, we have $\langle E\alpha, \beta \rangle = \langle \alpha, E\beta \rangle$. Thus, $E = E^*$.
Part 3: Matrix Representation Example
Objective:
Verify the self-adjoint property ($A = A^T$ for real matrices) using a specific numerical example in $\mathbb{R}^3$.
Setup:
Space: $V = \mathbb{R}^3$ with the standard inner product (dot product).
Subspace ($W$): Spanned by the single vector $\beta = (3, 12, -1)$.
Operator ($E$): The orthogonal projection onto $W$.
Calculation:
Projection Formula:
Since $W$ is 1-dimensional, the projection of any vector $\alpha = (x,y,z)$ onto $W$ is:
$$E(\alpha) = \frac{\langle \alpha, \beta \rangle}{\|\beta\|^2} \beta$$
Compute $\|\beta\|^2$: $3^2 + 12^2 + (-1)^2 = 9 + 144 + 1 = 154$.
Compute $\langle \alpha, \beta \rangle$: $3x + 12y - z$.
Formula: $E(x,y,z) = \frac{3x + 12y - z}{154} (3, 12, -1)$.
Determine Matrix Columns:
We find the image of the standard basis vectors $e_1, e_2, e_3$.
For $e_1 = (1, 0, 0)$:
Scalar = $\frac{3(1) + 0 - 0}{154} = \frac{3}{154}$.
Vector = $\frac{3}{154}(3, 12, -1) = \frac{1}{154}(9, 36, -3)$.
For $e_2 = (0, 1, 0)$:
Scalar = $\frac{0 + 12(1) - 0}{154} = \frac{12}{154}$.
Vector = $\frac{12}{154}(3, 12, -1) = \frac{1}{154}(36, 144, -12)$.
For $e_3 = (0, 0, 1)$:
Scalar = $\frac{0 + 0 - 1}{154} = \frac{-1}{154}$.
Vector = $\frac{-1}{154}(3, 12, -1) = \frac{1}{154}(-3, -12, 1)$.
Construct the Matrix:
$$[E] = \frac{1}{154} \begin{pmatrix} 9 & 36 & -3 \\ 36 & 144 & -12 \\ -3 & -12 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$$
Verification:
Observing the matrix, the element at row $i$, column $j$ is equal to the element at row $j$, column $i$ (e.g., $A_{12} = 36$ and $A_{21} = 36$).
Since the matrix is symmetric ($A = A^T$), the operator is self-adjoint, confirming the theoretical result. 30 Nov 2025, 18:32:39 GMT+05:30 Products: Gemini Apps Why is this here? Lecture 53: Unitary Operators - I
1. Introduction to Unitary Operators
Context:
The lecture builds upon the concept of isomorphisms in inner product spaces. A unitary operator is essentially an isomorphism of an inner product space onto itself.
Definition:
Let $V$ be an inner product space over a field $F$. A linear operator $T$ on $V$ is called a Unitary Operator if:
It is an isomorphism of the space onto itself.
This implies $T$ is one-to-one and onto (invertible).
$T$ preserves the inner product:
$$\langle T\alpha, T\beta \rangle = \langle \alpha, \beta \rangle$$
for all $\alpha, \beta \in V$.
2. Properties of Unitary Operators
Property 1: Composition of Unitary Operators
If $U_1$ and $U_2$ are unitary operators on an inner product space $V$, then their composition $U_1 U_2$ is also a unitary operator.
Proof:
Since $U_1$ and $U_2$ are isomorphisms (invertible), their product $U_1 U_2$ is also invertible.
We must show the product preserves the norm/inner product:
$$\|(U_1 U_2)(\alpha)\| = \|U_1(U_2(\alpha))\|$$
Since $U_1$ is unitary (norm-preserving):
$$\|U_1(U_2(\alpha))\| = \|U_2(\alpha)\|$$
Since $U_2$ is unitary:
$$\|U_2(\alpha)\| = \|\alpha\|$$
Thus, $\|(U_1 U_2)(\alpha)\| = \|\alpha\|$, proving the composition is unitary.
Property 2: Inverse of a Unitary Operator
If $U$ is a unitary operator, then its inverse $U^{-1}$ is also a unitary operator.
Conclusion: Group Structure
The set of all unitary operators on an inner product space forms a Group under the binary operation of composition.
3. Relationship with Adjoint Operators
Theorem:
Let $V$ be an inner product space (finite or infinite dimensional) and $T$ be a linear operator on $V$.
$T$ is a Unitary Operator if and only if the adjoint $T^*$ exists and:
$$T^* = T^{-1}$$
(Equivalently, $T T^* = T^* T = I$).
Proof:
"If" Direction ($\implies$):
Assume $T$ is unitary.
Then $T$ is invertible ($T^{-1}$ exists) and preserves inner products:
$$\langle T\alpha, T\beta \rangle = \langle \alpha, \beta \rangle$$
We can rewrite $\langle \alpha, \beta \rangle$ using the identity $I = T T^{-1}$:
$$\langle \alpha, \beta \rangle = \langle T\alpha, (T^{-1})^* T^* \beta \rangle$$
Alternatively, using the definition of adjoints directly:
$$\langle T\alpha, T\beta \rangle = \langle \alpha, T^* (T\beta) \rangle$$
Since $\langle T\alpha, T\beta \rangle = \langle \alpha, \beta \rangle$:
$$\langle \alpha, \beta \rangle = \langle \alpha, T^* T \beta \rangle$$
This implies $T^* T = I$, so $T^* = T^{-1}$.
"Only if" Direction ($\impliedby$):
Assume $T^*$ exists and $T^* T = I$ (i.e., $T^* = T^{-1}$).
Since $T$ is invertible, it is one-to-one and onto.
Check preservation of inner product:
$$\langle T\alpha, T\beta \rangle = \langle \alpha, T^* T \beta \rangle$$
Since $T^* T = I$:
$$\langle \alpha, I \beta \rangle = \langle \alpha, \beta \rangle$$
Thus, $T$ preserves inner products and is a unitary operator.
4. Example: Linear Operator on $\mathbb{C}^n$
Setup:
Let $V = \mathbb{C}^{n \times 1}$ (column matrices) with the standard inner product $\langle X, Y \rangle = Y^* X$ (conjugate transpose).
Define a linear operator $T(X) = AX$, where $A$ is an $n \times n$ matrix.
Condition for Unitarity:
For $T$ to be unitary, we need $\langle T\alpha, T\beta \rangle = \langle \alpha, \beta \rangle$.
Compute $\langle T\alpha, T\beta \rangle$:
$$\langle A\alpha, A\beta \rangle = (A\beta)^* (A\alpha) = \beta^* A^* A \alpha$$
Compute $\langle \alpha, \beta \rangle$:
$$\beta^* \alpha$$
For these to be equal for all $\alpha, \beta$, we require:
$$A^* A = I$$
Conclusion:
The operator $T$ is unitary if and only if the matrix $A$ satisfies $A^* A = I$.
5. Unitary Matrices
Definition:
An $n \times n$ complex matrix $A$ is called a Unitary Matrix if:
$$A^* A = I$$
(Where $A^*$ is the conjugate transpose of $A$).
Note: This implies $A^{-1} = A^*$. Consequently, $A A^* = I$ is also true.
Theorem: Matrix Representation of Unitary Operators
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional inner product space. A linear operator $U$ on $V$ is unitary if and only if its matrix representation relative to an orthonormal basis is a Unitary Matrix.
Proof Sketch:
Let $\mathcal{B} = \{\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n\}$ be an orthonormal basis.
Let $A = [U]_{\mathcal{B}}$.
The condition for preserving inner products translates to the columns of $A$ being orthonormal vectors in $\mathbb{C}^n$.
Orthonormal columns imply $A^* A = I$.
6. Orthogonal Matrices
Definition:
An $n \times n$ real (or complex) matrix $A$ is called an Orthogonal Matrix if:
$$A^T A = I$$
(Where $A^T$ is the transpose).
This is the real analogue of a unitary matrix.
It implies $A^{-1} = A^T$.
The rows and columns of an orthogonal matrix form orthonormal sets.
Determinant Property:
If $A$ is an orthogonal matrix, then $\det(A) = \pm 1$.
Proof: $\det(A^T A) = \det(I) \implies \det(A) \det(A) = 1 \implies (\det A)^2 = 1$.
7. Examples of Orthogonal and Unitary Matrices
1. One-Dimensional Case ($1 \times 1$ Matrix $A = [c]$):
Orthogonal: $c^2 = 1 \implies c = 1$ or $c = -1$.
Unitary: $c \bar{c} = 1 \implies |c|^2 = 1 \implies |c| = 1$.
Solution: $c = e^{i\theta}$ for any real $\theta$.
2. Two-Dimensional Orthogonal Matrix ($2 \times 2$):
Let $A = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}$.
For $A$ to be orthogonal ($A^{-1} = A^T$), and considering $\det(A) = \pm 1$:
Case 1: $\det(A) = 1$ (Rotation)
$$A = \begin{pmatrix} a & -c \\ c & a \end{pmatrix}$$
With constraint $a^2 + c^2 = 1$. If we set $a = \cos \theta, c = \sin \theta$:
$$A = \begin{pmatrix} \cos \theta & -\sin \theta \\ \sin \theta & \cos \theta \end{pmatrix}$$
Case 2: $\det(A) = -1$ (Reflection)
$$A = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ b & -a \end{pmatrix}$$
With constraint $a^2 + b^2 = 1$.
$$A = \begin{pmatrix} \cos \theta & \sin \theta \\ \sin \theta & -\cos \theta \end{pmatrix}$$ 30 Nov 2025, 18:06:22 GMT+05:30 Products: Gemini Apps Why is this here? 1. Introduction to Isomorphism in Inner Product Spaces
Context:
The lecture builds upon the standard definition of isomorphism in vector spaces (a one-to-one and onto linear transformation) and extends it to Inner Product Spaces (IPS). In an IPS, structure must be preserved—specifically, the inner product.
Definition:
Let $V$ and $W$ be two inner product spaces defined over the same field $F$. A linear transformation $T: V \to W$ is called an Isomorphism in Inner Product Spaces if:
$T$ is one-to-one (injective).
$T$ is onto (surjective).
$T$ preserves inner products.
This means for any $\alpha, \beta \in V$:
$$\langle T\alpha, T\beta \rangle_W = \langle \alpha, \beta \rangle_V$$
(Where $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle_W$ is the inner product in $W$ and $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle_V$ is the inner product in $V$).
2. Preserving Inner Products
Concept:
A linear transformation $T: V \to W$ is said to preserve inner products if the inner product of the images matches the inner product of the original vectors.
Key Consequence:
If $T$ preserves inner products, it is automatically one-to-one.
Proof:
Assume $T$ preserves inner products.
Then $\langle \alpha, \alpha \rangle = \langle T\alpha, T\alpha \rangle$.
This implies $\|\alpha\|^2 = \|T\alpha\|^2$, or $\|\alpha\| = \|T\alpha\|$.
If $T\alpha = 0$, then $\|\alpha\| = 0$, which implies $\alpha = 0$.
Since the kernel contains only the zero vector, $T$ is one-to-one.
Alternative Definition:
Sometimes, an isomorphism in IPS is defined simply as a surjective (onto) linear transformation that preserves inner products (since injectivity is implied by the preservation of the norm).
3. Theorem: Equivalent Statements for Finite Dimensional Spaces
Theorem Statement:
Let $V$ and $W$ be finite-dimensional inner product spaces over the same field $F$. Let $T: V \to W$ be a linear transformation. Then the following statements are equivalent:
$T$ preserves inner products.
$T$ is an isomorphism (in the inner product space sense).
$T$ carries any orthonormal basis of $V$ onto an orthonormal basis of $W$.
$T$ carries some orthonormal basis of $V$ onto an orthonormal basis of $W$.
Proofs of Implication:
1 $\implies$ 2:
If $T$ preserves inner products, it is norm-preserving and thus one-to-one.
Since $V$ and $W$ are finite-dimensional and presumably have the same dimension (implied for isomorphism candidates), a one-to-one map is automatically onto.
Therefore, $T$ is an isomorphism.
2 $\implies$ 3:
Let $\{\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n\}$ be an orthonormal basis for $V$.
Since $T$ is an isomorphism, it maps a basis to a basis. We must check orthonormality.
Check: $\langle T\alpha_j, T\alpha_k \rangle = \langle \alpha_j, \alpha_k \rangle$ (because $T$ preserves inner products).
Since $\langle \alpha_j, \alpha_k \rangle = \delta_{jk}$ (Kronecker delta), then $\langle T\alpha_j, T\alpha_k \rangle = \delta_{jk}$.
Thus, $\{T\alpha_1, \dots, T\alpha_n\}$ is an orthonormal basis for $W$.
3 $\implies$ 4:
This is trivial. If it holds for any basis, it holds for some basis.
4 $\implies$ 1:
Assume $T$ maps a specific orthonormal basis $\{\alpha_i\}$ of $V$ to an orthonormal basis $\{T\alpha_i\}$ of $W$.
Let $\alpha = \sum x_i \alpha_i$ and $\beta = \sum y_j \alpha_j$.
Then $\langle \alpha, \beta \rangle = \sum x_i \bar{y}_i$ (Parseval's identity logic).
Consider $T\alpha = \sum x_i T\alpha_i$ and $T\beta = \sum y_j T\alpha_j$.
Compute $\langle T\alpha, T\beta \rangle = \sum \sum x_i \bar{y}_j \langle T\alpha_i, T\alpha_j \rangle$.
Since $\{T\alpha_i\}$ is orthonormal, $\langle T\alpha_i, T\alpha_j \rangle = \delta_{ij}$.
Thus, $\langle T\alpha, T\beta \rangle = \sum x_i \bar{y}_i$.
Conclusion: $\langle T\alpha, T\beta \rangle = \langle \alpha, \beta \rangle$. $T$ preserves inner products.
4. Corollary regarding Dimension
Statement:
Let $V$ and $W$ be finite-dimensional inner product spaces over the same field. $V$ and $W$ are isomorphic if and only if $\dim(V) = \dim(W)$.
Proof Sketch:
Forward: If isomorphic, they must be one-to-one and onto, implying dimensions are equal.
Reverse: If dimensions are equal, construct orthonormal bases for both. Define $T$ mapping basis vectors of $V$ to basis vectors of $W$. This map is linear, bijective, and (as shown in the previous theorem) preserves inner products.
5. Examples
Example 1: Isomorphism to Coordinate Space ($F^n$)
Space $V$: A finite-dimensional IPS with dimension $n$.
Space $F^n$: The space of $n$-tuples with the standard inner product (dot product).
Transformation:
Let $\mathcal{B} = \{\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n\}$ be an orthonormal basis for $V$.
For any $\alpha \in V$, let $\alpha = \sum x_i \alpha_i$.
Define $T(\alpha) = (x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n)$.
Verification:
$\langle \alpha, \beta \rangle_V = \sum x_i \bar{y}_i$.
$\langle T\alpha, T\beta \rangle_{F^n} = \sum x_i \bar{y}_i$ (Standard inner product definition).
Since the values match, $T$ preserves inner products and is an isomorphism.
Example 2: Preserving Inner Product without Isomorphism (Infinite Dimensions)
Space $V$: Real-valued continuous functions on $[0,1]$ with inner product $\langle f, g \rangle_V = \int_0^1 t^2 f(t) g(t) \, dt$.
Space $W$: Same function space but with standard inner product $\langle f, g \rangle_W = \int_0^1 f(t) g(t) \, dt$.
Transformation: Define $T: V \to W$ by $(Tf)(t) = t \cdot f(t)$.
Analysis:
Compute $\langle Tf, Tg \rangle_W$:
$$= \int_0^1 (t f(t)) (t g(t)) \, dt = \int_0^1 t^2 f(t) g(t) \, dt$$
This is exactly $\langle f, g \rangle_V$.
So, $T$ preserves the inner product.
Conclusion:
$T$ preserves inner products (implies $T$ is one-to-one).
However, $T$ is not onto (not all functions in $W$ can be written as $t \cdot f(t)$ where $f$ is continuous, e.g., a function non-zero at $t=0$).
Therefore, $T$ is not an isomorphism, highlighting that the equivalence theorem relies on finite dimensionality. 30 Nov 2025, 16:52:11 GMT+05:30 Products: Gemini Apps Why is this here? The lecture begins by reviewing the concept established in the previous session: for any finite-dimensional inner product space, a linear functional can be represented as an inner product with a fixed unique vector in that space. The lecturer then poses the question: Does this hold true for infinite-dimensional inner product spaces?
1. Linear Functionals on Infinite-Dimensional Spaces
The answer is No. A counter-example is provided using the space of polynomial functions.
Counter-Example:
Space ($V$): Let $V$ be the space of all polynomial functions over the field of complex numbers $\mathbb{C}$.
Inner Product: Define the inner product for $f, g \in V$ as:
$$\langle f, g \rangle = \int_{0}^{1} f(t) \overline{g(t)} \, dt$$
Linear Functional ($L$): Fix a complex number $z \in \mathbb{C}$. Define $L: V \to \mathbb{C}$ by:
$$L(f) = f(z)$$
This is a valid linear functional.
Claim: There exists no non-zero function $g \in V$ such that $L(f) = \langle f, g \rangle$ for all $f \in V$.
Proof of Non-Existence:
Assume such a $g$ exists. Then $f(z) = \int_{0}^{1} f(t) \overline{g(t)} \, dt$.
Consider the polynomial $h(t) = t - z$. Note that $h(z) = 0$.
For any $f \in V$, let the test polynomial be $h(t)f(t)$. Then:
$$L(hf) = h(z)f(z) = 0$$
So, $\langle hf, g \rangle = 0$ for all $f$.
$$\int_{0}^{1} h(t)f(t) \overline{g(t)} \, dt = 0$$
Choose $f(t) = \overline{h(t)}g(t)$. The integral becomes:
$$\int_{0}^{1} |h(t)|^2 |g(t)|^2 \, dt = 0$$
Since $|h(t)|^2$ and $|g(t)|^2$ are non-negative, the integrand must be zero almost everywhere.
$h(t) = t-z$ is only zero at $t=z$. Thus, $|h(t)|^2 > 0$ almost everywhere.
This forces $g(t) = 0$, implying $g = 0$.
This contradicts the hypothesis that $g$ is a non-zero vector representing the functional. Thus, no such $g$ exists.
2. Existence of Adjoint Operators
For finite-dimensional inner product spaces, we can prove the existence of an adjoint operator using the representation of linear functionals.
Theorem:
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional inner product space over field $F$. Let $T$ be a linear operator on $V$. Then there exists a unique linear operator $T^*$ (called the Adjoint of $T$) on $V$ such that:
$$\langle T\alpha, \beta \rangle = \langle \alpha, T^*\beta \rangle$$
for all $\alpha, \beta \in V$.
Proof:
Fix a vector $\beta \in V$.
Define a function $\phi_\beta: V \to F$ by $\phi_\beta(\alpha) = \langle T\alpha, \beta \rangle$.
Check linearity of $\phi_\beta$:
$$\phi_\beta(c\alpha + \gamma) = \langle T(c\alpha + \gamma), \beta \rangle = c\langle T\alpha, \beta \rangle + \langle T\gamma, \beta \rangle = c\phi_\beta(\alpha) + \phi_\beta(\gamma)$$
Thus, $\phi_\beta$ is a linear functional on $V$.
By the Riesz Representation Theorem (for finite-dimensional spaces), there exists a unique vector $\beta' \in V$ such that:
$$\phi_\beta(\alpha) = \langle \alpha, \beta' \rangle$$
Therefore, $\langle T\alpha, \beta \rangle = \langle \alpha, \beta' \rangle$.
Define the operator $T^*$ such that $T^*(\beta) = \beta'$.
This defines a map $T^*: V \to V$.
Linearity of $T^*$:
Using the property $\langle \alpha, T^*\beta \rangle = \langle T\alpha, \beta \rangle$, one can show:
$$\langle \alpha, T^*(c\gamma + \beta) \rangle = \langle T\alpha, c\gamma + \beta \rangle = \bar{c}\langle T\alpha, \gamma \rangle + \langle T\alpha, \beta \rangle$$
$$= \bar{c}\langle \alpha, T^*\gamma \rangle + \langle \alpha, T^*\beta \rangle = \langle \alpha, cT^*\gamma + T^*\beta \rangle$$
Since this holds for all $\alpha$, $T^*(c\gamma + \beta) = cT^*\gamma + T^*\beta$. Thus, $T^*$ is linear.
Uniqueness: Follows from the uniqueness of the vector $\beta'$ in the Riesz Representation Theorem.
3. Matrix Representation of Adjoint Operators
The lecture explores how the matrix of an adjoint operator relates to the matrix of the original operator.
Setup:
Let $\mathcal{B} = \{\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \dots, \alpha_n\}$ be an orthonormal ordered basis for $V$.
Let $A$ be the matrix representation of $T$ relative to $\mathcal{B}$ (i.e., $[T]_\mathcal{B} = A$).
Let $B$ be the matrix representation of $T^*$ relative to $\mathcal{B}$ (i.e., $[T^*]_\mathcal{B} = B$).
Matrix Entries:
Any vector $\alpha$ in an orthonormal basis can be written as $\alpha = \sum \langle \alpha, \alpha_j \rangle \alpha_j$.
The entries of matrix $A$ are defined by $T(\alpha_j) = \sum_{k=1}^n A_{kj} \alpha_k$.
Using the inner product formula for coefficients in an orthonormal basis:
$$A_{kj} = \langle T\alpha_j, \alpha_k \rangle$$
Similarly for $B$ (matrix of $T^*$):
$$B_{kj} = \langle T^*\alpha_j, \alpha_k \rangle$$
Relationship between $A$ and $B$:
Consider the entry $B_{kj}$:
$$B_{kj} = \langle T^*\alpha_j, \alpha_k \rangle$$
Use the property of the adjoint $\langle u, T^*v \rangle = \langle Tu, v \rangle$:
$$B_{kj} = \overline{\langle \alpha_k, T^*\alpha_j \rangle} = \overline{\langle T\alpha_k, \alpha_j \rangle}$$
Recall that $A_{jk} = \langle T\alpha_k, \alpha_j \rangle$.
Therefore:
$$B_{kj} = \overline{A_{jk}}$$
Conclusion:
The matrix of the adjoint operator is the conjugate transpose of the matrix of the operator.
$$[T^*]_\mathcal{B} = ([T]_\mathcal{B})^*$$
Where $B_{kj}$ (element at row $k$, col $j$ of $T^*$) is the complex conjugate of $A_{jk}$ (element at row $j$, col $k$ of $T$). 30 Nov 2025, 14:55:58 GMT+05:30 Products: Gemini Apps Why is this here?
