% iterative_methods.m
%
% This script implements the Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel iterative methods for
% solving linear systems Ax = b.
%
% --- Convergence Condition Explanation ---
% The **Strict Diagonal Dominance (SDD)** condition is a *sufficient*
% condition to guarantee the convergence of both the Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel
% iterative methods.
% A matrix A is SDD if, for every row i, the absolute value of the diagonal
% entry is strictly greater than the sum of the absolute values of all other
% entries in that row:
% $$|A_{i,i}| > \sum_{j \neq i} |A_{i,j}|$$
% If this condition fails, the iterative method is skipped, as convergence
% is not guaranteed.
% -----------------------------------------

function isConvergent = checkConvergenceCondition(A)
    % checkConvergenceCondition
    % Checks if matrix A is Strictly Diagonally Dominant (SDD).
    % SDD is a sufficient condition for the convergence of Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel.
    % Returns true if SDD, false otherwise (including non-square matrices).

    [m, n] = size(A);

    % 1. Check if the matrix is square
    if m ~= n
        isConvergent = false;
        return;
    end

    % 2. Check for Strict Diagonal Dominance
    % For each row i, is |A(i,i)| > sum(|A(i,j)|) for all j ~= i?
    isConvergent = true; % Assume SDD until proven otherwise
    for i = 1:n
        diagVal = abs(A(i,i));
        % Calculate the sum of absolute values of off-diagonal elements
        offDiagSum = sum(abs(A(i,:))) - diagVal;

        if diagVal <= offDiagSum
            % Failure of strict diagonal dominance in row i
            isConvergent = false;
            return;
        end
    end
end

function [x, numIter] = jacobiMethod(A, b, tol, maxIter)
    if nargin < 3, tol = 1e-6; end
    if nargin < 4, maxIter = 100; end

    fprintf('\n Jacobi Method \n');

    % Check the convergence condition (Strict Diagonal Dominance)
    if ~checkConvergenceCondition(A)
        fprintf('[Warning] Jacobi Method: Convergence condition (Strict Diagonal Dominance) failed for this matrix. Skipping calculation.\n');
        n = length(b);
        x = NaN(n, 1); % Return NaN solution
        numIter = 0;   % Return 0 iterations
        return;
    end

    n = length(b);
    x_old = zeros(n, 1); % Start with initial guess x^(0) = 0
    x_new = zeros(n, 1);
    
    % Decompose A = D + R
    D = diag(diag(A));
    R = A - D;

    for numIter = 1:maxIter
        % Vectorized update rule: x_new = inv(D) * (b - R * x_old)
        % This is implemented efficiently as division by the diagonal elements:
        x_new = (b - R * x_old) ./ diag(A);
        
        % Check for convergence using the infinity norm
        if norm(x_new - x_old, inf) < tol
            break;
        end
        x_old = x_new;
    end

    x = x_new;
    fprintf('Converged in %d iterations.\n', numIter);
    fprintf('Solution x =\n'); disp(x);
    fprintf('Residual norm ||Ax - b|| = %.3e\n', norm(A*x - b));
end

function [x, numIter] = gaussSeidelMethod(A, b, tol, maxIter)
    if nargin < 3, tol = 1e-6; end
    if nargin < 4, maxIter = 100; end

    fprintf('\n--- Gauss–Seidel Method ---\n');

    % Check the convergence condition (Strict Diagonal Dominance)
    if ~checkConvergenceCondition(A)
        fprintf('[Warning] Gauss–Seidel Method: Convergence condition (Strict Diagonal Dominance) failed for this matrix. Skipping calculation.\n');
        n = length(b);
        x = NaN(n, 1); % Return NaN solution
        numIter = 0;   % Return 0 iterations
        return;
    end
    
    n = length(b);
    x = zeros(n, 1); % Start with initial guess x^(0) = 0
    x_old = x;

    for numIter = 1:maxIter
        for i = 1:n
            % Use already updated values (x(1:i-1)) for j < i
            sumBefore = A(i, 1:i-1) * x(1:i-1);
            % Use old values (x_old(i+1:end)) for j > i
            sumAfter  = A(i, i+1:end) * x_old(i+1:end);
            
            x(i) = (b(i) - sumBefore - sumAfter) / A(i,i);
        end

        % Check for convergence using the infinity norm
        if norm(x - x_old, inf) < tol
            break;
        end
        x_old = x;
    end
    
    fprintf('Converged in %d iterations.\n', numIter);
    fprintf('Solution x =\n'); disp(x);
    fprintf('Residual norm ||Ax - b|| = %.3e\n', norm(A*x - b));
end

% testIterativeMethods  Run Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel on sample systems

[xGS4, itGS4] = gaussSeidelMethod(A4, b4, tol, maxIter);

% Iterative_Methods.m
% Implements and tests Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel iterative methods for
% solving linear systems Ax = b.
% Includes a check for Strict Diagonal Dominance (SDD) which is a
% sufficient condition for convergence.

function checkConvergenceCondition(A)
    % Checks if matrix A is Strictly Diagonally Dominant (SDD).
    % SDD is a sufficient condition for the convergence of Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel.
    [m, n] = size(A);
    if m ~= n
        error('Matrix must be square.');
    end
    for i = 1:n
        diagVal = abs(A(i,i));
        % Calculate the sum of absolute values of off-diagonal elements in row i
        offDiagSum = sum(abs(A(i,:))) - diagVal;
        if diagVal <= offDiagSum
            % If the absolute value of the diagonal element is less than or equal to
            % the sum of the absolute values of the rest of the row, it fails SDD.
            error('Matrix is not strictly diagonally dominant. Modify the matrix to satisfy the convergence condition.');
        end
    end
end

function [x, numIter] = jacobiMethod(A, b, tol, maxIter)
    % Solves Ax = b using the Jacobi iterative method.
    if nargin < 3, tol = 1e-6; end
    if nargin < 4, maxIter = 100; end
    
    % Ensure A satisfies the SDD condition (for guaranteed convergence)
    checkConvergenceCondition(A);
    
    n = length(b);
    x_old = zeros(n, 1);
    x_new = zeros(n, 1);
    
    % Decompose A = D + R, where D is diagonal and R is the rest
    D = diag(diag(A));
    R = A - D;
    
    fprintf('\n Jacobi Method \n');
    for numIter = 1:maxIter
        % Vectorized update rule: x_new = inv(D) * (b - R * x_old)
        % Since D is diagonal, inv(D) is simply 1./diag(A)
        x_new = (b - R * x_old) ./ diag(A);
        
        % Check for convergence using the infinity norm
        if norm(x_new - x_old, inf) < tol
            break;
        end
        x_old = x_new;
    end
    
    x = x_new;
    fprintf('Converged in %d iterations (max: %d).\n', numIter, maxIter);
    fprintf('Solution x =\n'); disp(x);
    fprintf('Residual norm ||Ax - b|| = %.3e\n', norm(A*x - b));
end

function [x, numIter] = gaussSeidelMethod(A, b, tol, maxIter)
    % Solves Ax = b using the Gauss-Seidel iterative method.
    if nargin < 3, tol = 1e-6; end
    if nargin < 4, maxIter = 100; end
    
    % Ensure A satisfies the SDD condition
    checkConvergenceCondition(A);
    
    n = length(b);
    x = zeros(n, 1);
    x_old = x;
    
    fprintf('\n--- Gauss–Seidel Method ---\n');
    for numIter = 1:maxIter
        x_old = x; % Store the previous iteration for convergence check
        
        for i = 1:n
            % The key difference: use the already updated components of x(1:i-1)
            sumBefore = A(i, 1:i-1) * x(1:i-1);
            % Use the previous iteration's components for x_old(i+1:end)
            sumAfter  = A(i, i+1:end) * x_old(i+1:end);
            
            x(i) = (b(i) - sumBefore - sumAfter) / A(i,i);
        end
        
        if norm(x - x_old, inf) < tol
            break;
        end
    end
    
    fprintf('Converged in %d iterations (max: %d).\n', numIter, maxIter);
    fprintf('Solution x =\n'); disp(x);
    fprintf('Residual norm ||Ax - b|| = %.3e\n', norm(A*x - b));
end

function [x, numIter] = jacobiMethod(A, b, tol, maxIter)
    if nargin < 3, tol = 1e-6; end
    if nargin < 4, maxIter = 100; end
    %Make sure A is well-behaved
    checkConvergenceCondition(A);
    n = length(b);

    D = diag(diag(A));
    R = A - D;
    fprintf('\n Jacobi Method \n');
    for numIter = 1:maxIter

        end
        x_old = x_new;

    x = x_new;

    fprintf('Solution x =\n'); disp(x);
    fprintf('Residual norm ||Ax - b|| = %.3e\n', norm(A*x - b));
end
function [x, numIter] = gaussSeidelMethod(A, b, tol, maxIter)
    if nargin < 3, tol = 1e-6; end
    if nargin < 4, maxIter = 100; end
    checkConvergenceCondition(A);
    n = length(b);

    for numIter = 1:maxIter

            %Use old values for j > i

        if norm(x - x_old, inf) < tol
            break;
        end
        x_old = x;
    end
    fprintf('Converged in %d iterations.\n', numIter);
    fprintf('Solution x =\n'); disp(x);
    fprintf('Residual norm ||Ax - b|| = %.3e\n', norm(A*x - b));
end

Here's why: ACL uses Standard LaTeX: The ACL style files (using the acl.sty package) are based on standard LaTeX document classes, which respect the default float placement specifiers ( h , t , b , p , and ! ). General Recommendation: In the LaTeX community, [htbp] (Here, Top, Bottom, Page of floats) is widely considered the best practice combination to ensure a figure or table is placed quickly and appropriately. ACL Guidelines: The guidelines emphasize that figures and tables should be placed near where they are first discussed , which is exactly what the h (here) specifier is trying to achieve. Using [htbp] maximizes the chances of this happening without causing problems. The key is to use it within the standard figure or figure* environments: $$\begin{figure}[htbp]$$$$...$$$$\end{figure}$$ Note: If you are having trouble with placement, the original [hbt!] (or even [!htbp] ) is also commonly used to tell LaTeX to relax its internal spacing rules and prioritize placement, but [htbp] is a good, safe default. Here's a breakdown of the common placement specifiers and why [htbp] is a solid general alternative: Specifier Meaning h Here - Place the float approximately at the same point it appears in the source text. t Top - Place the float at the top of a page. b Bottom - Place the float at the bottom of a page. p Page of floats - Place the float on a separate page containing only floats. ! Override - Override LaTeX's internal parameters for determining float position (often used with h or other specifiers). Recommended Alternative The best common alternative to [hbt!] is [htbp] . This combination tells LaTeX to try placing the figure: h ere (where it is in the text). At the t op of a page. At the b ottom of a page. On a dedicated p age of floats. Using [htbp] is often preferred because it gives LaTeX the most options for placement, which usually resolves placement issues without resorting to the strict override of ! . Comparison and Context Your original specifier, [hbt!] , tells LaTeX to: Try h ere. Try the b ottom. Try the t op. ! Override LaTeX's normal aesthetic constraints (i.e., put it here or at the bottom/top even if it's aesthetically less pleasing to the algorithm). If you want a very close but perhaps slightly less aggressive alternative, you could use [htb] or [ht] . [htb] : Prioritizes here, top, then bottom. [ht] : Prioritizes here, then top. [H] : (Requires the float package) Places the figure exactly H ere, like a normal part of the text, but this should be used sparingly as it can lead to very poor page breaks. why my figures are not in correct postions in pdf 5 Oct 2025, 20:04:19 GMT+05:30 Of course. Your figures aren't appearing in the correct positions because you're using the figure environment, which in LaTeX is a "float" . The Core Reason: Floats in LaTeX In LaTeX, a figure or table is not treated like a normal character or paragraph. Instead, it's a "floating" object. LaTeX's main goal is to typeset a beautiful and readable document, which means it will move (or "float") large items like figures to a place where they fit best without creating ugly, large empty spaces in the text. When you write \begin{figure}[hbt!] , you are giving LaTeX a set of suggestions , not a command: h : Try to place the figure h ere, exactly where I put it in the code. b : If 'here' doesn't work, try the b ottom of the current page. t : If that doesn't work, try the t op of the next page. ! : Be more **!**nsistent and ignore some of LaTeX's internal aesthetic rules. The problem is that if you have many figures and not enough text, LaTeX cannot satisfy the h (here) request, so it moves on to the next best option ( b or t ), causing the figures to bunch up at the bottom or top of the page. How to Fix It You have two main solutions to force the figures to appear exactly where you want them. Solution 1: Use the float Package (Recommended) This is the best and easiest solution. It introduces a new placement option, [H] , which is much stricter than [h] and essentially means "Put it HERE and nowhere else." Add the float package to the preamble of your document (before \begin{document} ). \documentclass{article}
\usepackage{graphicx}
\usepackage{float} % <-- Add this line

\begin{document} Change [hbt!] to [H] for every figure you want to lock in place. % --- Your original code ---
% \begin{figure}[hbt!]
%   \centering
%   \includegraphics[width=8.7cm]{...}
%   \caption{My caption}
% \end{figure}

% --- The corrected code ---
\begin{figure}[H] % <-- Change [hbt!] to [H]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=8.7cm]{Annotation/figures/more figures/11_confusion_matrix_comparison.png}
  \caption{confusion matrix comparison}
  \label{fig:confusion_matrix} % It's good practice to have unique labels
\end{figure} Solution 2: Don't Use a Float at All If you don't need a formal "figure" with a number (e.g., "Figure 1"), you can place the image directly. If you still want a caption, you'll need the caption package. Add the caption package to your preamble. \documentclass{article}
\usepackage{graphicx}
\usepackage{caption} % <-- Add this line

\begin{document} Remove the figure environment and use \captionof instead. \subsection{Cost Analysis}

\begin{center}
    \includegraphics[width=8.7cm]{Annotation/figures/more figures/03_single_agent_costs.png}
    \captionof{figure}{Cost analysis for single-agent}
    \label{fig:single_agent_cost}
\end{center}

\begin{center}
    \includegraphics[width=8.7cm]{Annotation/figures/more figures/02_multi_agent_costs.png}
    \captionof{figure}{Cost analysis for Multi-agent}
    \label{fig:multi_agent_cost}
\end{center} Recommendation For your document, Solution 1 is the best approach . Simply add \usepackage{float} to your preamble and change all your \begin{figure}[hbt!] to \begin{figure}[H] . This will force the figures to appear exactly where you placed them in the code. Products: Gemini Apps Why is this here? ## Executive Summary

This analysis compares the performance of multi-agent (4 agents) versus single-agent fine-tuned models on bias classification tasks using 1000 samples each. The results demonstrate significant superiority of the multi-agent approach across multiple evaluation metrics.

### Key Results
- **Multi-agent Accuracy**: 77.2% (772/1000 correct)
- **Single-agent Accuracy**: 62.2% (622/1000 correct)
- **Accuracy Improvement**: +15.0 percentage points (+24.1% relative improvement)
- **Statistical Significance**: p = 3.40e-13 (highly significant)
- **Effect Size**: Cohen's h = 0.329 (medium effect)

## 8. Key Findings and Conclusions

### Primary Discoveries

1. **Significant Performance Improvement**: Multi-agent system shows 15 percentage point accuracy improvement with high statistical significance (p < 0.001).

2. **Balanced Classification**: Multi-agent provides more balanced performance across bias types, reducing systematic bias toward stereotype predictions.

3. **Token Complexity Effect**: Both systems struggle with longer texts, but multi-agent maintains superior performance across all complexity levels.

4. **Error Reduction**: Multi-agent system produces 150 fewer errors (39.7% reduction) compared to single-agent.

5. **Processing Time Trade-off**: Multi-agent requires 71% more processing time but delivers 24% better accuracy.

Question 2: Reaction of $\text{Cr(CO)}_6$ This question involves two sequential reactions starting with $\text{Cr(CO)}_6$: $$\text{Cr(CO)}_6 + \text{LiC}_6\text{H}_5 \rightarrow \mathbf{A}$$

The nucleophile , phenyllithium ($\text{LiC}_6\text{H}_5$ or $\text{LiPh}$) , attacks one of the electron-poor carbonyl carbons . This forms an intermediate anionic acyl complex , an example of a Fischer Carbene precursor . $$\text{Cr(CO)}_6 + \text{LiPh} \rightarrow \text{[Cr(CO)}_5\text{C(O)Ph]Li} \quad (\mathbf{A})$$ Structure of A: A pentacarbonyl chromium unit ($\text{(CO)}_5\text{Cr}$). The sixth position is occupied by the acyl anion group, $-\text{C(O)Ph}$ (or $-\text{C(O)C}_6\text{H}_5$). The lithium counter-ion ($\text{Li}^+$) is associated with the anionic oxygen. The geometry is octahedral with the acyl group being a monodentate ligand. Step 2: Formation of B (Alkylation/Electrophilic Attack) The anionic acyl oxygen in A is highly nucleophilic . The reagent, trimethyloxonium tetrafluoroborate $\text{[Me}_3\text{O}][\text{BF}_4]$ , is a strong methylating agent (electrophile). The $\text{O}$-alkylation occurs on the acyl oxygen atom. $$\text{[Cr(CO)}_5\text{C(O)Ph]Li} + [\text{Me}_3\text{O}][\text{BF}_4] \rightarrow \text{(CO)}_5\text{Cr=C(OMe)Ph} + \text{Me}_2\text{O} + \text{LiBF}_4 \quad (\mathbf{B})$$ Structure of B: A Fischer Carbene Complex . The $\text{O}$ atom gets methylated ($\text{-OMe}$). The resulting carbene ligand is $-\text{C(OMe)Ph}$ (or $-\text{C(OMe)C}_6\text{H}_5$). Comparing with the Options: The correct option must show: A as the anionic acyl complex $\text{[Cr(CO)}_5\text{C(O)C}_6\text{H}_5]\text{Li}$, where the $\text{Li}$ is near the $\text{O}$ atom of the acyl group. B as the neutral Fischer Carbene complex $\text{(CO)}_5\text{Cr=C(OMe)C}_6\text{H}_5$. Looking at the provided structures: (a) $\mathbf{A}$: shows the $\text{Li}$ complex with $\text{-C(O)C}_6\text{H}_5$. $\mathbf{B}$: shows the resulting carbene $\text{Cr=C(OCH}_3)\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$. This is the correct pair. (b) $\mathbf{A}$ is correct, but $\mathbf{B}$ shows an incorrect $\text{Cr=C(CH}_3)\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$ (an alkyl carbene, not an alkoxy carbene). (c) $\mathbf{A}$ shows the $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$ attached to a $\text{CO}$ ligand, not the $\text{Li}$ near the $\text{O}$. $\mathbf{B}$ is a $\text{Cr=C(OCH}_3)\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$ complex, but the geometry is unusual. (d) Both $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ have incorrect structures/ligand attachments. The structures of A and B respectively are represented in option (a) . Products: Gemini Apps Why is this here? The Architecture of Reason: A Comprehensive Analysis of Logic, Argumentation, and Critical Debate Introduction The study of logic is the systematic evaluation of arguments, a discipline that provides the foundational principles for correct reasoning.[1] In an era characterized by an unprecedented volume of information and persuasive rhetoric, the ability to distinguish sound reasoning from fallacy is not merely an academic pursuit but a requisite skill for intellectual autonomy and meaningful participation in society.[2] The principles of argumentation form the bedrock of scientific inquiry, legal deliberation, philosophical debate, and the everyday choices that shape individual lives.[2, 3] This report provides a comprehensive analysis of the core concepts in logic and argumentation. It begins by deconstructing the argument into its fundamental components, establishing a precise lexicon for analysis. It then explores the primary modes of reasoning—deductive, inductive, and abductive—that form the dynamic engine of inference. Subsequently, it establishes the rigorous criteria by which arguments are evaluated for their structural integrity and factual accuracy. The analysis extends to a taxonomy of evidence, the philosophical grounds of knowledge itself, and concludes by situating these elements within the larger, dialectical process of critical debate through which knowledge is produced, contested, and refined. Part I: The Anatomy of an Argument To analyze reasoning, one must first understand its constituent parts. An argument is not a simple assertion but a complex structure built from specific logical elements, each with a distinct function. This section dissects this structure to establish a clear and foundational vocabulary. 1.1 The Genesis of Argument: The Issue All argumentation originates from an Issue , which is the explicit or implicit question that sparks disagreement, invites inquiry, or presents a point of uncertainty. The issue is the catalyst for debate, representing a contested point that cannot be resolved through simple observation or universal agreement. For example, the question of whether pineapple is an acceptable pizza topping constitutes an issue that gives rise to arguments on both sides.[4] The issue frames the entire discourse, setting the boundaries within which all subsequent claims and evidence must operate to be considered relevant. 1.2 Propositions and Claims: The Substance of Discourse The building blocks of arguments are propositions, which are deployed strategically as claims. Proposition The most fundamental unit of logic is the proposition . A proposition is a declarative statement that asserts a particular state of affairs and, crucially, possesses a truth value—it must be either true or false.[5, 6] It is important to distinguish the abstract proposition from the specific sentence used to express it. For instance, the sentences "Smith loves Jones" and "Jones is loved by Smith" are linguistically different but express the identical proposition.[6] Questions, commands, and exclamations are not propositions because they cannot be judged as true or false.[5] Claim A claim is a proposition that has been put forward for acceptance within the context of an argument.[4] While all claims are propositions, a proposition becomes a claim when it serves as the primary assertion an arguer is attempting to establish. For example, in the statement, "The Los Angeles Chargers have the potential to make the NFL playoffs," the proposition about the Chargers' potential is functioning as the central claim to be defended.[4] A subtle but critical distinction exists here. A proposition is a static logical entity defined by its potential to be true or false. A claim, however, is a proposition that has been assigned a dynamic role within an argument: the assertion to be proven. This functional distinction highlights that argumentation is the art of strategically deploying propositions to serve specific purposes, either as the point to be proven (the claim) or as the reasons for that proof (the premises). 1.3 The Engine of Reasoning: Argument, Premises, Conclusion, and Inference These components form the core structure of reasoned persuasion. Argument An argument is a structured set of propositions in which one or more propositions, known as premises , are offered as support for another proposition, the conclusion .[5, 6, 7] An argument is more than a mere collection of related statements; it is defined by the purported logical connection between its parts.[6] Its purpose is to provide rational grounds for believing the conclusion is true.[5] Premises Premises are the propositions presented as reasons, evidence, or grounds for accepting the conclusion.[4, 7] An argument must contain at least one premise to justify its conclusion. In natural language, premises are often introduced by indicator words such as "because," "since," "for," "as," or "in view of the fact that".[4, 7] For example, the statement "...because they have three of the best players in the league" serves as a premise supporting a claim about a team's playoff potential.[4] Conclusion The conclusion is the main point of the argument—the proposition that the premises are intended to prove or support.[4, 6] It is the logical outcome derived from the premises. Conclusions are frequently signaled by indicator words like "therefore," "thus," "hence," "consequently," or "it follows that".[4] For instance, "Therefore, pineapple is a perfectly acceptable and delicious pizza topping" is the conclusion of an argument about culinary combinations.[4] Inference Inference is the mental process or logical transition that connects the premises to the conclusion.[5, 6, 7] It is the act of reasoning that allows one to move from the acceptance of the premises to the acceptance of the conclusion. While "argument" refers to the complete structure of propositions, "inference" refers more specifically to this logical leap. The essence of an argument lies not in the truth or falsity of its constituent propositions, but in the integrity of the inferential link between them. A set of propositions can all be true, but if no logical inference connects them, they do not form an argument.[6] For example, the statements "Grass is green" and "Snow is white" are both true, but they provide no logical support for the conclusion "Therefore, the ocean is blue".[8] The evaluation of an argument, therefore, must prioritize the assessment of its inferential structure. Part II: The Three Paths of Logical Inference Reasoning is not a monolithic process. Logicians and philosophers have identified three distinct modes of inference, each with its own logical flow, standard of certainty, and role in the pursuit of knowledge. Understanding their differences is essential for both constructing and critiquing arguments effectively. 2.1 The Logic of Certainty: Deductive Reasoning Deductive reasoning is a "top-down" form of inference that moves from one or more general premises to a specific conclusion that follows with logical necessity.[9, 10, 11] The defining characteristic of a deductive argument is that if its premises are true, its conclusion is guaranteed to be true.[5, 9] It is impossible for the premises to be true and the conclusion false without creating a logical contradiction.[6] This form of reasoning is often structured as a syllogism , a classic example being: Major Premise: All humans are mortal. (A general rule) Minor Premise: Socrates is a human. (A specific instance falling under the rule) Conclusion: Therefore, Socrates is mortal. (The necessary conclusion) [5, 12] The conclusion of a deductive argument is non-ampliative; it does not introduce new information about the world but rather makes explicit what was already contained implicitly within the premises.[13] Its function is not discovery but proof, clarification, and the application of established rules to particular cases. This makes it the primary mode of reasoning in fields that demand certainty, such as mathematics and formal logic, as well as in practical applications like legal reasoning and planning.[12, 14] 2.2 The Logic of Probability: Inductive Reasoning Inductive reasoning operates in the opposite direction of deduction. It is a "bottom-up" process that moves from a series of specific observations to a broader, probable generalization.[9, 10, 11] Unlike deduction, induction deals in probabilities, not certainties.[13] The structure of an inductive argument is based on identifying patterns within a sample of evidence: Observation 1: The sun rose this morning. Observation 2: The sun has risen every morning observed in the past. Conclusion: Therefore, the sun will probably rise tomorrow. [14] The conclusion of an inductive argument is ampliative, meaning it goes beyond the information provided in the premises to make a wider claim about the world.[13] This power to generate new knowledge comes at the cost of certainty. No matter how many confirming instances are observed (e.g., white swans), one can never be 100% certain that the next observation will not contradict the generalization.[11] The strength of an inductive conclusion is contingent on the quality, quantity, and representativeness of the evidence. Induction is the cornerstone of the empirical sciences, where theories are formed from experimental data, and it underpins most of our everyday learning and predictions based on past experience.[13, 14] 2.3 The Logic of Explanation: Abductive Reasoning Abductive reasoning is the process of forming a conclusion by seeking the best or most likely explanation for an observed phenomenon. Often called "inference to the best explanation," it begins with an incomplete set of observations and works backward to posit the most plausible cause or hypothesis.[9, 15, 16] The logical flow of abduction is from effect to a likely cause: Observation: A patient presents with a fever, cough, and fatigue. Possible Explanation 1: The patient has the common cold. Possible Explanation 2: The patient has influenza. Possible Explanation 3: The patient has COVID-19. Conclusion: Given the current prevalence of COVID-19 and the specific symptom cluster, the most plausible initial hypothesis is a COVID-19 infection, which should be tested. [14] The conclusion of an abductive inference is a plausible hypothesis, not a proven fact or a generalized rule.[17] Its strength lies in its explanatory power—its ability to account for the available evidence in the simplest and most coherent way. Abduction is the logic of discovery and diagnosis, essential for generating hypotheses in science, conducting medical diagnoses, and performing detective work.[9, 14, 15] These three modes of reasoning are not mutually exclusive but often work in a complementary cycle to produce knowledge. An inquiry may begin with a surprising observation, for which abduction generates a plausible hypothesis. Induction is then used to gather more data and generalize that hypothesis into a broader theory. Finally, deduction tests the theory by deriving specific, falsifiable predictions from it. This cyclical process—hypothesize, generalize, test—is a more robust model of scientific and critical inquiry than viewing each mode in isolation. This interplay also reveals a fundamental trade-off in reasoning. Deduction provides absolute certainty, but its conclusions are not informative in the sense of adding new knowledge about the world. Induction and abduction, conversely, are ampliative and expand our knowledge, but their conclusions are inherently probabilistic and fallible. This explains why fields like mathematics, which value certainty, are primarily deductive, while empirical sciences, which seek to discover new truths about the world, are grounded in inductive and abductive methods. | Attribute | Deductive Reasoning | Inductive Reasoning | Abductive Reasoning |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Logical Flow | Top-Down (General Rule to Specific Case) | Bottom-Up (Specific Observations to General Rule) | Effect to Cause (Observation to Best Explanation) |
| Conclusion Strength | Necessary / Guaranteed (if premises are true) | Probable / Likely | Plausible / Hypothetical |
| Key Function | Proof / Application of Rules | Generalization / Prediction | Hypothesis Formation / Explanation |
| Nature of Conclusion | Non-Ampliative (makes implicit knowledge explicit) | Ampliative (goes beyond the premises) | Ampliative (goes beyond the premises) |
| Classic Example | All humans are mortal; Socrates is human; ∴ Socrates is mortal. | The sun has always risen; ∴ The sun will rise tomorrow. | The grass is wet; It probably rained. | Part III: The Criteria for Critical Evaluation Understanding the structure of an argument is the first step; evaluating its quality is the second. The standards for judging an argument depend on the type of reasoning it employs. Deductive and inductive arguments, because of their different claims to certainty, are assessed using distinct but parallel sets of criteria. 3.1 Evaluating Deductive Arguments: Validity and Soundness Validity Validity is a formal property of a deductive argument that pertains exclusively to its logical structure.[18] An argument is valid if, and only if, it is impossible for its conclusion to be false assuming its premises are true .[6, 19] Validity is a test of the inferential link; it does not concern the actual truth of the premises themselves.[12] A valid argument can have false premises and a false conclusion. For example: "All birds are fish. Tweety is a bird. Therefore, Tweety is a fish" is a structurally valid argument, because if the premises were true, the conclusion would have to be true.[20] The only combination ruled out by validity is true premises and a false conclusion. Any argument with this combination is, by definition, invalid .[19, 20] Soundness Soundness is the highest standard for a deductive argument. An argument is sound if it meets two conditions: it must be valid , and all of its premises must be actually true .[5, 18, 19] Because a sound argument is valid and has true premises, its conclusion is guaranteed to be true.[8, 19] An argument that is valid but has at least one false premise is considered unsound .[8] The example "All birds are fish..." is valid but unsound. A sound argument, such as "All mammals are animals. All dogs are mammals. Therefore, all dogs are animals," provides the strongest possible form of logical proof.[18] 3.2 Evaluating Inductive Arguments: Strength and Cogency Because inductive arguments only claim that their conclusions are probable, they cannot be valid or sound. Instead, they are evaluated using the analogous concepts of strength and cogency. Strength Strength measures the degree of support the premises provide for the conclusion in an inductive argument. An argument is strong if it is improbable that its conclusion is false assuming its premises are true .[1, 8] Unlike the binary valid/invalid distinction, strength exists on a continuum from weak to strong.[18] A strong argument: "99% of all humans are right-handed. John is a human. Therefore, John is probably right-handed." A weak argument: "1% of all humans are ambidextrous. Jane is a human. Therefore, Jane is probably ambidextrous." Cogency Cogency is the highest standard for an inductive argument. An argument is cogent if it meets two conditions: it must be strong , and all of its premises must be actually true .[1, 7, 18] A cogent argument provides good reason to believe its conclusion is likely true.[18] However, because inductive reasoning is probabilistic, a cogent argument does not guarantee a true conclusion. It is still possible, though unlikely, for a cogent argument to have true premises and a false conclusion.[8, 20] For example, the argument "Most birds can fly. Tweety is a bird. Therefore, Tweety can probably fly" is cogent, but its conclusion would be false if Tweety turned out to be a penguin.[20] This framework reveals a fundamental division of labor in argument analysis. The first step, assessing validity or strength, is a purely logical task focused on the argument's internal structure. The second step, assessing soundness or cogency, adds an empirical task: one must go outside the argument to investigate the actual truth of the premises. This distinction allows for a precise diagnosis of an argument's flaws. An argument can be logically impeccable but based on false information (valid but unsound), or it can be composed of true statements that are logically disconnected (invalid). | | Deductive Arguments | Inductive Arguments |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Criterion for Logical Structure | Validity: If premises are true, conclusion must be true. | Strength: If premises are true, conclusion is probably true. |
| Criterion for Structure + True Premises | Soundness: Argument is valid AND all premises are actually true. | Cogency: Argument is strong AND all premises are actually true. | Part IV: The Foundations of Support: A Taxonomy of Evidence The truth of an argument's premises—a requirement for both soundness and cogency—depends on the evidence provided to support them. Evidence can take many forms, each with unique characteristics, strengths, and weaknesses. A skilled arguer must select the type of evidence most appropriate for the claim being made. 4.1 Statistical and Empirical Evidence Statistical evidence quantifies a phenomenon using numbers, percentages, surveys, and other numerical data.[21, 22] Empirical evidence is gathered through direct observation and measurement.[23] This category is often considered the strongest form of evidence because of its objective and verifiable nature.[21] It is particularly effective for demonstrating the scope or significance of an issue and for supporting general claims about populations.[22] For example, citing data on the number of annual deaths related to not wearing a seatbelt provides powerful, concrete support for an argument about traffic safety.[22] However, its reliability is contingent on the integrity of the methodology used for its collection; biased samples, flawed experiments, or deliberate manipulation can render statistical evidence misleading.[22, 24] 4.2 Testimonial Evidence Testimonial evidence is drawn from the statements of other people and can be divided into two main types.[25, 26] Expert Testimony leverages the findings or opinions of a recognized authority in a relevant field. Citing an expert lends credibility to an argument, showing that the position is supported by someone with deep knowledge and experience.[24, 27] Eyewitness Testimony consists of first-hand accounts from individuals who observed an event.[25] The strength of expert testimony depends on the expert's credentials and the relevance of their expertise to the topic at hand; an expert in one field is not an authority in another.[25] Eyewitness accounts can provide compelling, direct evidence but are susceptible to human error, including memory distortion, perceptual biases, and subjectivity.[25] 4.3 Anecdotal Evidence Anecdotal evidence consists of personal stories, individual experiences, or isolated examples.[21, 22, 26] While generally considered a weak form of evidence for establishing a general rule—as a single case may not be representative—it serves several important rhetorical functions. Anecdotes can make abstract issues more concrete and emotionally resonant, helping to engage an audience.[22, 24] More importantly from a logical standpoint, a single, well-chosen anecdote can serve as a powerful counterexample sufficient to disprove a universal claim. For example, the claim "All swans are white" is definitively falsified by the anecdotal evidence of a single black swan.[26, 27] 4.4 Analogical Evidence Analogical evidence supports a conclusion by drawing a comparison between two distinct things or situations.[21, 22] The argument posits that because the two analogues share certain relevant characteristics, they likely share the characteristic at issue as well. Analogies are particularly useful for explaining complex or unfamiliar topics in more accessible terms.[22] For instance, a doctor might explain a medical procedure by analogy to a more familiar mechanical process.[22] In cases where a topic is new or under-researched, analogy may be the only form of evidence available.[26] The weakness of this evidence type is that its strength is entirely dependent on the relevance and degree of similarity between the two things being compared. A flawed or "false" analogy, where the differences outweigh the similarities, offers no logical support.[22, 28] The effectiveness of evidence is not absolute but is highly contextual and depends on the nature of the claim being supported. To prove a statistical claim about a population, statistical evidence is indispensable and anecdotal evidence is nearly irrelevant. To refute a universal claim ("all X are Y"), a single piece of anecdotal evidence (an X that is not Y) is the most decisive form of proof possible. For a claim about a novel situation, a carefully constructed analogy may be the most persuasive evidence available. Therefore, critical evaluation requires not just identifying the type of evidence used, but judging its appropriateness for the specific argumentative task. Part V: The Philosophical Grounds of Knowledge: Kant's Theory of Judgement Beyond the mechanics of argumentation lies the deeper philosophical question of knowledge itself: What is the nature of the "truths" that premises and conclusions express? The philosopher Immanuel Kant provided a revolutionary framework for understanding the origins and types of human knowledge by introducing two fundamental distinctions that intersect to create a matrix of judgment. 5.1 The Epistemological Distinction: A Priori vs. A Posteriori This distinction concerns the origin of our knowledge. A Priori judgments are those that can be known through reason alone, independent of any specific sensory experience.[29, 30, 31] They are characterized by necessity (they could not be otherwise) and strict universality (they admit no exceptions). The truth of "2+2=4" is known a priori. A Posteriori judgments are those that can only be known through experience.[29, 30, 31] Their truth is grounded in and verified by sensory observation. They are contingent (they could have been otherwise) and lack strict universality. The truth of "The sky is blue" is known a posteriori. 5.2 The Semantic Distinction: Analytic vs. Synthetic This distinction concerns the relationship between the subject and predicate of a judgment. Analytic judgments are those in which the predicate concept is already contained within the subject concept.[29, 30, 32] Such judgments are explicative ; they analyze and clarify the meaning of the subject but add no new information. The statement "All bachelors are unmarried" is analytic because the concept [unmarried] is part of the definition of the subject [bachelor]. Synthetic judgments are those in which the predicate concept is not contained within the subject concept.[29, 30, 32] These judgments are ampliative ; they synthesize or add new information to the subject, thereby expanding our knowledge. The statement "All crows are black" is synthetic because the concept [black] is not part of the definition of [crow]. 5.3 The Crux of Kantian Philosophy: The Synthetic A Priori Before Kant, philosophers generally assumed these two distinctions aligned: all a priori judgments were thought to be analytic (truths of logic and definition), and all synthetic judgments were thought to be a posteriori (truths of fact derived from experience).[31, 33] Kant's groundbreaking insight was to argue for the existence and fundamental importance of a third category: synthetic a priori judgments . These are judgments that expand our knowledge of the world (synthetic) yet are known with the necessity and universality of pure reason (a priori).[29, 33] Kant found examples of such judgments in mathematics and the foundational principles of science: Mathematics: He argued that "7 + 5 = 12" is synthetic because the concept of '12' is not found by merely analyzing the concepts of '7' and '5'. It requires an act of construction or synthesis. Yet, it is known a priori with absolute certainty, not through repeated experiments.[30, 32] Metaphysics: The principle "Every event has a cause" is synthetic because 'having a cause' is not part of the definition of 'event'. Yet, Kant argued, it is a principle we know a priori, as it is a necessary precondition for our ability to make sense of experience at all.[31] Kant's solution to the puzzle of how such knowledge is possible was his "Copernican Revolution" in philosophy. He proposed that our minds are not passive recipients of sensory data but actively structure our experience according to innate cognitive frameworks. These frameworks include the "forms of intuition" (space and time) and the "categories of the understanding" (such as causality and substance). Synthetic a priori judgments are, therefore, knowledge not of a world as it is "in itself," but of the necessary and universal structures of our own experience.[31, 33] This radically redefines objectivity. For Kant, an objective truth is not one that corresponds to a mind-independent reality, but one that conforms to the necessary structures of any rational mind. | | Analytic (Explicative) | Synthetic (Ampliative) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| A Priori (Known via Reason) | Analytic A Priori: True by definition. Ex: "All triangles have three sides." | Synthetic A Priori: Necessarily true and expands knowledge. Ex: "7 + 5 = 12." |
| A Posteriori (Known via Experience) | (Impossible Category): Experience is not needed to analyze a concept. | Synthetic A Posteriori: Contingently true and expands knowledge. Ex: "The cat is on the mat." | Part VI: The Dialectical Process of Critical Inquiry The concepts of logic and argumentation are not static tools but are deployed within a dynamic, social process of critical debate and knowledge production. This final section models this process, integrating the previously discussed components into a lifecycle that moves from conflict to resolution and application. 6.1 Framing the Debate: Issue and Disjunction A critical inquiry begins with an Issue , the central question under consideration. The emergence of an issue immediately gives rise to a Disjunction : a state where two or more competing, often mutually exclusive, theories or positions are proposed as solutions.[34] This represents the initial state of intellectual conflict, the thesis and antithesis that set the stage for debate. 6.2 The Engine of Progress: Dialectical Form and In-Conjunction The Dialectical Form is the interactive process through which these disjunctive positions engage one another. It involves the presentation of arguments, the critical examination of evidence and reasoning, and the identification of contradictions both within and between the competing views.[35, 36] This is not simply a contest to determine a winner but a collaborative, albeit adversarial, process aimed at advancing understanding. The goal is to move beyond the initial opposition toward an In-Conjunction —a synthesis or reconciliation that resolves the conflict by forming a more comprehensive, higher-level understanding that often preserves the valid insights of the original positions while transcending their limitations.[37] 6.3 Achieving Resolution: Closure Statement and Summary Extraction The dialectical process culminates in a provisional resolution. A Closure Statement articulates the outcome of the debate, whether it is a definitive synthesized conclusion or a recognition of an ongoing stalemate and the reasons for it.[34] Following this, Summary Extraction is the cognitive act of distilling the essential knowledge gained. This involves identifying the core principles that have been established, the questions that have been answered, and the new lines of inquiry that have been opened. This extracted summary constitutes the new knowledge produced by the process. 6.4 The Scope of Application: Individualization, Culturalization, and Universalization The final stage of knowledge production involves defining the domain of validity for the extracted conclusion. This is a critical step that determines the applicability and authority of the new knowledge. Individualization: The conclusion is framed as a matter of subjective belief or personal truth. This perspective roots knowledge in the possessive individualism that is a hegemonic form of subjectivity in many modern societies.[38] Culturalization: The conclusion is understood as being true relative to a specific culture, community, or historical context. This approach uses culture as a primary explanatory framework. While it can respect diversity, it also risks "culturalization," where culture is treated as a static, all-encompassing explanation that can obscure other social or economic factors and create hierarchical divisions between groups.[39, 40] Universalization: The conclusion is posited as a universal principle that applies across all contexts. This approach seeks to establish general laws and objective truths but can be criticized for dehistoricizing phenomena and erasing meaningful local differences.[41, 42] This final stage reveals that the production of knowledge is not a purely abstract or logical endeavor. The act of defining the scope of a conclusion is laden with political and social implications. To universalize a finding is to grant it maximum authority, which may delegitimize other perspectives. To culturalize it can be a means of either respecting particularity or marginalizing a group as "other." To individualize it champions personal autonomy but may hinder collective understanding and action. The choice of scope is itself a claim that can be subjected to further critical debate, demonstrating that the process of knowledge creation is recursive, unending, and deeply embedded in the social world. Conclusion The architecture of reason is a multi-layered structure, extending from the fundamental logical unit of the proposition to the complex, societal dialectic of knowledge production. This analysis has demonstrated that a comprehensive understanding of argumentation requires not only a grasp of its static components—premises, conclusions, and evidence—but also an appreciation for the dynamic processes of inference that give it life. The distinct paths of deductive, inductive, and abductive reasoning each offer unique capabilities, trading certainty for informative power in a cycle that drives inquiry forward. The rigorous standards of validity, soundness, cogency, and the contextual use of evidence provide the critical tools needed to evaluate the quality of any argument. Ultimately, these logical structures are situated within the philosophical framework of how knowledge itself is constituted and the social framework of how it is debated and defined. Mastering this architecture is to acquire the essential means for navigating complexity, challenging falsehoods, and contributing constructively to the ongoing pursuit of understanding. 1. Gemini Apps Prompted tommorow is my exam teach me this give me proper intutions and examples with solutions general steps to solve this kind of problems Attached 1 file. - image_081dc7.png 22 Sept 2025, 12:53:48 GMT+05:30 Of course! Let's break down these notes and get you ready for your exam. We'll focus on the intuition behind the concepts, which makes them much easier to remember. Here's a structured explanation of your notes. ## 1. Stability of Numerical Problems: Well-Behaved vs. Poorly-Behaved 🤔 The Core Idea (Intuition) Imagine you're baking a cake. A well-conditioned (stable) recipe is one where if you add a tiny bit too much flour (a small input error), the cake still turns out great (a small output error). An ill-conditioned (unstable) recipe is one where a tiny bit too much flour makes the cake completely inedible (a huge output error). In numerical analysis, we're dealing with equations instead of recipes. A problem is stable or well-conditioned if small errors in your initial data lead to only small errors in the final answer. It's unstable or ill-conditioned if tiny, unavoidable errors in your input data can cause massive, disastrous errors in your final answer. Formal Definitions from Your Notes The Problem: You have an equation linking some data y to a solution x . Condition Number K(x) : This is the "error amplification factor". It formally measures how much the relative error in the output can be magnified compared to the relative error in the input.
$$K(x) = \frac{\text{Relative Error in Output}}{\text{Relative Error in Input}} = \frac{|\delta x / x|}{|\delta y / y|}$$ The Rule: If K is small (e.g., 1, 10, 100), the problem is stable . Your answer is reliable. If K is huge (e.g., 10⁹), the problem is unstable . Your answer could be garbage even if your input was almost perfect. Example: System of Equations Consider finding the intersection of two lines. Well-Conditioned Problem: x + y = 2 x - y = 0 The lines intersect at a clear angle. The solution is x=1, y=1 . If you slightly change the first equation to x + 1.001y = 2 , the solution barely moves. This is stable. Ill-Conditioned Problem: x + y = 2 x + 1.00001y = 2.00002 These lines are almost parallel. The solution is x=0, y=2 . But if we make a tiny change to the second equation: x + 1.00001y = 2.00003 , the new solution is x=-1, y=3 ! A microscopic change in the input (0.00001) caused a huge change in the output. This problem is ill-conditioned. ## 2. Finding Roots of Non-Linear Equations ( f(x) = 0 ) 🤔 The Core Idea (Intuition) For a simple equation like 2x - 4 = 0 , you can find the root x=2 directly. But for something like cos(x) - x = 0 , you can't just isolate x . So, we have to use clever guessing. This is what iterative methods are all about. It's like playing "hot and cold". You make a guess, the method tells you how to make a better guess, and you repeat this process until your guess is incredibly close to the actual answer. Methods from Your Notes Direct Methods: This is what you do for simple equations. You use a formula (like the quadratic formula for ax² + bx + c = 0 ) and get the exact answer in one go. Limitation: Only works for a very small class of (mostly linear) problems. Iterative Methods: The workhorse for most non-linear problems. Process: Start with an initial guess ( x₀ ). -> Use a rule to get a better guess ( x₁ ). -> Use the rule again to get an even better guess ( x₂ ). -> ... and so on. The sequence of guesses is {x₀, x₁, x₂, ...} . The method converges if this sequence gets closer and closer to the true root, ξ . The Convergence Theorem (The "Guarantee") How do we know our guessing game will actually lead to the right answer? That's what the theorem in your notes is for. The Theorem says: A sequence {xₙ} converges to the root ξ if you can show that the error at the next step is always a fraction of the error at the current step.
$$|x_{n+1} - \xi| \le C |x_n - \xi| \quad \text{for a constant } 0 < C < 1$$ Intuition: |xₙ - ξ| is your distance from the true answer (the error). The constant C is a "shrinking factor". If C=0.5 , this formula guarantees that with every step you take, you cut your distance to the true answer at least in half. Proof Sketch from your notes: By applying this rule repeatedly, the error at step n is |xₙ - ξ| ≤ Cⁿ |x₀ - ξ| . Since C is less than 1, when n gets very large, Cⁿ becomes incredibly small (it goes to zero). This forces the error to go to zero, meaning xₙ must converge to ξ . Example: Finding √3 Let's find the root of f(x) = x² - 3 = 0 . The true root is ξ = √3 ≈ 1.732 .
Let's use an iterative method called Newton's Method (the formula isn't important, just the process). Initial Guess: x₀ = 1 Iteration 1: The formula gives x₁ = 2 Iteration 2: The formula gives x₂ = 1.75 Iteration 3: The formula gives x₃ = 1.73214... Iteration 4: The formula gives x₄ = 1.73205... You can see the sequence {1, 2, 1.75, 1.73214, ...} is rapidly converging to the true root √3 . ## General Steps for Your Exam Identify the Problem Type: Is the question about whether a problem is sensitive to initial errors ? That's a stability/conditioning problem. Is the question about finding a solution x for an equation f(x)=0 ? That's a root-finding problem. If it's a Stability Problem: Think about the Condition Number K . Ask yourself: If I slightly change the numbers in the problem, does the final answer change a little or a lot? Look for things that cause instability, like trying to find the intersection of nearly parallel lines. If it's a Root-Finding Problem: Can you solve it directly (is it linear/quadratic)? If yes, do it. If not, it's iterative . You'll be given a starting point x₀ and an iteration formula. Your job is often to perform a few iterations to show you understand the process. Just plug the last answer back into the formula to get the next one. If asked about convergence, you need to refer to the convergence theorem . You've got this! Take a deep breath and focus on these core intuitions. Good luck with your exam! Products: Gemini Apps Why is this here? Here is a comprehensive guide covering the key concepts in neural networks, from the foundational Perceptron to modern Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). The Perceptron: The Original Neuron The key breakthrough of the Perceptron, introduced by Frank Rosenblatt in 1958, was its ability to learn from data. It was the first algorithm that could automatically learn the optimal weight coefficients to separate data into different classes, forming the foundation of machine learning. Logic Gates with a Perceptron A Perceptron computes a weighted sum of its inputs and passes it through a step function. The output ŷ is 1 if $w \cdot x + b > 0$ and 0 otherwise. AND Gate: We need the output to be 1 only if both inputs ($x_1, x_2$) are 1. Parameters: $w_1 = 1$, $w_2 = 1$, $b = -1.5$ Example: If $x_1=1, x_2=1$, then $(1 1) + (1 1) - 1.5 = 0.5 > 0 \implies$ output is 1. If $x_1=1, x_2=0$, then $(1 1) + (1 0) - 1.5 = -0.5 < 0 \implies$ output is 0. OR Gate: We need the output to be 1 if at least one input is 1. Parameters: $w_1 = 1$, $w_2 = 1$, $b = -0.5$ NOT Gate: (Considers only one input, $x_1$) Parameters: $w_1 = -1$, $b = 0.5$ Decision Boundary and Decision Function Decision Function: This is the linear equation the Perceptron computes before the step function: $f(x) = w_1x_1 + w_2x_2 + ... + b$. It defines a value for any point in the input space. Decision Boundary: This is the line (or hyperplane in higher dimensions) where the decision function is exactly zero: $w \cdot x + b = 0$. This boundary separates the input space into two classes. For example, the line $2x_1 + 3x_2 - 6 = 0$ is a decision boundary. Perceptron Learning Algorithm The algorithm iteratively adjusts weights to correctly classify training examples. Pseudocode: Initialize weights w and bias b (e.g., to zeros or small random numbers). Choose a learning rate η (e.g., 0.1). Loop for a fixed number of epochs or until convergence: For each training example ($x_i, y_i$): Compute the predicted output: $\hat{y}_i = \text{step}(w \cdot x_i + b)$ Calculate the error: $e = y_i - \hat{y}_i$ Update the weights and bias: $w_{new} = w_{old} + \eta \cdot e \cdot x_i$ $b_{new} = b_{old} + \eta \cdot e$ Example Parameter Update: Let's say we have a data point $x = [2, 1]$ with true label $y=1$.
Initial parameters are $w = [0.2, -0.1]$, $b = 0.1$, and learning rate $\eta=0.1$. Iteration 1: Compute Prediction: $w \cdot x + b = (0.2 * 2) + (-0.1 * 1) + 0.1 = 0.4 - 0.1 + 0.1 = 0.4$. Since $0.4 > 0$, the prediction $\hat{y} = 1$. Calculate Error: Error $e = y - \hat{y} = 1 - 1 = 0$. Update Parameters: Since the error is 0, the parameters do not change. $w = [0.2, -0.1]$, $b = 0.1$. Let's assume the next data point is $x = [-1, -2]$ with true label $y=0$. Iteration 2: Compute Prediction: $w \cdot x + b = (0.2 * -1) + (-0.1 * -2) + 0.1 = -0.2 + 0.2 + 0.1 = 0.1$. Since $0.1 > 0$, the prediction $\hat{y} = 1$. Calculate Error: Error $e = y - \hat{y} = 0 - 1 = -1$. Update Parameters: $w_{new} = [0.2, -0.1] + 0.1 \cdot (-1) \cdot [-1, -2] = [0.2, -0.1] + [0.1, 0.2] = [0.3, 0.1]$. $b_{new} = 0.1 + 0.1 \cdot (-1) = 0.0$. After two iterations, the updated parameters are $w = [0.3, 0.1]$ and $b=0.0$. Limitations of the Perceptron The primary limitation is that it can only learn linearly separable problems. It fails on problems where the classes cannot be separated by a single straight line, with the classic example being the XOR logic gate. Gradient Descent and Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) Derivatives and Gradient Descent To overcome the Perceptron's limitations, we need a way to learn non-linear boundaries. This is achieved using gradient descent , an optimization algorithm that finds the minimum of a function. Derivative: For a function $L(w)$, the derivative $\frac{dL}{dw}$ tells us the slope or the rate of change of $L$ with respect to $w$. Gradient ($\nabla L$): In higher dimensions (multiple weights), the gradient is a vector of partial derivatives that points in the direction of the steepest ascent of the function. Gradient Descent: We take steps in the opposite direction of the gradient to move "downhill" and minimize the loss function $L$. The update rule is:
$$w_{new} = w_{old} - \eta \nabla L(w_{old})$$ η (eta) is the learning rate . If it's too small, training is slow. If it's too large, we might overshoot the minimum and fail to converge. Example Calculation: Suppose our loss function is $L(w) = w^2$ and we start at $w=4$ with $\eta=0.1$.
The derivative is $\frac{dL}{dw} = 2w$. Iteration 1: Gradient at $w=4$ is $2 * 4 = 8$. $w_{new} = 4 - 0.1 * 8 = 4 - 0.8 = 3.2$. Iteration 2: Gradient at $w=3.2$ is $2 * 3.2 = 6.4$. $w_{new} = 3.2 - 0.1 * 6.4 = 3.2 - 0.64 = 2.56$. From Perceptron to MLP The Perceptron's step activation function has a derivative of zero almost everywhere, making it unsuitable for gradient descent. To fix this, MLPs use: Differentiable Error Functions: Instead of just counting misclassifications, we use functions like Mean Squared Error (MSE) that measure the magnitude of the error. Differentiable Activation Functions: We replace the step function with smooth, non-linear functions like the Sigmoid ($\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}$) or ReLU ($\text{max}(0, z)$). An MLP consists of an input layer, one or more hidden layers, and an output layer, allowing it to learn complex, non-linear decision boundaries. Gradient Computation (Backpropagation) Backpropagation is the algorithm used to efficiently compute the gradient of the error with respect to every weight in an MLP. It applies the chain rule of calculus, starting from the output layer and moving backward. For Output Layer Weights ($w_{jk}$): The gradient depends directly on the output error and the activation of the hidden neuron.
$$\frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{jk}} = (y_k - \hat{y}_k) \cdot \hat{y}_k(1-\hat{y}_k) \cdot h_j$$
(Assuming Sigmoid activation and MSE error) For Hidden Layer Weights ($w_{ij}$): The gradient depends on the gradients of the layer ahead of it, "propagating" the error backward. Designing a Neural Network Experiment 1. Experiment for a Non-Linear Decision Boundary Goal: Learn to classify data that is not linearly separable (e.g., an XOR-like problem). MLP Design: Input Layer: 2 neurons ($x_1, x_2$). Hidden Layer: 2 neurons ($h_1, h_2$). Output Layer: 1 neuron ($\hat{y}$). Activation Functions: Sigmoid for all hidden and output neurons. Error Function: Mean Squared Error (MSE): $E = \frac{1}{2}(y - \hat{y})^2$. Backpropagation Equations (Gradient Calculation): Let $w_{1h1}$ be the weight from input $x_1$ to hidden neuron $h_1$. Let $w_{h1o}$ be the weight from hidden neuron $h_1$ to the output neuron. Gradient for output weight ($w_{h1o}$): $$\frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{h1o}} = \frac{\partial E}{\partial \hat{y}} \cdot \frac{\partial \hat{y}}{\partial z_{out}} \cdot \frac{\partial z_{out}}{\partial w_{h1o}} = -(y - \hat{y}) \cdot \sigma'(z_{out}) \cdot h_1$$ Gradient for hidden weight ($w_{1h1}$): $$\frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{1h1}} = \left( \frac{\partial E}{\partial \hat{y}} \cdot \frac{\partial \hat{y}}{\partial z_{out}} \cdot \frac{\partial z_{out}}{\partial h_1} \right) \cdot \frac{\partial h_1}{\partial z_{h1}} \cdot \frac{\partial z_{h1}}{\partial w_{1h1}}$$
These gradients are then used in the gradient descent update rule: $w_{new} = w_{old} - \eta \frac{\partial E}{\partial w}$. 2. Experiment for Multi-Class Classification (3 Classes) Goal: Classify data into one of three classes. MLP Design: Input Layer: 2 neurons ($x_1, x_2$). Hidden Layer: (e.g., 4 neurons). Output Layer: 3 neurons, one for each class ($\hat{y}_1, \hat{y}_2, \hat{y}_3$). Activation Functions: Hidden Layer: ReLU or Sigmoid. Output Layer: Softmax . Softmax converts the outputs into a probability distribution, ensuring they sum to 1.
$$\text{Softmax}(\mathbf{z}) i = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum {j=1}^{3} e^{z_j}}$$ Error Function: Cross-Entropy Loss . This is ideal for comparing a predicted probability distribution with a true distribution. Training and Optimization Techniques Gradient Descent Variants Type Gradient Computation Pros Cons Batch Entire training set. Stable, deterministic convergence. Slow, requires huge memory. Stochastic (SGD) One random sample. Fast, escapes local minima. High variance (noisy updates). Mini-Batch A small batch of samples (e.g., 32-256). Balance of speed and stability. Standard for deep learning. Addressing Training Challenges in Deep Networks Vanishing Gradients: In very deep networks, gradients can shrink exponentially during backpropagation, effectively halting learning in early layers. Solution: Use activation functions like ReLU , which has a constant gradient of 1 for positive inputs, preventing shrinkage. Internal Covariate Shift: The distribution of each hidden layer's inputs changes as the weights in previous layers are updated. This forces layers to constantly adapt, slowing down training. Solution: Batch Normalization. This technique normalizes the inputs to a hidden layer for each mini-batch, stabilizing the distributions and accelerating training. Overfitting: The model learns the training data, including its noise, so well that it fails to generalize to new, unseen data. Solution: Dropout. During training, randomly "drop" (set to zero) a fraction of neurons in a layer for each forward/backward pass. This forces the network to learn more robust, redundant representations and prevents it from relying too heavily on any single neuron. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) Benefits of CNN over MLP for Image Data Parameter Sharing: An MLP would require a separate weight for every pixel-to-neuron connection. A CNN uses a small filter (e.g., 3x3) that is convolved across the entire image. The weights of this one filter are shared, drastically reducing the total number of parameters. Translation Invariance: Because the same filter is applied everywhere, a CNN can detect a feature (like an edge or a corner) regardless of where it appears in the image. An MLP would have to learn the same feature again for every possible location. The Convolution Operation Convolution is an element-wise multiplication of a filter (kernel) and a portion of the input, followed by a sum. Equation (Output Size): The size of the output feature map is given by:
$$O = \frac{W - K + 2P}{S} + 1$$
Where: $W$ = Input size $K$ = Kernel (filter) size $P$ = Padding $S$ = Stride Parameter Calculation: The number of parameters in a convolutional layer is: ( (kernel_width * kernel_height * input_channels) + 1_bias ) * num_filters Backpropagation in CNNs Backpropagation in a CNN follows the same chain rule principle as in an MLP, but the operations are different. Gradient w.r.t. Weights: The gradient for a filter weight is the sum of gradients from all patches of the input where that filter was applied. Gradient w.r.t. Input: The process to compute the gradient for the layer's input is mathematically equivalent to a "full convolution" using the rotated filter. Products: Gemini Apps Why is this here? explain like the teacher Attached 2 files. - image_49d869.png - image_49db15.png 19 Sept 2025, 19:25:18 GMT+05:30 Of course! Let's break down these optimization algorithms. Think of this process like trying to find the lowest point in a hilly, foggy valley. Your goal is to get to the very bottom, but you can only see the ground right at your feet. The "valley" is our loss function $f(w)$, and your position is the weight $w$. Finding the lowest point means minimizing the loss. 1. The Basic Hiker: Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) This is the simplest and most intuitive approach. The Strategy: Imagine you're the hiker in the foggy valley. To get to the bottom, you check the slope of the ground where you're standing. If it slopes down to your left, you take a step to the left. The steepness of the slope tells you the direction. This "slope" is the gradient ($g_t$). Your update rule is exactly this:
$$w_{t+1} = w_t - \eta \cdot g_t$$ $w_t$ is your current position. $g_t$ is the gradient (the direction of the steepest ascent). We subtract the gradient ($- g_t$) to move in the opposite direction (downhill). $\eta$ is the learning rate . This is your step size. It's a fixed value you choose beforehand. The Problem: What happens if you reach a flat plateau or a gentle slope (like a saddle point )? The gradient $g_t$ becomes very small, close to zero. Your next step ($\eta \cdot g_t$) will be tiny, and you'll barely move. You might get stuck and think you've reached the bottom, even though the real valley floor is much further away. 2. The Smart Hiker: RMSProp (Root Mean Square Propagation) This hiker is a bit smarter. They realize that a fixed step size ($\eta$) isn't ideal. Sometimes you want to take big leaps (on gentle slopes) and other times small, careful steps (on steep cliffs). The Strategy: RMSProp adapts the learning rate. It keeps track of a moving average of the squared gradients. The core idea is: If the slope has been steep recently (large gradients), it means we're in a "bumpy" or "cliff-like" area. RMSProp gets cautious and reduces the step size to avoid overshooting the target. If the slope has been gentle recently (small gradients), RMSProp gets confident and increases the step size to move faster through the flat regions. The Result (as seen in your image): Look at your first graph. RMSProp starts moving downhill, but when it reaches the saddle point around $w=0$, the gradient is almost zero. While RMSProp tries to adapt, it doesn't have a strong sense of "direction" or "history" to push it through this flat area. It slows down and gets stuck. The red trajectory is very short because it gave up too early. 3. The Pro Athlete: Adam (Adaptive Moment Estimation) Adam is the gold standard for a reason. It combines the smart adaptive step size of RMSProp with another powerful concept: Momentum . The Strategy: Think of Adam as a heavy bowling ball rolling down the valley instead of a hiker. Adam uses two key concepts: 1. Momentum (First Moment): This is the $m_t$ in your formula.
$$m_t = \beta_1 \cdot m_{t-1} + (1-\beta_1) \cdot g_t$$
This keeps a moving average of the gradients. A bowling ball doesn't just stop instantly on a flat surface; its momentum carries it forward. Similarly, Adam doesn't just consider the current gradient ($g_t$); it also remembers the directions it was recently moving in ($m_{t-1}$). This momentum helps it to "roll" right through flat regions like saddle points. 2. Adaptive Learning Rate (Second Moment): This is the $v_t$ in your formula, which is basically the RMSProp part.
$$v_t = \beta_2 \cdot v_{t-1} + (1-\beta_2) \cdot (g_t \odot g_t)$$
Just like RMSProp, this part looks at the average of squared gradients to scale the step size. It slows down in "bumpy" areas and speeds up in "smooth" ones. (Side Note: The m_hat and v_hat are just "bias correction" steps to make sure the estimates are accurate at the very beginning of the training). The Result (as seen in your image): Now look at your second graph. Adam reaches the saddle point, where the gradient is near zero. An optimizer like SGD or RMSProp would get stuck. But Adam's momentum ($m_t$) remembers it was rolling downhill before, so it has the "force" to push through the flat area. At the same time, its adaptive learning rate ($v_t$) ensures the step sizes are appropriate. The result is clear: the red trajectory is long, confidently passing the saddle point and rolling all the way down to the true minimum (the blue dot). Summary Optimizer Analogy Strength Weakness SGD A blind hiker taking fixed steps. Simple, easy to compute. Gets stuck on flat regions (saddle points) and can be slow. RMSProp A smart hiker who adjusts their step size. Adapts step size to the terrain. Lacks momentum to escape plateaus effectively. Adam A heavy bowling ball with momentum. Combines momentum and adaptive step sizes. The best of both worlds; robustly navigates complex terrains. Products: Gemini Apps Why is this here?  1. What is SnT?
The Science and Technology (SnT) Council is a student-led body that unifies IISER TVM's scientific clubs. Our purpose is to nurture curiosity and collaborative innovation across all disciplines.
We achieve this by organizing talks, workshops, and competitions. Our flagship initiative is Anvesha, the institute's annual science fest, which serves as a vibrant platform to make science accessible and exciting for thousands. We are dedicated to connecting the academic community with the public and championing excellence in science education.

2. What clubs are under SnT?
The Science and Technology (SnT) Council is the parent body for the following student clubs:
Coding Club of IISER-TVM (CCIT)
Exhibit A 
Ecological Society of IISER-TVM (ESI)
Parsec (Astronomy Club)
Quizzing Society of IISER-TVM (QSI)
Other technical clubs on campus are typically affiliated directly with their respective schools or departments.

3. How to access Crucible?
Accessing Crucible is a two-step process, depending on your need.
1. For General Access to the Workspace:
The main Crucible area is an open space for all students to collaborate, ideate, and work on projects. The key can be collected from the Medical Center reception desk to access this common area.
2. For Access to Specialized Labs & Equipment:
To use the specialized labs (e.g., physics lab, chemistry lab), you must first receive approval from the SnT Council. Please follow this procedure:
Step 1: Draft an email explaining the project you wish to work on. Be sure to mention the specific lab or equipment you require and the purpose of your work (e.g., course project, club activity, personal innovation).
Step 2: Email the SnT Council at [stc@iisertvm.ac.in].
Step 3: The council will review your request. Once approved, you will be notified and granted access to the specific lab resources.
Please note: Access to specific equipment may require a brief safety and training orientation.

4. What work does SnT do?
The SnT Council is the engine of our campus's tech and innovation ecosystem. Our job is to empower students by:
Supporting and overseeing the student-run science clubs.
Organizing the institute's massive annual tech-fest, Anvesha.
Creating opportunities for learning through workshops, competitions, and speaker sessions.
We are the central hub for any student looking to build, innovate, and explore the world of science.

5. How to volunteer for events?
We'd love for you to join our team! Volunteering is one of the best ways to get hands-on experience and become part of the vibrant SnT community.
The best path to volunteering is to connect directly with the event's organizers. This could be a specific club (like the Coding Club for a hackathon) or the SnT Council itself. Check out our [Clubs Page] to find contact details and links to their community groups.
Don't hesitate to reach out—new volunteers are always welcome!

6. Who manages the council?
 The management of the SnT Council is a collaborative effort. It is led by the SnT Secretary who collaborates closely with the council's Faculty-in-Charge and the Dean of Student Affairs (DoSA).
The Secretary drives the initiatives, while the faculty and DoSA provide invaluable mentorship, support, and administrative oversight, ensuring the council's success.

7. Are there faculty-in-charge for SnT and clubs?
Yes, both the SnT Council and the clubs (that are not under SnT) are supported by faculty advisors. These advisors provide valuable guidance and oversee their activities to ensure they run smoothly.
Please visit the website's' Leadership' section for a detailed list of the current faculty advisors for both the council and the clubs.

8. How do you approach SnT for any query?
Please email us at [stc@iisertvm.ac.in]. Additionally, don't hesitate to talk to any of our council members when you see them on campus. We're a friendly team happy to help you with your questions.

9. Who are the SnT council members?
The members of the SnT Council are elected for each academic year. To view our current council members' complete list and roles, please visit the website's 'Leadership' section.

10. How to volunteer for Anvesha?
Volunteering for Anvesha is handled through a time-bound application process. Official calls for volunteers and application forms are disseminated via institute-wide emails during the designated recruitment phase. It is crucial to submit your form before the announced deadline.
For late inquiries or if the deadline has passed, please get in touch with a member of the Anvesha committee to check for any remaining possibilities.


11. When is Anvesha?
Anvesha is the annual tech-fest that happens in the Varsha semester.
It is a grand stage where we invite the brightest minds to showcase groundbreaking projects, learn from research visionaries through talks and workshops, and compete in events pushing science's boundaries. It is a place for everyone to explore their passion, gain new skills, and connect with like-minded peers.
To begin your quest, explore the Anvesha Section to find out more.


12. What is the duration of Anvesha?
Anvesha unfolds over two main periods. A series of build-up events, workshops, and preliminary rounds spans approximately one month. This all leads to the main attraction: a concentrated and high-energy 3-day festival.
To find out the specific dates for this year, please check the official Anvesha schedule on our website.

                <p>
The Science and Technology Council (STC) at IISER Thiruvananthapuram is committed to promoting scientific inquiry, technological advancement, and interdisciplinary research within the institute. Its mission is to cultivate an intellectually stimulating environment where students and researchers are encouraged to explore innovative solutions to complex problems. By organizing academic seminars, workshops, outreach programs, and collaborative projects, the STC seeks to enhance scientific thinking, foster creativity, and build leadership skills among its members. The council also emphasizes the importance of responsible and ethical research, aiming to bridge the gap between scientific knowledge and a student's understanding of research.</p>
            </div>

                <h2 class="section-title-sub">Our History</h2>
                <p>
The STC was established to serve as a central platform that connects the diverse academic interests of students and faculty at IISER TVM. Founded by a group of enthusiastic students, in response to a growing interest in scientific clubs and platforms for discussion, the council began as a forum to exchange ideas and support research initiatives across various scientific disciplines. Over the years, it has expanded its activities to include seminars, talks, exhibitions, school outreaches, and public engagement efforts. Through its continued dedication to excellence in science and technology, the STC plays a vital role in shaping the research culture of IISER TVM, inspiring innovation, and nurturing the next generation of researchers.</p>
            </div>
            <div class="about-section">
                <h2 class="section-title-sub">Our Structure</h2>
                <p>The Science and Technology Council (STC) is a constituent body of the Students’ Affairs Council (SAC) of IISER Thiruvananthapuram. STC is led by a Secretary, supported by council members who serve as representatives of the student community. Together, they work to promote scientific awareness, collaboration, and communication across the campus.

The council functions under the guidance of the Faculties-in-Charge (FIC) and the Dean of Student Affairs (DoSA).

STC oversees several affiliated clubs, each dedicated to a particular domain of science or technology. These clubs together with council actively organize events, discussions, and hands-on activities, and are responsible for planning and conducting Anvesha, the annual science fest of IISER Thiruvananthapuram.</p>
            </div>
